#7879. Three Cats, One Rabies Outbreak: What Happens Next?

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Every time the topic of vaccines comes up, thereâs always someone who questions whether our pets really need them. Asking questions about medical care is perfectly reasonable (in fact, informed pet parents should!), but dismissing vaccination without understanding the risks is another story.

Rabies is a perfect example. This is not some historical disease or something that only affects animals in remote areas or underdeveloped countries. It can infect mammals, including our own cats, dogs, and even us. Whatâs even scarier is that once the clinical signs appear, rabies is almost always fatal, making prevention essential.

Recent events in Quebec offer a timely reminder. Amid an emerging wildlife outbreak, three domestic cats tested positive for raccoon-strain rabies in 2026. Although these numbers pale in comparison to the number of infected wildlife recorded since December 20241, it demonstrates how a disease circulating in wild animals can reach our pets.

And this isn't just a Canadian concern. Rabies variants and wildlife risks differ by region, but keeping pets appropriately vaccinated is a responsibility shared by pet parents everywhere.

Despite its name, raccoon-strain rabies isn't exclusive to raccoons; they are simply the reservoir species of this particular variant of the rabies virus. Skunks and other mammals â including cats â can also become infected.

Rabies attacks the central nervous system. It spreads mainly through the bite of an infected animal, when virus-containing saliva enters the body. Saliva can also transmit the virus if it reaches an open wound, the eyes, nose, or mouth.

Raccoon rabies had been eliminated in Quebec following an outbreak between 2006 and 2009, but the virus resurfaced in 2024. Since then, more outbreaks have appeared, and case numbers have climbed sharply in 2026, particularly in MontÃ©rÃ©gie. By October 29, 328 animals had tested positive for raccoon-strain rabies across the province. The three infected cats are examples of how a virus circulating in wildlife can also reach our pets, even though cats are not the main reservoir responsible for spreading this variant.

Cats are naturally curious, territorial predators. They investigate unfamiliar scents, watch moving animals, explore hidden spaces, and sometimes pursue creatures that would be better left alone. These behaviors are normal expressions of feline biology, not evidence that a cat is being reckless.

Unfortunately, wildlife encounters can turn dangerous very quickly. A raccoon searching for food near a house may cross paths with an outdoor cat. A skunk hiding beneath a shed may be investigated by a curious feline. Even a sick or disoriented wild animal can catch a cat's attention, and one of the hallmarks of rabies infection in wild animals is a reduced fear of humans and predators as the infection attacks the nervous system. And cats being cats, curiosity can get them into trouble! These encounters don't just happen deep in the woods. A backyard, garage, or garden fence can be enough.

One of the infected cats was believed to have contracted rabies after contact with a wild animal. Another case led to three people receiving preventive treatment following possible exposure.

Rabies doesn't always turn an animal into a movie villain, either. Early signs can be subtle, which is why recognizing unusual behavior and reporting possible exposure is so important.

When people think of rabies, they often picture a snarling animal, dripping saliva, and attacking everything in sight. Hollywood certainly loves that version! Unfortunately, rabies doesn't always come with such obvious special effects.

In cats, the first signs can be surprisingly subtle. A normally friendly kitty may suddenly become grumpy, hide more than usual, vocalize differently, lose interest in food, or behave in ways that seem completely out of character. Since cats are already experts at keeping their humans guessing, a sudden behavior change can sometimes be easy to dismiss. But when a cat starts acting noticeably different from their usual, wonderfully weird self, it's worth paying attention.

As the disease progresses, neurological signs become more apparent. Affected cats may become disoriented, walk unsteadily, have difficulty swallowing, drool excessively, develop weakness, or eventually become paralyzed. Some become unusually aggressive or sensitive to touch, sounds, and light.

There is also a less dramatic presentation called paralytic rabies, sometimes referred to as âdumb rabiesâ. Instead of becoming aggressive, affected animals may become unusually quiet, weak, or withdrawn. Difficulty swallowing, a drooping jaw, and progressive paralysis can follow. So no, a rabid animal doesn't necessarily look like it's auditioning for a horror movie.

Of course, these signs can also occur with other neurological conditions, injuries, and intoxications. Nobody should attempt to diagnose rabies based on behavior alone. A cat showing sudden, unexplained neurological changes needs prompt veterinary attention, particularly if wildlife exposure is possible.

Here's another catch: rabies can take weeks, sometimes even months, to show itself. A cat may seem perfectly fine after an encounter with an infected animal, but that doesn't mean the virus isn't already in its body. So if a possible exposure happens, don't wait for your cat to look sick before calling the vet. By then, it may be too late.

Sadly, once rabies reaches the clinical stage, there is no cure, and the outcome is almost always fatal. That's why a suspected exposure should never be a wait-and-see situation. Don't wait for signs to appear; contact your veterinarian right away. With rabies, prevention isn't just better than treatment; it's our best chance to protect our cats in the first place.

Think your indoor cat doesn't need a rabies vaccine? Think again! Indoor cats have fewer opportunities to encounter wildlife, but escapes happen, doors get left open, and sometimes wildlife finds its way indoors. Nobody plans these little adventures, least of all the cat!

Rabies vaccination is also required by law for cats in many countries and jurisdictions. Even where it isn't mandatory, keeping your cat vaccinated is an important part of preventive care. Ask your veterinarian about the appropriate schedule for your cat.

And remember, vaccination doesn't mean ignoring a possible exposure. If your vaccinated cat is bitten by a potentially rabid animal, contact your veterinarian right away.

If your cat is bitten or scratched by a wild animal, contact your veterinarian immediately, even if your cat seems perfectly fine. Bite wounds can hide beneath all that lovely fur, and waiting for signs to appear is not an option.

Keep your cat away from other animals and don't try to catch or handle the wild animal. Report suspicious wildlife to local authorities and let trained professionals deal with it.

If a person is bitten or scratched, or infected saliva enters an open wound or contacts the eyes, nose, or mouth, wash the area thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes and seek medical attention immediately. Post-exposure treatment can prevent rabies from developing, so don't delay.

And please, leave dead wildlife alone. No bare-handed investigations or impromptu rescue missions!

Quebec is also fighting the outbreak through wildlife surveillance and vaccination campaigns using vaccine baits. These efforts help protect wild animals and reduce further spread.

Cats will be cats. A rustling bush can become the most fascinating thing in the universe, and a passing raccoon may look like an invitation to investigate. We can't blame them for being curious. We can give them safer ways to enjoy their adventures.

#7877. The Most Common Fatal Diseases in Cats, and How to Avoid Them

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Nobody enjoys thinking about serious illness in a pet, and itâs natural to want to look the other way. But considering many serious feline health conditions respond well to early intervention, a little knowledge can go a long way. Here are eight of the most serious, what they tend to look like, and practical steps that can help lower the risk. The aim isnât to worry anyone, just to help owners feel prepared.

Heart problems are notoriously hard to spot in cats, even during a routine health check, because the usual signs, like a murmur, donât always show up during an exam. The most common form of cardiac disease â hypertrophic cardiomyopathy â causes the heart muscle to thicken so it canât work as well, and it can cause sudden death. Vets rely on heart scans, chest X-rays, and blood tests to discover heart disease.

Lowering the risk: Genetics play a big part, so anyone buying a kitten from a breeder should ask whether the parentsâ hearts have been checked, particularly if your breed of choice is one with a higher incidence of cardiac disease, like purebred Maine Coons, Siamese, Sphynx, Ragdoll, and Burmese. A high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet formulated for cats is a vital ingredient in promoting heart health. Cat food must contain the amino acid taurine because cats cannot make it themselves, and a diet lacking this essential nutrient is a fast track to heart disease.

Kidney disease is common in older cats. The kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter waste, which shows up as drinking and urinating more, tiredness, weight loss, and a scruffy coat. It can also lead to high blood pressure and low red blood cell counts, which cause pale gums, weakness, and fast breathing.

Lowering the risk: Although kidney disease canât be entirely prevented, regular checkups with blood and urine tests can catch changes early. A balanced diet helps, and maximizing a catâs water intake by feeding wet food and providing a range of enticing water options can make a significant difference.

Feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) is prevalent in cat populations around the world and is the most common cause of feline cancer. FeLV attacks the bone marrow, and the clinical signs of infection can be quite variable, but often include lethargy, weight loss, poor appetite, and weakness. Because FeLV cripples the immune system, affected cats are more susceptible to disease, and an otherwise simple infection can be deadly.

Lowering the risk: Vaccination is the best protection. Keeping cats indoors and away from possibly infected cats helps, as does quarantining newcomers and regularly cleaning dishes, toys, bedding, and litter boxes.

This is the most common hormone disease in cats, affecting about 10% of cats over age ten. It can lead to heart problems, kidney disease, blindness, and death. Cats lose weight quickly despite a huge appetite, and some suddenly go blind because of high blood pressure. Fortunately, the outlook is good with treatment, including medication, surgery, or radioactive iodine.

Lowering the risk: Hyperthyroidism canât be prevented, so spotting changes early and getting annual blood screening are the best weapons.

Up to one in a hundred cats develops diabetes in their lifetime, either because they donât make enough insulin or canât use it properly. Left untreated, it can cause serious complications. Signs include weight loss, drinking and urinating more, accidents outside the litter box, and bloody urine. Treatment is usually insulin injections, but if caught early, it can sometimes be managed through diet.

Lowering the risk: Feeding a high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet with low carbohydrate levels can help reduce the risks. The most common form of diabetes in cats is Type 2 (insulin resistance) and the best way to avoid this disease is by maintaining a lean, healthy body condition.

Rabies is almost always fatal, and cats are the domestic animal most likely to get it. It spreads through bites and scratches, often from wildlife such as bats, skunks, raccoons, and foxes. Some infected cats become withdrawn, others irritable or aggressive, and drooling and wide pupils are common. It is dangerous for people too.

Lowering the risk: Vaccines protect for one to three years. If contact with rabies is suspected, veterinary attention must be sought immediately. The disease is invariably fatal once clinical signs of rabies appear, so donât wait.

Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP) is caused by a mutated form of feline coronavirus. Early signs are mild, such as tiredness, but many cats develop a swollen belly from fluid, and it can progress fast. Until recently, FIP was almost always fatal, though newer treatments are changing this.

Lowering the risk: Good hygiene between cats and isolating newcomers until theyâre healthy reduce exposure. Keeping cats healthy and up to date on other vaccines may also help.

Spread by mosquitoes, heartworms are less common in cats than in dogs, but they can still cause serious disease, including sudden death. Wheezing and coughing are the most common signs, and the infection is hard to detect.

Lowering the risk: A monthly preventive is the best defense. If you live in an area where heartworm is present, it takes only one mosquito, so even indoor cats can be exposed.

Not every disease on this list can be prevented, but many can be avoided or managed simply by providing your cat with a high-quality diet and keeping up with regular vet checks. Blood and urine tests, appropriate vaccines, and monthly flea, tick, and heartworm protection all help, and keeping cats indoors lowers exposure to injury and illness. Catching problems early is often what makes treatment most effective, and a vet can help tailor a plan for each cat.

#7876. When Art Meets Animal Rescue: A Creative Way to Help Dogs Find Homes

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

We often turn to art for pleasure, curiosity, or a feeling we canât quite put into words. A painting catches our attention; a sculpture makes us pause. But art inspiring us to adopt a dog? Now thereâs a plot twist.

The Rescue Collection is an exciting project created through a collaboration between The Sato Project, creative agencies BLKJ Havas Singapore and Havas New York, and Brooklynâs Powerhouse Arts. The program brings adoptable dogs into the art gallery and uses observations of their responses to create individual artistic profiles. The aim is to help potential adopters see the dogs beyond their appearance, breed, or uncertain past.

Itâs an unusual approach to a familiar challenge: helping rescue dogs get noticed in a crowded adoption landscape.

At Powerhouse Arts in Brooklyn, animal welfare scientist Dr. Holly Molinaro observed dogs from The Sato Project as they explored different artworks. The dogs first had time to sniff around and become comfortable in the unfamiliar space. Their responses were then observed, including whether they looked at, sniffed, or moved away from particular pieces, or chose to lie down nearby.

Rudolph, for example, chose to lie down in front of some sculptures but ignored others. These observations helped shape profiles associating the dogs with artistic styles such as Surrealism, Minimalism, Figurative art, and Abstraction.

The concept is playful, but its purpose is practical. A standard adoption photograph may show what a dog looks like; a creative profile offers another reason to stop scrolling and learn more about the animal behind the image.

Someone might come for the art and leave wanting a dog. Turns out, the best thing in the gallery might have four legs and be up for adoption.

The Sato Project rescues dogs in Puerto Rico and helps place them in homes, including in the northeastern United States. Some arrive with limited information about their histories, and assumptions about a dogâs background can influence how potential adopters perceive them.

A dogâs history can help rescue teams understand what support an animal may need and how to approach introductions to a new home. But the past doesnât tell the whole story. A complicated backstory might tell us where a dog has been. It doesnât tell us everything about who they are. Dogs, much like people, are so much more than their basic profile.

Dogs respond to the world as individuals. One may eagerly approach a stranger, while another prefers to observe from a safe distance. Neither reaction alone defines the dogâs personality or tells us what kind of companion they might become with time and appropriate support.

The Rescue Collection offers a different starting point. Instead of focusing on what is known about a dogâs past, it invites people to become curious about the dog in front of them. That first spark of interest can matter, especially for dogs who might otherwise be overlooked.

Dogs explore their surroundings through several senses, and their behavior around unfamiliar objects can offer clues about what attracts their attention. But interpreting those responses requires care.

Dogs also see color differently from humans. People typically have three types of color-sensitive cone cells in their retinas, while dogs have two, a form of vision known as dichromacy. Dogs distinguish blues and yellows relatively well but have more difficulty differentiating reds and greens. Their visual experience of the world is therefore different from ours.

That doesnât mean dogs see the world in black and white. Color is only one possible influence on how they respond to an object. Shape, contrast, texture, scent, movement, and the surrounding environment may also play a part.

Nor does spending longer near a sculpture necessarily mean a dog prefers its artistic style. The dog may be interested in its shape or position, or simply feel comfortable resting there.

A single gallery visit cannot establish an animalâs overall personality or predict how they will behave around children, other dogs, or visitors at home. Behavior is best understood across time and situations.

A sculpture might have us admiring its color and form. The dog? They might be more interested in giving it a sniff. Different critics, different criteria.

Although the profiles are not scientific personality assessments or guarantees of compatibility, they do invite us to learn more about each dog. Conversations with the rescue team and time spent meeting the dog remain essential to finding a suitable match.

Rescue work involves far more than finding adopters. Veterinary care, foster placements, transportation, behavioral support, and follow-up all require time and resources. Helping the public connect with the dogs is only one part of that work, but an important one.

The Sato Projectâs adoption and foster manager, Alessandra Migliore, said the organization was excited to explore new ways of showcasing its dogsâ personalities. The campaign is part of the organizationâs broader work to help dogs rescued in Puerto Rico find homes in the northeastern United States.

A creative campaign cannot guarantee adoption, and an appealing profile is only the beginning. But an unexpected introduction may reach someone who wasnât actively looking for a dog, or encourage a prospective adopter to look beyond their first impressions.

The Rescue Collection hopes to help more rescue dogs connect with potential adopters. Its message says it best: âSee the masterpiece inside every dog.â

Art might catch someoneâs eye, but getting to know the dog is what matters. And if a sculpture-loving visitor leaves the gallery thinking about adoption, thatâs a pretty good review.

These festive houseplants bring color, fragrance and greenery to your home long after the decorations come down...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Christmas tree might be the star of the living room in December, but once the holidays are over, it usually gets packed away or recycled. Festive houseplants, on the other hand? Well, they can stick around for years – and some might become so beloved that you can't imagine your home without them.

Whether you're looking to make your Christmas décor a little more lasting, or simply a self-confessed crazy plant lady in need of more houseplants (I'm right there with you!), then you should absolutely consider choosing a living plant this year.

From spectacular seasonal blooms to fragrant herbs and miniature trees, these five festive favorites offer plenty of reasons to keep growing long after the last present has been unwrapped.

I'm a huge fan of Christmas cactus, having inherited one that lived for an incredible 27 years before recently dying. (RIP, Noel; we barely knew ye!) It was a reminder of just how long these festive houseplants can last, and how attached we can become to them over time.

Christmas cactus (Schlumbergera) produces beautiful flowers in shades of pink, red, purple and white, usually just in time for the holidays. Even when it's not in bloom, though, its arching stems make an attractive display, particularly in a hanging pot.

Give it bright indirect light, keep it away from harsh sunshine and don't let its roots sit in soggy compost (mine loved life on our bathroom windowsill), and remember: a cooler spell and shorter days in fall help encourage flowering.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Few festive houseplants make quite as dramatic a statement as amaryllis (Hippeastrum). Its tall stems and oversized trumpet-shaped flowers bring a splash of color indoors when much of the garden is dormant, making it a favorite for Christmas displays.

Somehow, I have managed to keep my own diva alive for several years now (it's sitting on my desk as I type this, in fact), so I urge you not to discard the bulb once flowering finishes. Instead, remove the faded flowers, keep the leaves growing, give it light, water and occasional feeding as it grows, then follow a suitable resting period to encourage another round of blooms. With a little patience, the same bulb can reward you with flowers for many seasons.

You can pick up a bag of Amaryllis bulbs easily enough from the Garden State Bulb Store, if you fancy giving it a go; they'd make excellent holiday presents once you've gotten them started!

If you'd prefer something compact and relatively easy to care for, Flaming Katy (Kalanchoe blossfeldiana) is a solid choice. This succulent produces clusters of bright flowers in red, pink, orange, yellow or white, and it's widely available during the festive season.

Its fleshy leaves store water, so it doesn't need constant watering (making it ideal for even the most forgetful plant parents everywhere). All you have to do is place it somewhere bright, allow the compost to dry a little between drinks, and avoid leaving it sitting in water.

Blooming in the fall and winter, what could be prettier than this Flaming Katy at Christmas?

Flaming Katy can be encouraged to flower again by providing a steady stint of uninterrupted nights in autumn, making it a holiday plant that's well worth keeping after its first colorful display.

Rosemary is a lovely way to bring fragrance into the home over the holidays, especially when sold clipped into a miniature living Christmas tree shape. Its evergreen needles look festive, while its scent adds a little something extra to the season – and you can snip sprigs for cooking, too.

I have actually kept my own rosemary going for a long time, bringing it in and out of the house with the seasons until it grew so large that it eventually had to move permanently into the garden. It just goes to show that a small festive plant can have quite a future ahead of it!

Rosemary (even one like this Rosemary Christmas Tree from the Three Company Store) needs plenty of light and well-drained compost. Don't overwater it, and remember that it generally prefers cooler and brighter conditions than a hot room right next to a radiator.

For something a little different, why not choose a small tree? Fig, olive and citrus trees can all make beautiful container plants, bringing Mediterranean charm to a bright home.

A fig tree offers attractive foliage and the possibility of homegrown fruit, while an olive tree has silvery-green leaves and a timeless look. And there's no denying that a calamondin or miniature orange tree is particularly festive, with glossy foliage, fragrant flowers and colorful fruit that can linger on the branches.

Naturally, these trees need the brightest spot you can offer, and citrus in particular appreciates warmth and consistent care. Indoor conditions aren't always ideal year-round, so check each tree's needs and consider moving it outdoors during suitable warmer months.

A living Christmas plant is a gift that doesn't have to end when the festivities do. Choose yourself, then, a festive houseplant that suits your space, give it the care it needs, and you could be enjoying your festive favorite for many Christmases to come.

Or, you know, you could ask Santa to bring you one. Either or...

#7874. From Cat-astrophe to Cat-tastic: The Story of Snickers the Smiling Cat

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Snickers is a calico cat born in Owensboro, Kentucky, USA, whose adorable âsmileâ has hundreds of thousands of fans. Her life journey hasnât always been smooth, but this remarkable cat touches the heart of every person she meets along the way. It was her fierce personality that inspired her pawrent, Kelly DeWeese, to go to great lengths to ensure Snickers gets to live her best life.

June 2020 was a challenging time for Kelly. She had recently lost her mother, leaving her in a state of grief, and in an attempt to find solace and cope with her loss, she took up running. It was during one of these runs, only her second, that a tiny, fragile kitten crossed her path.

Kelly was jogging past vast cornfields, and her mind was hyper-focused on the pleasing sound of the stalks rustling in the wind when a small calico kitten appeared out of the blue. She was alone, sick, and desperately in need of help.

Snickers, as she would later be christened, was in terrible shape. Her eyes were crusted shut; she couldn't meow, and she had severe respiratory issues, including sneezing. Her frail body was covered in fleas, and it was clear she was suffering.

Moved by compassion, Kelly scooped up the little kitten and carried her the two miles back to her home, where she was given a much-needed bath and plenty of TLC. The following day, Kelly took her to the local veterinarian, who ran various tests and initiated a series of treatments.

Despite the efforts of the local vet, the situation didn't improve, and the bills were mounting. Snickers' condition was dire.

Despite the financial strain, Kelly's determination to save Snickers was unwavering. After several trips to the vet, it became clear that this brave little kitten needed specialized care. Snickers was referred to a specialist in Louisville, Kentucky, two hours away. There, a CT scan revealed the root of her health issues: large polyps behind her eyes and deep within her inner ear.

The specialist recommended two major surgeries to remove the polyps. The surgeries were spaced six weeks apart and were extremely expensive. The first surgery was a great success, but the second operation had a life-altering consequence. During the procedure, one of the polyps slipped into her neck, temporarily cutting off oxygen to the brain. She essentially died for a few seconds before the surgical team managed to resuscitate her with CPR. Tragically, Snickers woke up from the operation blind.

The prognosis was uncertain, with a 50/50 chance of her regaining her eyesight. But Kelly, determined and resolute, refused to give up on her beloved feline companion. She watched over Snickers as she adjusted to her newfound blindness, never losing hope.

Remarkably, a couple of months later, a miracle occurred. One day, while she was waving something in front of Snickers, the catâs reaction gave Kelly a glimmer of hope. It appeared that Snickers might be regaining her eyesight. Ecstatic about this newfound possibility, Kelly promptly took Snickers back to the specialist, who confirmed the miraculous news: Snickers had indeed regained her eyesight.

Now, Snickers is a thriving and healthy six-year-old cat, bearing her distinctive, always-smiling face. Her remarkable journey from a sickly, abandoned kitten to a joyful, beloved family member is a testament to the power of love and determination. Her infectious smile serves as a constant reminder that sometimes, in the face of adversity, the most extraordinary things can happen. Kelly's unyielding commitment to Snickers proves that every life, no matter how small, is worth fighting for.

All those present at the veterinary clinic will agree that Snickers' recovery was nothing short of a miracle, and her journey to health and happiness continued to inspire those who heard her story. Kelly, who had been enduring a challenging period in her life when she found Snickers, felt that the little calico had rescued her just as much as she had rescued the cat. Their bond deepened as they supported each other through adversity.

As Snickers regained her eyesight and settled into her new, loving home, it was increasingly evident that she was not your typical feisty calico. Her sweet and calm disposition was a stark contrast to the naughty tortie stereotype, with endearing quirks that set her apart, such as sitting with a posture that resembled a human's. Snickers took an interest in watching television and enjoyed playing fetch, showcasing her unique personality.

Her joyful demeanor and cheerful, almost constant smile brought a special kind of happiness to Kelly's life. She couldn't help but feel that Snickers was fully aware of her love. The little calico has found her forever home and is living her best life.

Snickers' story didn't end with her recovery. She quickly became a star on Kelly's Instagram, captivating her followers with the charming and humorous poses she struck. Snickers has an uncanny ability to assume positions that make it appear as though she were a human in a cat's body. She gazes intently at the camera as if she knew she was a star.

Not only does Snickers sport a perpetual smile on her face, but she also has a surprise waiting on one of her pawsâa smiley face marking. This unique and heartwarming feature only adds to her charm.

Kelly's devotion to Snickers, both emotionally and financially, is unwavering. She recognizes that many people might not have been willing to invest the considerable amount she did to save a sick kitten, especially one that had a grim prognosis. Many might have chosen to take the easier path and euthanize the cat.

Yet Kelly saw past the hardships and the steep financial costs. Snickers had been loving and sweet from the moment she entered Kelly's life, and Kelly simply couldn't give up on her. The life insurance money she had received after her mother's passing became a lifeline for Snickers, a way to provide the specialized care and surgeries that ultimately saved her life.

For Kelly, the choice to sacrifice a significant portion of her savings was clear. She believed it was a way to honor her mother's memory by making a difference in the life of a helpless creature. Money became secondary in the face of compassion and determination, and over $10K in donations from the public showed how generous people can be when they see someone in need of support.

Snickers and Kelly's story is a testament to the extraordinary transformations that can occur when we refuse to give up, even in the face of daunting challenges. Snickers, with her perpetual smiling face and smiley paw, embodies the spirit of resilience and the profound impact that love and dedication can have on a life, no matter how small or furry.

Their story continues to serve as a beacon of hope and a reminder that sometimes, in the most unexpected moments, we find our greatest sources of joy and inspiration.

Originally from San Diegoâs sunshine and now living amongst Kentuckyâs rolling hills, I've built a cozy life powered by cat love and everyday warmth. I'm the kind of person who turns simple moments into little rituals, especially with my favorite feline co-star, Snickers.

Itâs that time of year again. Before BublÃ© comes out of his cave and Mariahâs bank balance gets its annual influx, we find ourselves surrounded by candy, costumes, and a plethora of giant orange cucurbits.

Carved into ghoulish jack-oâ-lanterns for Halloween or baked into a delicious Thanksgiving pie, pumpkins have myriad uses, both decorative and delicious, and unlike many festive foods, theyâre also something our dogs can enjoy.

A member of the gourd family (Cucurbitaceae), the pumpkin is a cultivated squash, technically a fruit, with both savory and sweet culinary applications. While some countries wouldnât dare serve a roast dinner without a generous helping beside their potatoes, in the US, the nutritious pumpkin is usually relegated to seasonal decorations or the key ingredient in the eponymous pie.

There are more than 100 varieties of pumpkin with slightly different textures, flavors, and recipe applications. What they all have in common is that they are low in calories, high in antioxidants, rich in vitamins & minerals, and, when prepared correctly, safe for dogs to eat.

Compared with the potato, a vegetable commonly used in both human and canine recipes, the pumpkin is higher in fiber, much lower in carbohydrates, and is far more digestible. It is often included in diets for cats and dogs with digestive problems due to its beneficial impact on intestinal health and function.

Even the seeds of certain pumpkin varieties, when properly prepared, have been found to help eliminate intestinal parasites.1

And the cherry atop this pumpkin pie? Most dogs find the taste of pumpkin irresistible.

Though there are certainly some dogs that challenge this notion, we shouldnât use our dogs as an eco-friendly alternative waste disposal unit. While the occasional table scrap â provided the food is safe for dogs â is unlikely to cause any major catastrophes, offloading ex-display jack-oâ-lanterns and leftover pie is not a good idea.

Yes, pumpkin is a safe and healthy food we can share with dogs, but there are some dos, donâts, and precautions to be aware of.

Pumpkin is a delicious, healthy, and nutritious food that deserves to be seen as more than just a Halloween decoration or pie ingredient. Dogs love the taste, and their digestive systems will thank you.

Old-style holiday bulbs that run hot can help reduce the chill for potted plants on a frosty night. But there are a few details to get right before you try it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every November, boxes of holiday lights come down from the attic, and a few gardeners start eyeing those tangled strands for a second job. On paper, Christmas lights frost protection sounds like a neighbor's tip over coffee – string up a potted lemon tree, plug it in, and hope it makes it to morning.

There's some truth to it. Gardeners have relied on heat from old-style bulbs for years, and it can work alongside the usual steps for winterizing container plants, like covering pots or moving them under shelter. When used safely with a suitable cover or enclosure, that heat can nudge the temperature around a plant up a few degrees.

The catch is that only certain bulbs produce enough heat to help, and most modern porch strands won't help at all. But using the right bulbs comes with its own risks. Mix hot bulbs, fabric covers, and unprotected electrical connections outdoors carelessly, and you have a fire and shock hazard.

Christmas lights keep plants warm only if the bulbs run hot. Old-fashioned incandescent bulbs, like these C7 Christmas lights from Amazon, give off a fair amount of heat along with their light, so running a strand beneath a properly supported frost cover or inside a cold frame can warm the small area around a plant. University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources advises home citrus growers to use traditional non-LED lights to provide extra warmth, with or without a frost blanket.

Colorado State University Extension measured the effect in cold frame trials in Fort Collins. One string of 25 mid-size C7 bulbs hung inside a covered cold frame, with a space blanket over the frame, kept each frame noticeably warmer than the night outside. A string also beat a single large bulb at warming the cold corners.

If you want to recreate an enclosed space like that, use a cold frame or mini greenhouse, but only if the structure allows the lights to be safely suspended away from the plants and covering.

Pick up a string of Christmas lights in a store today, and you'll likely find they're LEDs. They convert far more of their electricity into light, leaving little heat behind – fine for decoration but useless for shielding a citrus tree on a 28°F (-2°C) night. When it comes to LED lights, frost protection just isn't on the table – they don't generate enough warmth.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

University frost guidelines specifically recommend incandescent bulbs when you need real heat. Traditional incandescent mini lights can provide some warmth, while larger C7 and C9 bulbs, like these from Novelty Lights Store, produce more heat per bulb.

Any set used should carry an outdoor rating and be suitable for the intended setup. With incandescent Christmas lights, plants under a properly supported cover can gain extra heat, but the same heat makes the bulbs a hazard if they touch foliage or covering materials.

Several vulnerable container plants could benefit, but growers most often protect potted citrus this way. Cold damage can begin around 30°F (-1°C), depending on the variety and duration of exposure, with limes generally more sensitive than mandarins. A potted lemon on the patio faces a specific risk that an in-ground tree doesn't. Its roots are far less cold-hardy than its branches, and the small amount of potting mix around them can cool and freeze much faster than the soil around an in-ground tree.

That means the lights can help through brief cold spells – just a few nights with light frost. They're not enough to protect tropical plants during weeks of hard freezes. A larger container holds more potting mix and can provide some extra insulation for the roots, so a pot like the ModernNest fiberstone planter from Walmart, designed to withstand freezing conditions, gives a citrus tree a sturdier home but won't prevent its roots from freezing.

Hot incandescent bulbs can cause damage if they come into contact with foliage or covering materials. Incandescent bulbs can burn leaves if they touch them directly. Frost cloth, sheets, plastic wrap, and space blankets should never be pressed against the lights, where they can scorch, melt, or become a fire risk. Hang the strand so each bulb has enough clearance from surrounding materials, and use a separate frame, stakes, or supports to keep covers up and away from the bulbs. Make sure the lights are securely positioned so they cannot shift into contact with the covering.

Water and electricity can create hazards on cold nights. Use only outdoor-rated lights and cords outside, and plug them into a GFCI-protected outlet. Throw out any strand with cracked sockets or frayed wire instead of hanging it. Keep indoor strands and household power strips indoors, and don't rely on tape to waterproof electrical connections. Follow the manufacturer's limits on how many strings can be connected end to end, and follow the safety instructions packed with the product.

Start by moving the pot. An unheated garage, shed, or closed-in porch that stays above freezing can carry a citrus tree through a cold snap with no wiring. Pots that stay outside belong together, up against a house wall or in a corner out of the wind. Water them well before the cold comes, since moist potting mix freezes more slowly than dry.

Covers and wraps add another layer. Lowe's sells a 2-ounce frost blanket that can go over the plant on cold nights and come off during the day. Around the container, slip on an Eonox drawstring pot insulation cover to keep cold wind off the root zone.

For plants that need steady heat for weeks, a thermostatically controlled heater inside a greenhouse built to house one is the safer setup – the Dr Infrared greenhouse heater has an adjustable thermostat.

Under a cover or in a cold frame, old incandescent holiday lights can add a few degrees, maybe enough to see potted citrus through a short, light frost. You can't count on them, though, and the method needs careful setup, even though it's recommended by several university extension services. An LED strand won't give a cold plant any real protection.

Using hot bulbs with fabric and outdoor power for improvised heating carries risks that are easy to underestimate. Proper shelter, insulation, and a good frost blanket are generally safer options, although they won't always provide as much warmth as a safely heated enclosure.

For most gardeners, the simplest solution is to keep the twinkling lights on the porch this year and move your lemon tree into a frost-free garage when cold weather hits. It'll still be green when the holiday decorations go back in the attic.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7869. Is That Really A Service Dog?

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

For years, business owners and property managers have wrestled with the same question: how do you tell the difference between a legitimate service animal and a pet that someone is trying to pass off as one?

Itâs a question John Bradford spent years trying to answer, first as a property manager overseeing thousands of rental units, and now as the founder of PetScreening, a platform used to verify animal accommodation requests across more than 7 million rental units nationwide.

With the rising number of service dogs and emotional support animals leading to incidents of confusion, conflict, and exploitation, John sets the record straight on how to verify a real service animal from one that isn't, and what you are legally allowed to ask.

The truth is that most people donât fully understand the laws around service animals and emotional support animals, and even well-meaning questions can come across as anything but. That gray area and confusion can create real risk. Ask the wrong question, and a business can face a discrimination complaint. Ask no questions at all, and policies and rules become easy to bend, which leads to potentially dangerous situations.

Getting this right protects everyone involved, including the people who genuinely rely on these animals every day.

Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), service animals are defined as:

âDogs that are individually trained to do work or perform tasks for people with disabilities.â

Disabilities vary widely, from physical and sensory to psychiatric, intellectual, and neurological. The needs of each person are different, so the trained tasks may look different from person to person.  The ADA cites that the service animal must be a dog or, in rare cases, a miniature horse. Federal law does not require certifications, registrations, vests, or ID cards for these animals.

Beyond the specification that the animal must be trained to perform tasks, the legal standard is limited, so it can be difficult to easily identify which animals are legitimately service dogs and which are not. This is where public confusion starts.

There are plenty of ways to make a dog look like a service animal, like labeled vests, âregistrationâ certifications, and IDs, but none of these are federally supported. A dog wearing a vest isnât automatically a service animal, and a dog without one isnât automatically a pet. What matters legally is not appearance or paperwork. Itâs the dogâs trained ability to perform certain tasks.

This is the distinction many find hardest to grasp, and it matters because different laws apply to each. Service dogs are protected under the ADA and, due to their training and the tasks they perform, they are permitted in public spaces such as restaurants, retail stores, and hotels. That could mean guiding someone who is visually impaired, alerting an owner to an oncoming seizure, or reminding them to take medication. Service animals are also protected under the Fair Housing Act and require paperwork if the disability or need for the animal is not obviously understood.

Emotional support animals (ESAs) are different. Their value comes from the comfort their presence provides. They donât necessarily have to be dogs, they arenât required to be trained to perform specific tasks, and theyâre not covered by the ADA to be allowed in public spaces like restaurants.

They are, however, protected by the Fair Housing Act. Under this, landlords are generally required to make allowances for an ESA if a tenant has appropriate documentation from a licensed healthcare provider establishing a disability-related need. Examples of disabilities warranting an ESA include, but are not limited to, anxiety disorders or autism.

ESA accommodations are supposed to come through legitimate means, typically an established relationship with a licensed medical or mental health professional who can document the need. But some people have found loopholes for this by filling out forms online or paying fees for instant letters, which only fuels public skepticism about the legitimate need for these animals. Not to mention, this abuse can make people wary of service dogs, too.

While there is no foolproof visual test, trained service animals typically display consistent, recognizable behaviors. These dogs show exemplary discipline and obedience to the commands of their handler. They have the ability to ignore external distractions from other dogs, people, food, sounds, and smells while focusing on the needs of their handler. They display a calm temperament and are not aggressive or anxious. It is also expected that these animals be quiet, unless they are tasked with alerting an owner to a medical issue, and that they are housebroken and trained to walk on a leash without unnecessary pulling or circling.

This is where business owners and landlords need to tread carefully. When it isnât obvious that a dog is a service animal, staff are permitted to ask:

Is this dog required because of a disability?

What task has it been trained to perform?

Thatâs the full extent of it. Staff should not ask about the nature of a personâs disability, demand documentation or proof of training, or require dogs to demonstrate their tasks. Asking beyond the two questions, even if it comes from a place of genuine curiosity or caution, can expose a business to discrimination claims.

News stories about supposed service animals harming bystanders in public continue to raise questions about the legitimacy of those animals, and businesses are often caught in the crossfire. These incidents are symptoms of a larger problem: businesses and property owners navigating without clear guidance, while people with legitimate needs are met with suspicion.

Service animals and emotional support animals play an essential role in the lives of the people who rely on them, and protecting that role starts with understanding the rules.

If you own a business or manage a property, you donât need to become legal experts overnight, but you do need a consistent, fair process that respects peopleâs rights and keeps everyone safe. When everyone knows where the lines are, the people who truly depend on these animals can go about their lives without facing doubt at every door.

#7868. Kika USA Cat Food Review 2026: Our Expert’s Opinion

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

This article was created in sponsorship with Kika USA, which helps make content like this possible.

We give Kika USA a rating of 4.7 out of 5 stars.

A healthy cat is a beautiful cat. Okay, that might be a bit of a stretch, but your catâs skin and coat are indeed a window into their overall health.

Skin is the bodyâs largest organ, and signs of poor health and nutritional deficits often show up here before larger problems develop. So when a food supports a lustrous coat and healthy skin, itâs usually good for your catâs overall health as well.

Thatâs the approach Kika USA has taken with their cat food. Their wet and dry food formulas are uniquely designed to meet the demands of the largest organ, using high-protein, high-omega formulas that support not only skin and coat health, but also the immune and digestive systems. Because, in the end, itâs all connected to your kitties' overall health.

I had a chance to try Kika USAâs dry food options, including their White Cats formulaâwith the help of my white cat, Makoaâand their wet food toppers. Keep reading to find out if these unique coat-specific diets are the key to your cat's health and beauty.

Did you know that your catâs skin accounts for about a quarter of their body weight? With that in mind, it should be no surprise that your catâs skin uses an incredible amount of the nutrients they consume, especially protein. In fact, fur is composed of approximately 95% protein, and hair growth and skin renewal can account for roughly 25 to 30% of daily protein requirements.1 Dietary fats are equally important, as essential fatty acids help maintain the skinâs protective barrier and support a soft, supple coat.

Because of this, if your cat isnât getting enough protein, omega fatty acids, and other essential nutrients in their diet, it is often the skin that shows the first signs. A dull, brittle coat, excessive shedding, flaky skin, or hair loss may signal nutritional deficiencies.

The larger problem? Many cat foods on the market donât provide enough protein to meet the needs of the skin and coat, as well as the rest of their body. And even fewer foods provide enough quality fatty acids.

Kika USA grew from a family business started in Lithuania in 1991 by a passionate group of cat and dog show groomers and breeders. They knew how important nutrition is in building a strong, healthy, lustrous coat, and they brought that knowledge to their line of specialty cat and dog foods that would eventually make their way to the US.

These diets prioritize high amounts of quality animal protein, omega fatty acids, and other unique nutrients proven to support skin and coat health. Uniquely, Kika USA offers specific dry food formulas for different coat colors. Their White Cats, Dark Cats, and Red Cats formulas are made with the same base ingredients, but with special attention to specific amino acids and superfoods, including L-tyrosine, L-cysteine, L-tryptophan, dried carrots, and flaxseed.

Together, these ingredients support overall coat health while specific recipe tweaks help maintain coat pigment and reduce staining.

Kika USA is best suited for adult cats over one year old who might benefit from extra support for healthy skin and coat.

The dry food comes in recipes for red, dark, and white coats, making this brand especially useful for cats struggling with pigmentation issues, dullness, and staining.

The wet food range is primarily designed as a supplemental topper for adult cats, adding variety and moisture to regular meals, rather than a complete diet. There is also a kitten formula topper for immune support in younger cats.

Kika USAâs dry cat food formulas feature herring meal as their primary ingredient, providing a concentrated source of animal protein to support muscle maintenance, healthy skin, and coat condition. Poultry fat and salmon oil supply dietary fats, including omega fatty acids that help maintain a soft, glossy coat. Dried eggs offer additional animal-based protein, while ingredients such as flaxseed contribute beneficial fatty acids.

The recipes also include taurine, an essential nutrient for feline heart and eye health, alongside vitamins, minerals, and biotin to support overall wellness.

The majority of the ingredients in Kikaâs recipes are great, but there are some less desirable additions. Pea and potato protein boost the formulasâ overall protein content but provide less species-appropriate nutrition than animal sources. Potatoes and peas in whole form also feature prominently, meaning plant-based ingredients play a substantial role.

Although Kika USA offers separate dry food formulas for red, dark, and white-coated cats, their ingredient lists are remarkably similar. All three feature herring meal as the primary protein, alongside poultry fat, salmon oil, plant-based proteins, and essential vitamins and minerals.

The main differences lie in a few additions and minor variations in guaranteed nutrient levels. The red formula uniquely includes dried carrots, while both the red and dark formulas contain supplemental L-tyrosine, L-cysteine, and L-tryptophanâamino acids involved in various physiological processes, including pigmentation. Studies have shown that insufficient dietary L-tyrosine can cause black cats' fur to turn reddish-brown, while higher dietary concentrations can help maintain black pigmentation.2

The dark and white formulas guarantee slightly more crude protein than the red formula, while the white formula has marginally less crude fat.

Kika USAâs wet food offers adult cats two seafood-based options: tuna and tuna with shrimp. Both feature tuna as the primary ingredient, providing animal-based protein, while the shrimp formula adds another seafood source with unique micronutrients. The recipes also include tuna extract, a small amount of rice, and added ingredients such as taurine and vitamins, depending on the formula.

Their high moisture content can help supplement a catâs daily water intake, while the soft texture and seafood flavors may appeal to picky eaters. Marketed as supplemental toppers, these products are designed to add variety to an existing diet rather than replace a complete and balanced food.

For kittens, Kika USA also offers a tuna-and-sea-bass kitten formula with added vitamin E, vitamin C, and zinc to support a growing catâs nutritional needs.

Kika USA also offers a few supplements that are worth mentioning. These products focus on targeted mineral support for different life stages.

There are three formulas, including a puppy and kitten supplement for bone strength, joint health, and detox, an adult performance formula focused on bone strength and muscle recovery, and a senior formula targeting bone health, neuromuscular balance, and healthy aging.

Kika USA products are available directly through the official Kika USA website, which offers its full range of cat food formulas, wet-food toppers, supplements, and treats. You can also shop online through Petco, Chewy, Amazon, and Walmart.

For in-person shopping, Kika USA is stocked at select Petco stores and grooming salons, though availability varies by location.

This isnât my first encounter with Kika USA. I recently had the opportunity to try their Superior Care White Dogs Grain-Free Small Breed Dog Food, and while my Dalmatian mix was a little larger and "spottier" than their intended clientele, she still enjoyed it. And it is now my friendâs go-to food for her Maltese. So I was very excited to get the opportunity to try the brandâs cat food recipes.

I received bags of the White Cats, Dark Cats, and Red Cats dry food formulas, each of the wet food topper recipes, and their MZG System supplement.

I started my product testing with a deep dive into their recipesâ ingredients. Mostly, I wanted to know if there really was a difference between the three coat color options. As I mentioned in the product breakdown above, there actually are some slight differences.

The Dark and Red formulas have added amino acids proven to affect pigmentation, while the white formula lacks these. The Red formula also contains carrots, though I didnât find any research supporting carrots or beta-carotene influencing pigmentation in cats.

All three formulas contain ingredients to support overall coat health, and compared to the average cat food, they all have high amounts of protein and omega fatty acids. While I am not a huge fan of the inclusion of pea protein, potatoes, or peas, I was happy to see herring meal listed as the first ingredient, as this provides a natural source of those omega fatty acids and plenty of species-appropriate protein.

The wet food options are also made from a fish base, in this case tuna, with some key added ingredients.Taurine ensures cats get enough of this essential amino acid, while added sodium aluminosilicate helps detoxify the gut.

Once I was satisfied that the ingredients were up to snuff, it was time to let Makoa conduct his product tests.

Iâm not sure what specifically it is about this dry food, but Makoa really does seem to love it! True, he is a glutton and has never met a food he didnât like, but he seems especially excited about this dry food, even without the toppers, and attacked all three dry formulas with enthusiasm.

Currently, I am feeding only the White Cats variety, in the hope that it will help improve his tear stains â so far, so good!

Not surprisingly, Makoa is also a big fan of the wet food toppers. I mix a little in with his dinner each night, and he just gobbles it all up. I love that they add moisture and some fun new flavors to his meals, as well as extra protein.

I have also been using the MZG System supplement that came with my review package. This mineral-based supplement is marketed as supporting healthy bones, joints, and teeth, as well as aiding in detoxification.

Makoa happily eats the supplement mixed into his food, and I am hopeful that it will also help to keep his tears clear through those detoxing effects.

Overall, I am a fan of this food. While the differences in formulas might be slight, the ingredients alone are worth the buy. The focus on skin- and coat-supporting ingredients makes them a great option for cats struggling with dull fur, dandruff, and other common coat problems.

Kika USA's wet foods are marketed as toppers, meaning they donât contain everything needed to be a complete meal. They make a great addition to the companyâs dry food or your dry food of choice.

Kika USA dry food, wet food toppers, and supplements put skin and coat health first, knowing everything else will follow. #7867. Ask Dr. Paola - HELP! What Happens If Cherry Eye Is Left Untreated? (November 2, 2026)

My dog, Reggie, has Cherry eye. If left untreated, can it have a negative effect on his vision? Money is an issue for me right now.â

Cherry eye happens when the gland of the third eyelid, which helps produce tears, slips out of its normal position and becomes visible as a pink or red cherry-looking bulge in the corner of your dog's eye. I understand that veterinary expenses can be difficult to manage, and it is important to know what needs attention right away and what can safely wait a bit longer.

Cherry eye does not usually cause blindness directly, but leaving it untreated can put Reggie's eye health at risk. The exposed gland can become irritated, inflamed, or damaged, and its tear production may be reduced over time. Because this gland contributes to keeping the eye moist and protected, reduced tear production can increase the risk of dry eye, a condition that can lead to corneal damage, scarring, and impaired vision if it becomes severe. Think of the gland as part of the eye's built-in lubrication system. Even if the eye looks comfortable today, problems can develop gradually.

If surgery is not financially possible right now, please arrange a veterinary examination to confirm the diagnosis, assess tear production, and check the cornea.

Talk to your vet about a payment plan, or you might be able to find a veterinary teaching hospital or nonprofit clinic that may offer lower-cost care. Your veterinarian may recommend a suitable lubricating eye product while you work toward surgery, but lubrication will not reposition the gland. Please make sure you avoid human eye drops, leftover medications, or steroid eye drops unless specifically prescribed, as some of these can worsen an undiagnosed corneal ulcer. The gland should generally be repositioned and preserved rather than removed. If the gland is removed, you would need to use eye drops to supplement Reggieâs tear production for the rest of his life.

Please seek same-day veterinary care if you see Reggie squinting, holding the eye closed, rubbing it persistently, developing a cloudy or bluish cornea, or producing thick yellow or green discharge. These can be signs of a painful or more serious eye problem. If the eye is comfortable and clear, it may not be an immediate emergency, but I would not leave cherry eye unassessed for weeks or months. The most important first step is protecting the eye while finding an affordable treatment option.

#7865. Better a Bald Head Than a Cat That’s Dead: This Common Hair Growth Formula Is Killing Pets

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Humans have a rather complex and contradictory relationship with their hair. Many of us willingly put ourselves through torturous procedures to remove it from our legs, armpits, and just about anywhere else, while, at the same time, the quest to keep a full and lustrous head of hair fuels a billion-dollar hair growth industry. Since the 1980s, a chemical called Minoxidil has become increasingly popular as both a topical and oral treatment for baldness, but what few people realize is that the very product promising hair growth poses a serious risk to their pets. The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) is warning consumers about minoxidil toxicity in cats and dogs, highlighting a danger that deserves considerably more attention.

Anyone who shares a home with a cat knows that personal space is more of a suggestion than a household rule. Cats rub against our heads, groom our hair, curl up on our pillows, and somehow manage to investigate just about everything we touch. These perfectly normal feline behaviors can turn deadly when minoxidil enters the picture.

The history of minoxidil shares similarities with another well-known human drug: Viagra, which essentially took a common side effect of the heart medication, sildenafil, and turned it into its primary purpose. In the 1970s, researchers developing a new blood pressure medication found that a common side effect of the drug, minoxidil, was hypertrichosis, aka excessive hair growth. Like the story of sildenafil, the makers of minoxidil leaned into this side effect, repurposing the drug as a treatment for hair loss.1

In 1988, the FDA officially approved minoxidil, and it quickly gained popularity in products like Rogaine. Minoxidil works by widening blood vessels, a process called vasodilation, and altering the hair growth cycle to stimulate hair growth. But what helps us fight hair loss can be dangerous for our feline roommates.

A 2021 study published in the Journal of the American Animal Hospital Association examined 211 reported cases of topical minoxidil exposure in dogs and cats. Of the 87 animals that developed signs of poisoning, 62 were cats, and 25 were dogs. Eight cats died. A 2025 review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology identified another 94 reported cases, including 68 cats, ten of which died. Notably, 55 of 57 cases involving accidental exposure to a person's minoxidil treatment involved cats.

How does this happen? Topical minoxidil is applied directly to the scalp, either as a liquid using a dropper or as a foam spread with the fingers. Medication can remain on the hands, hair, or nearby surfaces. Cats don't need to break into the medicine cabinet; a little grooming, an affectionate head rub, or a snooze on a contaminated pillow may be enough to expose them. Some were even exposed through everyday contact with their follicle-challenged cat parents.

Minoxidil works by relaxing blood vessels and improving blood flow. In cats, however, the effects can become dangerously disruptive.

When absorbed, it can cause blood pressure to drop dramatically, a condition called hypotension. To compensate, the heart beats faster, but this doesn't necessarily solve the problem. Serious complications can follow, including fluid accumulation in the lungs (pulmonary edema) or in the space surrounding them (pleural effusion). Breathing becomes increasingly difficult, and severe poisoning can progress to cardiovascular and respiratory failure.

Now, what should you look out for? You might notice unusual tiredness, weakness, vomiting, or a sudden loss of appetite. More concerningly, your kitty may start breathing faster than usual or appear to struggle for air. And here's the tricky part: some cats may initially seem perfectly fine.

That's why a suspected exposure should never be brushed off simply because your cat appears normal. Waiting for visible signs of poisoning can waste valuable time.

Now that we are beginning to appreciate the risks this product poses to our pets, we have to wonder how many unexplained cat and dog deaths could be attributed to unknown minoxidil exposure.

Rapunzel may have had a tower to keep her hair safe, but cat owners need a different strategy: keeping minoxidil well away from curious paws.

If you use topical minoxidil, make sure you apply it in a room your cat cannot access. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water immediately afterward, and clean up any spills promptly. Used tissues, cotton pads, applicators, and empty containers should go straight into a secure bin. That tissue you casually leave on the bathroom counter? To your cat, it might look like just another interesting thing to investigate.

And what about bedtime? If you apply minoxidil in your bedroom, make closing the door part of your nighttime routine. Your cat may protest being left out of the bedroom, especially if your pillow is their favorite sleeping spot, but keeping them away from treated hair, skin, pillows, and bedding can help prevent accidental contact with medication residue. Remember, allowing the product to dry does not guarantee that every surface is free from contamination.

You might be wondering whether switching to oral minoxidil would solve the problem. Unfortunately, not entirely. Oral minoxidil is also toxic to cats if they accidentally ingest a tablet. Whichever formulation you use, keep the medication securely stored and well out of paws' reach. Or better yet, look into options that donât put your pet at risk.

Discuss your household's furry residents with the prescribing dermatologist and establish a routine that prevents accidental exposure. Cats are wonderfully persistent creatures. They may not appreciate a closed door or understand why their favorite pillow is suddenly off-limits, but a little inconvenience is a small price to pay for keeping them safe.

If your cat licks minoxidil, contacts a spill, or may have groomed contaminated fur, contact your veterinarian or an animal poison control service immediately, even if your kitty seems perfectly fine.

Treatment depends on the exposure and your cat's condition. It may involve hospitalization, cardiovascular monitoring, oxygen therapy, intravenous support, and medications to manage complications such as low blood pressure or fluid accumulation.

Never attempt to induce vomiting or administer home remedies unless specifically instructed by a veterinary professional. If medication is still on your cat's coat or skin, ask your veterinarian how to handle decontamination safely rather than delaying emergency care.

Unfortunately, not every cat survives minoxidil poisoning, making every accidental exposure a veterinary emergency.

hhttps://www.instagram.com/reel/DeF7upKOC-1/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&dmpr=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ==

Hair loss can affect confidence, and wanting to treat it is perfectly understandable. Minoxidil can be a valuable treatment for people experiencing certain types of hair loss, but sharing a home with a cat adds an important responsibility.

Preventing accidental poisoning starts with awareness. As pet parents, we need to be mindful of the products we bring into our homes, even those that seem perfectly harmless to us. From seemingly innocent houseplants and everyday foods to cleaning products, medications, and personal care treatments, many things we use routinely can pose risks to our feline companions. Before introducing something new into your home, take a moment to consider whether it is safe for your cat. A little research and a few precautions can make a world of difference.

Cats will continue doing what cats do best: following their humans, investigating everything, claiming the pillows, and showing affection on their own terms. We cannot expect them to understand why a particular patch of skin or a freshly treated pillow is suddenly off-limits. That responsibility belongs to us.

Thinning hair can be frustrating, even damaging to self-esteem, but itâs not a life-threatening condition. Losing a beloved pet to an avoidable medication exposure is a tragedy no one should have to experience.

Better bald than catless. Every single time.

#7864. Is Your Dog Weird Enough for Times Square?

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Does your pup have a bedtime routine that makes no sense, a suspicious obsession with household objects, or dramatically howl at their own reflection in the oven door? Congratulations. You might be living with a contender for the World's Weirdest Dog. Embark Veterinary has officially launched its search for canine oddballs, inviting pet parents to submit photos and videos of their furballâs most gloriously bizarre behaviors before November 15, 2026. The winning pup will earn the ultimate claim to canine fame: their face on a Times Square billboard, the official title of World's Weirdest Dog, and a $200 gift card.

The contest celebrates the behaviors that make dogs funny, unique, and truly memorable; the ones that make us smile when we think about them, while also highlighting  Embark's Behavior Insights & Training feature, which explores how canine DNA may influence behavior.

Sock Thieves, Bathtub Sleepers, and Other Household Oddballs

Furry weirdos have interesting, different habits; Embark's examples include a dog who sleeps upside down in the bathtub, one who carries a sock around without chewing it, and a canine who spins exactly three times before lying down. Not two. Not four. Three.

Then there's the dog who refuses to walk past one particular house, or the dinner diva who won't touch a meal until someone has given it the full restaurant treatment.

Such behaviors are entertaining partly because they are so unique and specific. Most pet parents can share at least one story that would make a perfectly reasonable person wonder what goes on inside that furry little head.

A sock might be a very treasured object, a source of comfort, a reminder of their favorite personâs scent, or simply something fun to carry. A particular walking route might feel uncomfortable for reasons a person cannot detect, most likely a scentâ¦ but then again, who knows? And a bedtime ritual may have started with nothing more mysterious than finding a comfortable position.

Of course, some dogs are just little weirdos, and that's part of their charm. But there's a difference between a pup who has always slept with their legs in the air and one who suddenly starts acting strangely. If your pup begins staring at walls, repeating the same movements, or turning down food when that's not normal for them, don't automatically label it as a new amusing personality trait. Pain, illness, and anxiety can all show up as changes in behavior. If something feels off, put the camera down and call the vet.

Genes can influence behavioral tendencies, but they don't write a complete script for an individual dog's life. Learning and environment play a big role, too, sometimes in ways pet parents never intended.

Take the sock thief. A dog grabs a sock, their pet parents react with dramatic excitement, and suddenly the household is involved in a thrilling chase. From our perspective, it's a laundry crime. From the pup's perspective, it may be an excellent new game.

Behaviors that lead to positive or rewarding outcomes are more likely to happen again. Attention, play, food, and access to preferred activities can all reinforce behavior, even when nobody is training anything on purpose.

Genetics can contribute, too. Inherited tendencies may influence a dog's motivation to chase, retrieve, explore, or seek food. But a predisposition doesn't guarantee a particular behavior, nor does it explain every individual habit. A dog's behavior comes from a combination of biology and learned experience, which is often less convenient than blaming everything on their breed, but it is much closer to reality.

A 2022 study published in Science looked at the behavior and DNA of thousands of dogs. Researchers found that a dog's breed explained only about 9% of the differences in behavior between individual dogs. In other words, dogs of the same breed can have very different personalities and behaviors. Genetics plays a role, but it doesn't tell the whole story.

That doesn't mean genetics is irrelevant. The researchers found evidence that many behavioral traits do have a heritable component. Rather, the findings show why breed alone is a poor crystal ball for predicting how an individual dog will behave.

Some dogs may be especially motivated to retrieve, chase, or investigate, reflecting tendencies shaped partly by their ancestry and breeding history. But individual dogs still vary, and experience helps shape how those tendencies appear. However, with more data, we may learn new things; science is ever evolving along with our technologies.

Embark's Behavior Insights & Training feature connects genetic information with behavioral insights and training guidance. Genetic results can be useful, but they are one piece of the puzzle and not a personality prediction.

Behavior is best understood in context. Has the habit been present for years, or did it start last week? What happens before the behavior? Could pain, fear, stress, or another medical issue be contributing?

If a pup is safe and comfortable, there's often no reason to stop a peculiar routine unless itâs a problem. A dog who carries a favorite toy around the house doesn't need a corrective training plan. When a behavior does create a problem, redirection and positive reinforcement can help teach an alternative response without relying on intimidation or punishment. This is the science of behavioral modification.

The goal isn't to turn every pup into a perfectly polished obedience champion, but to help us understand what each dog needs and help them become great family members.

Pet parents can enroll their weirdos through November 15, 2026, by uploading a photo or video of their pup's strangest behavior, with an optional short story, at Embark's official contest page. No weird dog? No problem. You can still get involved by casting your vote for the weirdest dog through the official voting page.

The first-place winner will receive the World's Weirdest Dog title, a Times Square billboard feature, and a $200 gift card. Second through fifth place will receive $150 gift cards each, while sixth through fifteenth place will receive an Embark Breed + Health Dog DNA Test with the Behavior Insights & Training upgrade.

So, if you know your furry pal is a weirdo, this may be their moment. Let that freak flag fly!
