A mower that's running perfectly now might not be so cooperative after months in storage. A little preparation can help prevent costly surprises.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ah, the last lawn-cutting Saturday comes and goes, so it’s the happy end of mowing for the entire calendar year. All you want to do is push that lawn mower into the shed and close and lock the door. But you can’t, and you’ll regret it if you do. Come the following spring, you’ll pull out a mower that is sluggish, with stale fuel, clogged carburetors, and broken parts. It’s entirely possible that that lawn mower won’t start in spring at all.

You can’t just put that mower to bed for a long winter’s nap without first doing some lawn mower maintenance. It’s not as nice as tucking that mower away and drinking a cool beer, but it’s not all that difficult either. Once you learn how to winterize a lawn mower, you’ll find that it’s easier to jump in and do the work before you move your machine into winter storage.

I'm here to walk you through the steps to prepare your lawn mower for its winter rest. Just follow this practical step-by-step approach. It won't take long if you tackle it alongside your other garden winterizing chores.

It only takes a month for the gasoline in a gas-powered motor to start to break down. When it does, it leaves gummy deposits in the carburetor. This doesn’t do anything good for the mower. You can tackle this in either of two ways.

First, and some would argue best, is to add a lawn mower fuel stabilizer to the remaining fresh gasoline in the tank. Sta-Bil, available on Amazon, is a good choice, but Sea Foam and Ethanol Shield are other popular options. But check your mower manufacturer's recommendations, as some don't advise this step.

To use a fuel stabilizer, first check the product instructions for the correct amount to add based on the gasoline volume. Add the stabilizer to the tank, then top up with fresh gasoline, leaving a little room for expansion. Run the engine for around 5-10 minutes, or as directed on the product label, to allow the treated fuel to circulate through the fuel system. This helps prevent gasoline from deteriorating during winter storage, reducing the risk of deposits forming in the carburetor and causing starting problems in spring.

The second option to winterize a gas mower is to empty the tank so that there is no gasoline to break down. You can do this easily by running the mower until it is totally out of gas. You can also empty the tank by draining the tank and carburetor bowl manually.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Before you start, switch off the engine, let it cool completely, and disconnect the spark plug wire for safety. If you need to tip the mower to access the underside, tilt it with the air filter and carburetor facing upward, as tipping it the wrong way can allow oil or fuel to leak into the air filter or engine intake.

Next, clean the underside of the mower, scraping away grass clippings and dirt with a plastic scraper or stiff nylon brush. Leaving damp debris in place over winter can cause corrosion on steel mower decks.

Once the underside is clean and completely dry, apply a protective coating. Mo-Deck Non-Stick Mower Deck Spray helps prevent grass clippings and debris from sticking to the deck, making cleanup easier when mowing season returns. Follow the product instructions and allow it to dry before storing the mower.

Draining the oil is not fun, but it’s not that difficult either. First, check your mower's manual, as some newer engines only require oil top-ups rather than regular changes. If yours needs an oil change, run the mower for a few minutes to warm the oil, then switch off the engine, let it cool enough to work safely, and disconnect the spark plug wire before proceeding.

Drain the old, dirty oil into a suitable container, following your mower's instructions. A Briggs & Stratton oil extractor kit makes the job much less messy, allowing you to remove oil through the fill tube without tipping the mower.

Does your mower have an oil filter? If so, change it now, using a replacement designed for your engine. Then refill with the correct amount of fresh motor oil. This will depend on your model, but common options include SAE 30 and synthetic 5W-30. Check the oil level with the dipstick to avoid overfilling, and take the used oil to a recycling facility.

Your lawn mower blade needs to be sharp and free of cracks. With the engine off and the spark plug wire disconnected, follow your mower's instructions to safely access and remove the blade. Wear thick gloves and check carefully for nicks, cracks, bends, or dull edges.

You can sharpen a dull blade with a hand file, but it's easier to use a proper lawn mower blade sharpener, like this Sporgain lawn mower blade sharpener and balancer from Amazon. However, if your lawn mower blade is cracked or badly damaged, it's better to replace it.

If you sharpen the blade yourself, follow the manufacturer's recommended angle and make sure it's properly balanced before reinstalling it. An unbalanced blade can cause excessive vibration and damage the mower.

At the same time, inspect the spark plug for wear, corrosion, or heavy carbon buildup. Remove it using a spark plug socket (this Milwaukee set from Home Depot has three sizes), and if the plug is damaged, badly worn, or heavily coated, it's best to replace it with a new one recommended for your mower. Otherwise, gently clean away any light buildup with a soft brush before putting it back. Check your mower's manual for any specific instructions.

The great thing about winterizing a battery-operated mower is that you don’t have to worry about gasoline issues. On the other hand, you do have to worry about looking after the battery. This is also important if your gasoline-powered mower has an electric starter.

Proper winter storage is essential. If the battery is removable, take it out of the mower and store it in a cool, dry place indoors, away from freezing temperatures and extreme heat. Check your manufacturer's recommendations for the ideal storage temperature, as requirements vary between batteries.

For lithium-ion batteries, most manufacturers recommend storing them partially charged, rather than fully charged or empty. Check the charge periodically throughout winter and top it up if needed.

However, if your mower uses a lead-acid battery, you generally need to keep it fully charged during storage. A compatible battery maintainer can help prevent them from going flat. The Noco Genius1 Smart Battery Charger and Maintainer maintains the battery's charge throughout winter so it's ready to go when mowing season returns. Do make sure any charger or maintainer you use is suitable for your battery type.

Move your mower into a dry shed, garage, or other sheltered space where it will be protected from rain, snow, and ice. Ideally, keep it on a clean, dry surface, as sitting on damp ground over winter can cause rust and corrosion.

A breathable, water-resistant lawn mower cover, like this Himal Outdoors Push Lawn Mower Cover from Amazon, is a good idea because it helps keep dust, dirt, and moisture off the mower when it's not in use. Make sure the mower is completely cool and dry before covering it.

Avoid storing your mower near corrosive household chemicals, fertilizers, or pool chlorine, as their fumes or spills can damage metal components over time. If you're storing it in a garage or shed, leave enough space around the machine for ventilation and easy access.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#7847. War Dogs of History: Sergeant Stubby and the Birth of the American War Dog Legend

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Long before the United States military established an official war dog program, one small stray taught the Army what a dog could do in combat. His name was Stubby, and by the time the First World War ended, he had become the most decorated dog in American military history.

Stubbyâs story began in the summer of 1917 at Yale Field in New Haven, Connecticut, where the 102nd Infantry Regiment of the 26th âYankeeâ Division was training before deployment to France. A short-tailed, brindle-colored dog of uncertain breeding, likely part Boston terrier and part American bull terrier, wandered into camp and was adopted by Private J. Robert Conroy. Soldiers were not permitted to keep pets, but Stubby won over the men, and eventually the officers, by learning to mimic military customs. He reportedly marched in step with the troops and raised a paw to his brow in a passable salute.

When the 102nd Infantry shipped out for France, the transport ships barred dogs. Conroy smuggled Stubby aboard the SS Minnesota hidden beneath his overcoat. Conroyâs commanding officer discovered Stubby during the crossing, but his salute reportedly charmed the officer into letting him stay.

Once in France, Stubbyâs role shifted from morale booster to something closer to that of a working soldier. He entered combat on February 5, 1918, at Chemin des Dames, enduring shelling for over a month, and went on to serve through 17 battles over 18 months on the Western Front.

After surviving a mustard gas attack, Stubby developed a heightened sensitivity to the smell of gas. Historians and contemporary newspaper accounts credit him with warning his regiment of subsequent gas attacks before the men could detect it themselves. This allowed soldiers time to don their masks. He was also credited with locating wounded soldiers in no manâs land and comforting them until stretcher bearers arrived.

Stubbyâs most famous exploit occurred when he discovered a German soldier mapping the layout of Allied trenches. According to accounts preserved by military historians, Stubby seized the man until American soldiers arrived to take him prisoner. For this act, Stubby was informally promoted to the rank of sergeant, making him, according to most accounts, the first dog to receive a rank in the United States Armed Forces. This was, of course, an honorary and unofficial designation rather than a formal commission, since the military does not commission dogs.

During the April 1918 German offensive on the town of Seicheprey, France, Stubby was wounded in the chest and leg by grenade shrapnel while accompanying the 102nd Infantry in combat. After recovering, he returned to visiting wounded soldiers in the hospital, walking the wards to lift the spirits of recovering men.

Stubby returned home a celebrity. He led parades, attended war bond rallies, and met three sitting or future presidents: Woodrow Wilson, Warren G. Harding, and Calvin Coolidge. General John J. Pershing personally honored him at a 1921 ceremony for the 102nd Infantry Regiment, presenting him with a gold medal from the Humane Education Society, an award that, while not an official military commendation, cemented his reputation as the greatest war dog of his era.

Conroy went on to attend Georgetown University Law Center, and Stubby went with him, becoming the unofficial mascot of the Georgetown Hoyas football team. At halftime, he would nudge a football around the field to the delight of the crowd.

Stubby died in 1929, reportedly in Conroyâs arms. His remains were preserved and are held today by the Smithsonianâs National Museum of American History, where he wears the medals and blanket he wore during his years of service. In 2018, an animated film called Sgt. Stubby: An American Hero introduced his story to a new generation. That same year, the descendants of Conroy dedicated a life-sized bronze statue of him at the Connecticut Trees of Honor Memorial in Middletown, Connecticut.

Stubby served nearly a quarter century before the United States Army established a formal War Dog Program in 1942. He had no training pipeline, no breeding program, and no structure to recognize what he did. He was, in the truest sense, an amateur who became indispensable through instinct, loyalty, and repeated exposure to danger alongside the men who fed and sheltered him. Later advocates of formal military working dog programs often cite his legacy as early proof of concept: a dogâs senses, courage, and bond with a handler could save human lives on a modern battlefield.

Every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

Support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

Keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

Follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

These dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

If Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

#7846. Outmarket AI: Head of Growth

Outmarket AI · Remote (US) · Full-time · Reports to the SVP of Marketing

Insurance still runs on manual work. Most policies are sold through agents and brokers, and the people who know the work best are buried in the documents: checking policies line by line, comparing quotes, building proposals, on nights and weekends. We think that's backwards. The best people in insurance should spend their time advising clients.

Outmarket, the AI platform built for insurance, makes that possible. Account teams drop in their documents and get back finished work to review, with every finding linked to the page it came from. Outmarket connects to the systems they already use. The judgment stays with the person; the groundwork doesn't.

It's working. More than 10,000 people at over 300 agencies use Outmarket, including 30 of the top 100 U.S. insurance brokers. Most of those agencies found us through other customers. We raised a $34.5M Series B led by SignalFire four months after announcing our Series A because customers were pulling us forward faster than we planned.

Demand that already exists. Customers recommend us to each other. Your job is to turn that word of mouth into an engine we can plan around.

Ground floor. You'll join marketing while the team is being built, alongside a new Head of Product Marketing and Head of Content. You'll have room to shape the function instead of inheriting a playbook.

A direct line. You'll work with the SVP of Marketing, the CRO, the founders and customers, and you'll see your decisions show up in pipeline within weeks.

You own marketing's pipeline number. That means qualified meetings with the right brokers and the sales-accepted opportunities and dollars that follow, not leads. You'll run the programs (named-account campaigns, event follow-through, webinars, paid and nurture), own the programs budget, and work closely with the CRO and the account executives.

There are two motions. Independent agencies buy through an outbound and events engine. Large brokers buy through a named-account program aimed at a buying committee: principal, producers, operations and often the person who runs their agency management system. You'll run both.

A growth marketing associate reports to you from day one. The SVP of Marketing runs demand gen until you arrive and hands it to you in your first month.

Own the marketing-sourced pipeline number and report it weekly with sales: meetings, sales-accepted opportunities, pipeline dollars and cost per opportunity.

Run the named-account program for our top 10 broker targets: choose accounts with sales, run buying-committee plays, and coordinate outbound, paid and event touches.

Plan and run the campaign calendar, including renewal-season campaigns, customer webinars and one experiment a month.

Own paid media on LinkedIn and search, favoring short customer videos over vendor claims. Cut whatever doesn't produce meetings.

Turn events into pipeline with our Director of Industry Events & Programs: pre-show targeting, meeting booking and post-show follow-up.

Build nurture and follow-up so no event lead or demo request goes stale, and own lead routing and the marketing tools you run on.

Get the customer stories and video made by the Head of Content in front of the right buyers.

5+ years in B2B demand generation or growth marketing

You've run named-account or ABM programs aimed at a buying committee and can show what they produced in opportunities, not MQLs.

You've worked with a field sales team in an events-heavy motion and know how to turn a conference into meetings.

You're hands-on with HubSpot or Salesforce, LinkedIn Ads and outbound tools, and you can build a campaign yourself before you hand it off.

You've managed at least one person or a contractor team and can set priorities without hand-holding.

You have startup experience at Series A to C, and you built a demand gen function

High agency: you find the work instead of waiting for it.

Ownership: you carry a number and a function, not a task list.

Startup pace: we ship weekly instead of planning quarterly.

You don't need to know insurance. You'll spend your first month in agencies and on calls with producers. Curiosity is the requirement, and becoming fluent is part of the job.

No forms. Just smart, optimized applications.

Remember every detail and next step, without a meeting bot.

#7845. Arianne and Micah’s Small Urban Minneapolis Garden

Hi GPOD! I’ve recently gotten a few emails from readers asking about submissions they entered through the website link at the end of every GPOD. Unfortunately, I haven’t received any submissions through the form in quite a while. I’m not sure what the problem is, but hopefully there will be a resolution soon. In the meantime, you can submit your photos and captions through the email linked below instead.

Today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota. And while looking through their latest photos, I kept forgetting that I was looking at a garden in the Midwest! Arianne has shared their garden with us before, and I’m excited to see what they’ve been growing this year. Here’s Arianne:

In Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden! It’s packed with flowers I start from seed—like zinnias, cosmos, statice, strawflower, celosia, and amaranth—along with overwintered dahlias. I love cutting fresh bouquets to gift to friends, family, and coworkers. When we’re not admiring the blooms, my husband is cooking outdoors—making wood-fired pizzas, wok dishes, and hosting family birthday celebrations right in the heart of our cozy yard.

Arianne packs plenty of interest into the garden along in the front yard and along the curb strip. Plants in this section of the garden include dwarf purple smokebush, threadleaf bluestar (Amsonia hubrichtii, Zones 5–8), boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), lamb’s ear (Stachys byzantina, Zones 4–8), purpleleaf sand cherry (Prunus × cistena, Zones 2–8), coreopsis (Coreopsis cvs., Zones 3–9), alliums (Allium cvs., Zones 3–9), sedum, and artemisia. It’s a great mix of foliage colors and textures even when everything isn’t in bloom.

I love the placement of the patio and pathway. It’s a really useful design technique for maximizing every square inch of a small garden while still leaving plenty of room for outdoor living.

Absolutely gorgeous section of the garden! This is where we really start to feel like we’re in the tropics. ‘Mars Madness’ hardy hibiscus (Hibiscus ‘Mars Madness’, Zones 4–9) has all the tropical drama while still being hardy enough for a Minneapolis winter. And it’s hard to miss those giant cannas and the colorful foliage on the coleus. I love all the red blooms too!

One of Arianne’s fabulous container combinations features Tropicanna Gold canna (Canna ‘Mactro’, Zones 8–11), purple shield (Strobilanthes dyerianus, annual), begonias (Begonia cvs., annual), flowering kale (Brassica oleracea, annual), and parrot’s beak (Lotus berthelotii, annual). So much of the color and interest here comes from foliage!

There is so much to look at in this section of the garden! Those variegated geranium leaves are striking, and I could go on and on about Arianne’s use of color and texture. The apple tree surrounded by all these ornamentals is an unexpected but lovely touch.

Just around the corner from the photo above. Another gorgeous tropical container, and ‘Blue Shadow’ fothergilla (Fothergilla × intermedia ‘Blue Shadow’, Zones 5–8) grows on the left in this view.

Another view of the backyard borders. There are so many plants packed into this garden, you would never believe this is a small urban backyard. And, if my eyes are working correctly, I’d say that’s a clover lawn?!

A shady combination of hostas, ‘Banana Boat’ sedge (Carex siderosticha ‘Banana Boat’, Zones 4–9), painted fern, purple shield, coleus, and impatiens.

Zinnias, statice, amaranth, and overwintered dahlias are just some of the blooms that make their way into bouquets for friends, family, and coworkers. So pretty!

Thank you so much for sharing your garden with us again, Arianne! It’s always a treat to see what you and Micah are growing, and I think I could spend hours wandering around this garden and still find something new to admire.

#7844. Ask Dr. Paola - HELP! What Does It Mean When a Dog’s Hackles Go Up in Different Places? (November 16, 2026)

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every other Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their dog's health and well-being.

Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned dog lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your furry friend happy and healthy. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your dog, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your canine companion.

âHaveâ a âquestion? Send it in here!

I have a question about my dog, Jethro. Sometimes when he alerts, the hackles between his shoulders rise. Other times they are prominent along his lower back. What does each appearance indicate about how he is responding?â

That is a great observation! When a dogâs hackles rise, it is an involuntary response controlled by the autonomic nervous system called piloerection, and it tells us that his arousal level has increased. However, the location of the raised hair does not reliably tell us which emotion a dog is experiencing.

When the hackles rise between his shoulders, it can accompany alertness, excitement, uncertainty, or concern. When they appear along his lower back, the same range of emotional responses is possible. Neither pattern automatically indicates aggression, fear, or a particular level of threat. Think of hackles as a little emotional alarm bell; they tell us Jethro is experiencing heightened arousal, but not exactly why.

Different dogs will respond to different stimuli in different ways, so thereâs no âone size fits allâ explanation for why different areas are triggered. I would pay close attention to what is happening around him when this occurs. Is he alerting to a stranger approaching the house, another dog walking past, an unfamiliar noise, or something unexpected in the environment? You might want to start keeping a record of what is going on before and after Jethroâs hackles are raised, and whether itâs his shoulders or lower back that is involved.

Combine that context with his facial expression, ear position, tail carriage, posture, muscle tension, and ability to disengage. Looking at the whole picture helps us understand whether Jethro is curious, excited, uncertain, or uncomfortable, and, most importantly, how we can best support him. These details, together with what triggered the alert, give us a much clearer picture of how Jethro is feeling.

It's easy to recreate the look in your own garden with beautiful white roses – and November is the perfect time to plant.

If there's one thing Miley Cyrus knows how to do, it's make a statement. And her recent wedding to musician Maxx Morando has given us plenty of inspiration – particularly when it comes to the flowers.

The couple's romantic ceremony featured masses of beautiful white roses, with a breathtaking floral arch creating a dreamy backdrop for the celebrations. It's classic, understated and wonderfully romantic. And, honestly? We're already dreaming about recreating the look in our own backyards. The good news is that November is one of the best times to get started. Bare-root roses are coming into season, making this the perfect opportunity to plant your own romantic rose display – often for considerably less than you'd spend on established container-grown plants.

So, while Miley might have had a team of florists to bring her wedding vision to life, you can take a slightly more long-term approach. Plant now, give your roses time to establish over winter, and you could be enjoying your own beautiful floral display come spring and summer. After all, as Miley herself once reminded us, we can absolutely buy ourselves flowers. But growing them ourselves? Even better.

There's something wonderfully timeless about an all-white flower display. While colorful planting schemes certainly have their place, sticking to one color can create a much more elegant look – and white roses, as Miley Cyrus' wedding photos have proven, are particularly lovely for this.

The beauty of this look is that you don't need hundreds of individual plants to make an impact. A well-positioned rose bush, a climbing variety trained over an arch or trellis, or even a small collection of white roses along a garden path can create a n atmosphere that's just as romantic.

Better still? Well, there's no need to wait until spring to start planning your own rose garden, because November is actually the ideal time to get planting. Bare-root roses become available from late fall and are generally much more affordable than their container-grown counterparts, making them a brilliant option if you're hoping to plant several together.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If you're looking for something that combines good looks with wildlife appeal, this shrub rose produces fragrant white blooms, followed by ornamental rose hips that provide additional seasonal interest.

For something a little closer to the full-bodied blooms seen at Miley's wedding, this floribunda variety produces gorgeous double white blooms, sometimes with the faintest blush of pink.

Of course, if it's the dramatic floral arch you're hoping to recreate, you'll want to consider a climbing rose. This pretty variety is ideal for training over arches, pergolas and trellises.

The good news? You don't need an elaborate wedding installation to achieve that same Miley Cyrus-inspired look; you just need a sturdy garden arch like this pergola from Outsunny, and pop it somewhere that gets plenty of sunlight. (Most roses need at least six hours of direct sunlight each day).

Next, plant a climbing rose on either side of your structure, allowing the canes to grow and training them horizontally and upwards as they develop. Be patient, though, as your rose arch won't become an overnight sensation, and it may take a couple of growing seasons to achieve the look you're craving.

And there you have it: a little celebrity-inspired garden magic without the celebrity price tag. Miley Cyrus' wedding might have lasted just one day, but with the right roses and a little patience, you can enjoy your own romantic floral display year after year. Talk about a love story worth growing, eh?

Sayulita, on the coast of Nayarit, Mexico, is a dog-friendly surf town. Many pups spend their mornings with their paws in the sand while their owners head into the water to catch some waves. They dig the sand, run and play along the shore, and many sit patiently waiting for their parents to return. But, dogs being dogs, it's not hard to imagine how some of them have naturally followed their human right into the water to discover what the fun is all about.

For a surprising number of beach-going canines, surfing has become part of their world, and this year, the first dog-surfing contest in Sayulita took place as part of the International DÃ­a de Muertos Surf Tournament, held October 29 through November 1, 2026, at Playa Principal. Twelve dog-and-handler teams participated, making this a pawticularly special addition to the town's surf calendar. The main tournament, now in its third edition, brought together more than 120 athletes across several surfing disciplines.

The official program listed the dog category as an exhibition, with a prize pool of 10,000 Mexican pesos distributed among the top three. But for the pups, there was no question about the attraction: a surfboard, some waves, the chance to have fun with their favorite person, and a beach full of admirers? Paw me in!

Sayulita has been part of my life for a long time. As a teenager, I spent many weekends camping there, long before the main entrance road was paved or I imagined I would return as a veterinarian or spend time pet-sitting here.

In July and August this year, I looked after a wonderful rescue pup in Sayulita, and our daily walks took us along the main beach, past the local cemetery, for our daily swim in the beautiful Playa de los Muertos. It was a lovely way to experience the town beyond its busy surf beaches.

Sayulita is genuinely pet-friendly. Dogs are welcome on its beaches, and most restaurants accommodate four-legged visitors. They are part of the scenery, whether accompanying their pet parents through town or waiting patiently on the sand while someone catches a wave.

That makes the new dog-surfing event feel like a natural progression. Dogs have long been part of the local beach scene. This time, they got their own chance to take to the spotlight in the water.

The first Sayulita dog-surfing competition brought together 12 teams: Suleiman Navarro and Toto; Risa Mara Machuca and Chia; Lia Carbajal and Nita; Emiliano Cordova and Pelusa; Fernando Stalla and Miky; Carlos Rocha and Paddel; Eno James and Nemo; Nique Miller and Roy; Monse AcuÃ±a and Trinity; Luis Becerra and Knacki; Buzz Moro and LeÃ³n; and Kory De Jean and GÃ¼ero.

First place went to Suleiman Navarro and Toto, a blind Pug from Punta de Mita. Toto's visual impairment didn't keep him from joining the fun and riding the waves with Sule. Second place went to Fernando Stalla and Miky, who already enjoy surfing in Sayulita from time to time.

Risa Mara Machuca, known through @surfitoutmexico, helped bring the dog-surfing category to the event. Her own surfing partner, Chia, is already familiar with the sport beyond Sayulita. In August 2025, Chia and Risa became the first Mexican team to compete in the World Dog Surfing Competition in Pacifica, California.

Their surfing story began when Chia, who loved following Risa into the ocean, climbed onto a soft-top surfboard one day and headed straight for the front. Risa looked up at the sky and shouted, "Thank you, universe!"

It's hard not to appreciate a pup who discovers and genuinely enjoys a hobby shared with her favorite person. Chia's enthusiasm has helped give Sayulita a local connection to a sport attracting canine-human teams internationally.

My visit to Sayulita during DÃ­a de Muertos offered another glimpse into how much the community values their pups. The plaza and surrounding streets were specially decorated for the occasion. On the evening of November 1, we watched a procession leave the plaza as people gathered to honor loved ones who had passed away. Families continued the tradition of remembering the departed through decorations, flowers, and time spent together.

Many local establishments created traditional altars dedicated to their departed pets, with photographs and little tributes to beloved dogs included among the traditional decorations. It was lovely to see these four-legged family members remembered and celebrated as part of the town's DÃ­a de Muertos traditions.

October 27 has become a popular date in Mexico for remembering pets during the DÃ­a de Muertos season. Families may prepare small altars with photographs, favorite treats, toys, and water. This particular observance is a relatively recent popular custom rather than an ancient tradition followed everywhere, but it has found a meaningful place in many households.

Anyone who has loved and lost a dog can understand why. Pets become part of our daily routines, our families, and our memories. Seeing their photographs included in these celebrations gave me a lovely glimpse into the affection people in Sayulita have for their canine companions.

It also brought together two sides of the human-animal bond: remembering the dogs who are no longer with us while celebrating the ones still sharing our adventures.

Surfing isnât an activity for every dog, and thatâs okay. Like any activity, surfing should be reserved for dogs who voluntarily enjoy swimming and feel comfortable on a board. A well-fitted safety vest is always a good idea, like the cute one Chia wore, complete with its little shark fin! Not every dog is a water enthusiast, and that deserves just as much respect as celebrating the confident pups happy to take the spotlight. Waiting on the beach for their pet parents is a perfectly wonderful way to spend the day, too. As long as everyone is happy and the beach is left clean, that's a win for dogs and people alike.

Of course, the fun of watching dogs surf is only part of what made this event special. It also brought together two things that are so much a part of Sayulita: its surf culture and its affection for dogs.

The 2026 dog-surfing event added something genuinely new to the International DÃ­a de Muertos Surf Tournament. While the main competition celebrated its third year, the dogs were making their own history and adding to the unique charm of the event.

One of the nicest parts of returning to town was seeing how naturally dogs fit into both everyday life and local traditions. From the pups waiting patiently on the beach as their owners enjoy the waves, to the little altars honoring those who had passed away, there were reminders everywhere of the special place dogs hold in this community. Watching these dogs enjoy the waves alongside their pet parents was a lovely addition to a weekend already filled with celebration, music, and remembrance. Seeing just how much dogs are woven into Sayulita's culture, thereâs surely no better place for a doggy surfing competition.

Outmarket AI · Remote (US) · Full-time · Reports to the SVP of Marketing

Insurance still runs on manual work. Most policies are sold through agents and brokers, and the people who know the work best are buried in the documents: checking policies line by line, comparing quotes, building proposals, on nights and weekends. We think that's backwards. The best people in insurance should spend their time advising clients.

Outmarket, the AI platform built for insurance, makes that possible. Account teams drop in their documents and get back finished work to review, with every finding linked to the page it came from. Outmarket connects to the systems they already use. The judgment stays with the person; the groundwork doesn't.

It's working. More than 10,000 people at over 300 agencies use Outmarket, including 30 of the top 100 U.S. insurance brokers. Most of those agencies found us through other customers. We raised a $34.5M Series B led by SignalFire four months after announcing our Series A because customers were pulling us forward faster than we planned.

Customers who want to talk. About 300 agencies use Outmarket, and most will go on record about it. Few content leaders start with that many stories ready to tell.

First in the seat. You'll be our first content hire, joining alongside a new Head of Product Marketing and Head of Growth. You'll decide what Outmarket sounds and looks like.

Real creative room, and a budget to use it. There's budget for specialist contractors such as editors, shooters and designers, and you'll have room to make work that doesn't look like typical B2B content.

A direct line. You'll work with the SVP of Marketing, the founders and customers, and you'll see what your work does for pipeline within weeks.

You own video, social, customer stories and written content. You'll build the function hands-on: you script, interview, direct and write yourself, and you work with a small group of specialist contractors instead of an in-house crew. Our buyers are owners, producers and operations leaders at commercial insurance agencies. It's a relationship-driven industry, and we're still learning where these buyers spend their attention online. Part of your job is finding out, then making the content that reaches them there.

Run the customer story program. Make it easy for busy customers to say yes, and never over-ask the same ones.

Ship every week. Build a steady publishing rhythm with a bench of specialist contractors. Find them, brief them clearly, know what things should cost, and review closely so quality holds as volume grows.

Turn our events into content. Work with our Director of Industry Events & Programs to plan what to capture at the conferences and customer dinners we already run, and publish soon after.

Find where brokers pay attention, whether that's LinkedIn, YouTube, industry media or events. Put our effort where the audience is, not where content teams usually start.

Build leaders' voices. Help our founders and other leaders post every week, each in their own voice.

Own written content, including the site, social and long-form pieces, and keep everything we publish clear and sharp.

Measure what your content does for pipeline and use that to decide what to make next.

If you see evergreen shrubs with dead leaf tips in late fall or early winter, it's a sure sign you need to protect plants from frost, freezing temperatures and cold winds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The mild fall in many areas this year allowed many shrubs to delay dormancy and even put out fresh growth. Without the time to build cold resistance before winter weather arrives, evergreen foliage is left vulnerable to leaf damage.

Blackened or brown evergreen leaf tips don't necessarily mean your shrubs are dying, but they are cause for concern and a clear sign you need to prepare your garden for winter. Understanding what's caused the damage is important so you know what to do next to save your beloved evergreen shrubs. So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your evergreen shrubs with black or brown leaf tips in late fall or early winter.

If your shrubs are experiencing damage related to our mild fall this year, you're likely to spot these symptoms:

If the damage is confined to a few leaf and needle tips, there's no need to worry: your shrub will recover, and it's a good idea to take steps to prevent further damage. If the damage is more significant, there's still a high chance of recovery but you should better protect plants from frost and have plenty of patience.

There are two primary and most likely causes of dark, dry tips on your evergreen shrubs. The distinction matters because the underlying cause determines how you help your shrub recover.

Your shrubs naturally harden off for winter, a process triggered by less daylight and gradually dropping temperatures. They slow their growth and undergo some internal processes that allow them to better withstand freezing winter temperatures. To get more specific, soluble sugars begin to accumulate in the cells of leaves and needles. These sugars make it harder for water in the cells to freeze and allow the plant to better regulate water movement. As the youngest leaves go through this process, they become woodier, more mature, and more resistant to freezing injuries.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

During a mild fall, as many of us have experienced this year, some evergreens might continue producing new, soft growth instead of entering the dormancy period. This disrupts the vital process of winter hardening-off, leaving cells with high water content and underdeveloped protection. So, when temperatures finally drop, the water in cells freezes more readily. These frozen cells then rupture. Affected leaves, needles, and tips die as a result of the damage and turn brown or black.

Some of the evergreens most susceptible to this type of damage include hebe, choisya, camellia, and photinia. Even plants that normally tolerate cold winters can be affected after an unusually warm fall.

Desiccation or wind scorch, also known as winter burn, is another potential cause of black or brown evergreen foliage, and this can occur regardless of an unseasonable fall. Evergreen shrubs lose moisture through their leaves, even as growth slows, and cold air, winter winds and bright sun increase this moisture loss. Once the ground – and the moisture held in the soil – freezes, the shrubs’ roots can't take up water to replace what's being lost. This moisture imbalance can cause leaf and needle tissue to dry out and turn brown or black, and damage often begins at foliage tips and margins.

Distinguishing leaf damage caused by winter desiccation from new foliage that's died in the first cold snap is easy: if wind scorch is the issue, damage will be on the windy side of the shrub. You’ll also see that the outer leaves and needles are most affected, with the inner foliage protected. The damage from wind scorch is typically gradual rather than suddenly appearing after a frost or freeze, too.

Evergreens with shallow roots like arborvitae, boxwood, rhododendron, yew, juniper and holly are particularly susceptible to winter desiccation. Any evergreen can be damaged this way, however, depending on moisture in the soil, wind levels and how protected the shrub is.

First – and most importantly – of all, don’t rush to snip off those black tips. You can’t recover that dead tissue, and cutting it off now can cause more damage. If your shrubs are victims of the poor hardening-off that resulted from a mild fall, trimming could trigger more vulnerable growth, and also expose currently sheltered foliage to further harm. Similarly, the damage on a wind-scorched shrub will protect the foliage beneath.

The next step depends on the cause of the leaf damage.

Now you know your shrub isn’t ready for the cold, protect it from the rest of the winter weather to come. A zip-up plant jacket is an easy way to winterize shrubs that only need protecting ahead of a predicted cold snap rather than being wrapped up all winter. Another option is to wrap plants up in burlap – rolls of hessian are available from Walmart – or horticultural fleece such as this from Amazon, unwrapping plants after the cold weather has passed.

When covering shrubs, be sure to do so loosely and use stakes inserted in the soil to hold fabric away from leaves. If your shrub is growing in a container, then wrapping the pot in bubble wrap and burlap protects roots during a prolonged freeze, too. Choose the level of protection based on your zone and how badly damaged your evergreen shrub is.

If those dead leaf tips are caused by a wind and moisture imbalance, first check the moisture in the soil around the plants. If you're using a moisture meter, make sure it's one with a long probe like this moisture meter on Amazon so you get a reading where it matters. If the soil is dry and the ground isn’t frozen, give the root zone a good soak.

Next, apply a layer of mulch made from natural materials like Back to the Roots Organic Mulch, available from Amazon, around the base of each shrub. This will help conserve moisture and insulate the soil. Just be sure to keep the mulch a few inches away from the stems to prevent moisture accumulating there and causing rot or fungal disease.

Now you need to protect your shrub from further damage from wind scorch. You could pop a frost jacket on your shrub whenever high winds are forecast, or use burlap to create a windbreak. You don’t necessarily need to cover the whole shrub; just provide a barrier from the prevailing winds. Keep checking shrubs throughout the winter, adding windbreaks and watering when the soil thaws as needed.

These steps will help prevent more damage, but they won’t reverse the damage that has already occurred. Now, you’re probably wondering when you can remove those unsightly dead leaf tips – and you're going to have to be patient. It’s important not to prune off dead leaves or branches now as this can trigger new growth, introduce damage or disease at the cut areas, and leave interior foliage vulnerable.

Wait to prune until spring when there is no more risk of a severe frost, then use clean, sharp shears to remove dead tips. If larger areas have browned or blackened, cut these stems back to the first healthy, live bud. You can check if a branch might regrow by scraping back the outer layer with your fingernail. If it’s brown underneath, it’s dead and should be removed. If you see green, it could still sprout new growth.

Keep your pruning light in spring. Trim back the damaged parts and then let healthy branches and leaves grow back in before you do any heavier pruning or shaping.

The damage for this year is done and gone, but you can learn from the incident to save your evergreen shrubs from harm next year:

Dead leaf tips on evergreen shrubs are usually a cosmetic issue, not a death sentence for your favorite plants. Follow these guidelines and your shrubs should recover, ready to shine again next year.

#7839. Bored, Overtired, or Just Being a Dog? What Makes Puppies Hyper

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Puppyhood is a huge learning curve â for both owner and dog â and managing a puppyâs energy can be one of the hardest parts of it. Hyperactivity is common, and the good news is that knowing what causes it makes it much easier to help a puppy calm down. The reasons range from ordinary puppy exuberance to, on rare occasions, a health problem.

Puppies burn energy by exploring and playing, but they can run out of things to do. A mix of toys, activities, and walks helps manage their energy. Without it, boredom and frustration can lead to destructive behavior or aggression, or to zooming around the house. A puppy with no good outlet, such as a sturdy chew toy, will release that pent-up energy by barking, running around, or jumping on people.

The opposite problem is just as real. Just like toddlers who throw tantrums when theyâre overtired, puppies that have too much going on can become hyperactive because they donât understand that they need a nap, and the discomfort frustrates them. Finding the balance gets easier as an owner learns a puppyâs energy levels. Plenty of activities and training sessions help, as do regular quiet times for cooling off and a quick nap to recharge.

Puppies learn quickly, and that includes behaviors that owners donât mean to encourage. If a puppy gets attention every time it becomes overexcited during play, even when the owner is trying to say stop, the puppy sees it as a reward, and the next time it feels neglected, hyper behavior may seem like a good way to get noticed. The fix is to interact when the puppy is gentle or relaxed, and to become less interesting when it gets overexcited, by dropping the tug toy and stepping away.

All puppies have energy, but the amount varies by breed, and a breedâs original purpose matters as much as its size. Border Collies, bred to herd sheep all day, require lots of physical and mental stimulation to keep up with their boundless energy. A more sedate breed, like the French Bulldog or King Charles Spaniel, tends to have far less energy to burn. A Border Collie puppy has less stamina than an adult, but it still has plenty of energy to manage.

Food affects everything from digestion to brain development, and it can influence sleep cycles, energy levels, and skin health. The wrong diet may contain too much of certain ingredients, often protein, which can lead to hyperactivity. Researching a puppyâs nutritional needs and checking the ingredients with a vet is worthwhile.

Obedience training teaches a dog how to manage its behavior, and socialization helps it get used to people, other pets, and new situations. Without them, a puppy doesnât know how to react, and a quick play session can end with an overexcited puppy that canât calm down. A tiny puppy climbing on people or nipping fingers may seem cute, but puppies donât always stay small, and an adult dog that bites or jumps can be dangerous, especially around a child or a stranger.

Most of the time, hyperactivity is easily corrected and comes down to diet, breed, or limited exercise. Health problems are a rare cause. If a puppy is still hyper after changes to diet, activity, and training, a vet check to rule out any health issues is always a good idea. The earlier a problem is diagnosed, the easier it is to treat.

Puppies are still learning what their bodies are telling them. One of the most common signs is becoming hyper or restless when they need to go. An older puppy getting used to house training may be asking to go out, while a younger one may not understand the signal and burst into a case of the zoomies until it figures it out.

Most hyperactivity simply comes from being a puppy. Younger dogs are more excitable, and they need lots of energy to explore the world without yet knowing how to manage it. Puppies steadily grow out of it. They may still get the zoomies later on, but they settle and learn better control. Rewarding calm behavior, working on obedience, and giving a working breed a job to do all help.

Researching a breed before bringing a puppy home matters, since a high-energy herding breed can be too much for some households. Time matters too, because a long workday followed by evening chores may leave little room for the exercise a puppy needs.

Activity is the best way to manage energy, and it shouldnât be only physical. Puzzles and other mental activities keep a brain busy as well. Calm behavior deserves rewards with treats and attention, and disengaging when a puppy gets overexcited teaches that playing nicely keeps the game going longer. Training helps too, because some hyper behavior is really bad manners learned along the way, such as jumping up or racing around when the leash comes out.

Most puppies grow out of their boundless energy as they reach adulthood and learn self-control, which can take between one and two years depending on breed. Some breeds are naturally quieter and happier to laze around, while more active breeds never lose their energy. A routine tailored to a dogâs needs is essential, along with choosing a puppy that suits the family.

A puppyâs energy can come from exuberance, overstimulation, tiredness, boredom, diet, or, on rare occasions, health issues. Working out which one applies, and adjusting the daily schedule to match, is the key to keeping it manageable.

#7838. Fall Color in Nancy’s Massachusetts Garden

Hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy. Nancy sent in photos of the trees and shrubs winding down the season in her garden, along with one of the last flowers still hanging on.

This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.

My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.

My paperbark maple (Acer griseum, Zones 4–8) has had a hard time coping with our summer droughts and water restrictions, but it looked a lovely red this fall.

This is another native tree that many people are not familiar with, fringe tree (Chionanthus virginicus, Zones 4–9), which has fragrant white flowers hanging from its branches in late spring to early summer. As you can see, it also looks beautiful in its yellow fall foliage.

In the front of this picture is a young sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua, Zones 5–9), which has spectacular red color in the fall and develops spiky seed balls as it matures. In the distance is a blackhaw viburnum (Viburnum prunifolium, Zones 3–9) showing its orange fall color.

‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla (Fothergilla ‘Mount Airy’, Zones 5–8) glows red and orange in front of fragrant abelia (Abelia mosanensis, Zones 4–8), whose fall color is beginning to fade. The abelia will charm us all again in spring with its fragrant blooms.

Sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus, Zones 5–9) on the right has turned a lovely yellow. Amazingly, all three sweetshrubs shown here had the bark eaten off around every trunk by rabbits last winter, killing every one. They all grew back from the roots, showing just how resilient they are. On the left, ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla is showing off its red fall foliage, and in back is ‘Alice’ oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Alice’, Zones 5–9) with maroon fall foliage.

One of the only flowers left blooming is ‘Sheffield Pink’ chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum ‘Sheffield Pink’, Zones 5–9), which complements the dark foliage of Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) behind it.

Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Nancy! Nancy says she’s ready to wander the garden, make her list of what needs dividing in spring, and figure out what new plants need to be bought. Sounds like a good way to spend the off-season to me!

Would a mini greenhouse or a cold frame be best for your garden needs this winter? Here's everything you need to know to decide…

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When the forecast drops below freezing for the first time in late fall, half the neighborhood rushes out to tuck bedsheets over their mums – unless they have a greenhouse, that is. But while most folk don't have the space or the budget for a full-size glasshouse, a mini greenhouse or cold frame is the affordable option to get plants through winter unscathed. But which is best when it comes to protecting plants from winter weather?

A mini greenhouse is a tall but narrow enclosure with wire-mesh shelves zipped inside a clear plastic cover. A cold frame is a low, bottomless box with a see-through lid that sits right on the dirt. Both catch sun all day, but they handle the night very differently, making the best one for you dependant on what you grow. And a Georgia winter is a very different beast from a Minnesota one, which affects how you winterize your garden in late fall.

Here's everything you need to know to make the right decision to protect your plants from frost and snow this winter.

Most mini greenhouses are made from a light steel frame with two to four tiers of wire-mesh shelves. This is covered with a PVC or polyethylene cover that zips up the front, or some designs have rigid polycarbonate panels, which is why they're often referred to as 'plastic greenhouses'. To vent, you unzip and roll up the door.

Mini greenhouses are cheap and give you a lot of growing space for a small footprint, but the plastic cover can wear out and be hard to replace, and not all products stand up to winter winds unless they're positioned in a sheltered spot. If you only use a mini greenhouse in winter, it's easy to pack up and store away for summer, or if you can remove the shelves then they're useful for growing tomatoes.

Cold frames are typically made from wood, aluminum or brick with a hinged glass or polycarbonate lid that can be propped open on warm days. Only holding one layer of pots, a cold frame and will only fit fairly low-growing plants. They generally cost more, unless you put your DIY skills to the test and build your own cold frame, but a sturdy design with a rigid lid lasts for years. A cold frame doesn't buy you any extra growing room, however.

Plants will usually come through a harsh 20°F (-7°C) night better in a cold frame than a mini greenhouse. Because the frame has an open base and sits directly on the ground, it benefits more from the heat of the sun. Soil soaks up the solar heat all day, which is why it's a good idea to prop the lid open a few inches on sunny days if temperatures rise above 40°F (4°C). But close the lid by late afternoon and the interior stays warm as the soil gives the heat back overnight, and the frame's solid sides slow the loss. For extra warmth, it's an easy task to bank straw or soil against the walls. too.

So, vegetables such as lettuce, spinach, kale and other winter greens will keep growing slowly under a cold frame lid into early winter. Low perennials and young transplants often do well too, and so do plants that rot when winter rain sits on their crowns.

Space is where a mini greenhouse wins over a cold frame. With several tiers of shelves, you can stack seedling trays, rooted cuttings and pots of hardy herbs in a space about the size of a doormat. However, a mini greenhouse sitting on paving has no soil to draw from, so it doesn't stay as warm overnight. While the interior still heats up in the day (so needs venting), thin plastic sides allow the warmth to quickly escape, so it doesn't take long for the air inside to drop to the same temperature as the air outside. A tall mini greenhouse catches every gust of wind, too, and cold air finds any gaps around zippers and seams.

If you have a sheltered sunny wall to stand a mini greenhouse against, however, that structure will absorb the sun's heat during the day and give it back through the night, helping to stabilize temperatures. Still, don't trust thin plastic in a hard freeze – but a mini greenhouse does a great job at keeping wind and rain off hardy container plants.

A mini greenhouse gives you extra growing space on a balcony or in a small urban garden, too.

When buying a cold frame, it's good to know that wood insulates better than metal if you live in a harsh climate. It's heavier, though, so if you want to be able to move your cold frame, then an aluminum frame also has the advantage it won't rot. Either way, look for a sturdy frame that doesn't wobble and a lid that props open at more than one height. Automatic venting is a useful upgrade if you're not at home during the day, as a temperature-activated hinge lifts the lid as the inside warms up.

Cedar wood frame, 3.5mm polycarbonate insulation and fully opening lid with venting positions.

Aluminum frame, 4mm polycarbonate panels and a collapsible design for easy summer storage.

Cedar and powder-coated steel, double-wall polycarbonate lid and temperature-activated automatic lid opening.

When buying a mini greenhouse, there's a balance to be had between budget and cover quality. A mini greenhouse with polycarbonate panels is more expensive but holds heat far better than a floppy plastic cover. If you opt for a cheaper flexible cover then look for one made of PE (polyethylene), preferably reinforced PE, rather than PVC.

PE stays flexible in freezing temperature and copes with long-term UV exposure well. PE that's reinforced with mesh also means any rips are easily fixed, and still lets in around 85% of sunlight. PVC (polyvinyl chloride) is usually clearer so lets more light through, but tends to split and yellow over time.

Look for a stiff, robust frame because a wobbly one means the cover flaps until the seams gape. It's vital that you can anchor the mini greenhouse down, too, and that the method used is suitable for the ground you plant to stand it on. Most designs will have base flaps that you can weigh down with bricks or stones, while some offer additional anchoring with ground stakes – useful if your garden is at all exposed.

Double-layer roof design for ventilation, UV-resistant PE cover and zip-up door. Measures 50" H x 27.6" W x 19.7" D.

Reinforced PE cover, mesh racks and 4 ropes and ground stakes. Measures 76.8" H x 57.9" W x 30.3" D.

4mm polycarbonate panels, roof vent, sliding door and rain gutter. Measures 71.65" H x 75.98" W x 27.16" D.

It's a simple task to upgrade a cold frame or mini greenhouse when winterizing your garden, and the cheap fixes go a long way. You could save bubble wrap to repurpose in the garden, clipping a layer inside the cover for an extra layer of trapped air. Always pick big bubbles since they generally insulate better, like this 24-inch-wide roll of large-bubble clear wrap from Amazon. Bubble wrap does cut some light, however, and packing-grade wrap breaks down in the sun faster than horticultural film.

On a bitter night, spreading frost cloth like this from Amazon over the plants inside also helps to insulate them, and it's easily pulled off in the morning.

A tall mini greenhouse can tip in strong wind, and even if anchoring stakes are included, they're usually flimsy. A shed anchor kit like this from Amazon with 18-inch ground screws and steel cable will do a much better job of holding your mini greenhouse down through winter weather.

If you mostly grow winter greens and low perennials, buy the cold frame since the open soil base and solid sides will give plants steadier nights. If you need plenty of space for seedlings, cuttings or taller pots, go with a mini greenhouse and expect bigger temperature swings.

Whichever you pick, park it in a sunny spot out of the wind, and hang a cheap digital max/min thermometer like this from Amazon in there so you know just what degree of winter protection your plants are getting. Neither a cold frame nor a mini greenhouse will protect frost-tender plants in severe cold weather without extra insulation or a safe heat source, so bring them inside before a hard freeze. And if you do add heat, do it carefully – a soil-heating cable on a GFCI outlet turns a cold frame into a hotbed, but keep heaters away from plastic and never run a fuel-burning heater in a small closed structure.

#7836. War Dogs of History: Chips

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

If Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

Chips was a mix of German Shepherd, Collie, and Husky, born around 1940 and raised as a family pet by Edward Wren and his family in Pleasantville, New York. In 1942, the Wrens donated Chips to the newly formed Dogs for Defense program, part of the Armyâs larger War Dog Program, formally authorized on March 13, 1942. Chips trained at the War Dog Training Center in Front Royal, Virginia, and was partnered with Private John P. Rowell. The two served in the 3rd Military Police Platoon, 30th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, under General George S. Patton.

Chips and Rowell landed in North Africa during Operation Torch in November 1942 and served through campaigns in Sicily, Italy, southern France, and the Rhineland and central European theaters. He was also present as a sentry dog at the 1943 Casablanca Conference, guarding the meeting between Winteon Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Chips earned his fame during the Allied invasion of Sicily, Operation Husky, on the morning of July 10, 1943. As Rowell and Chips came ashore, a hidden machine gun nest opened fire and pinned down their platoon. Chips tore free of his handler and charged the position alone, seizing the gunner by the throat and forcing the crew to surrender. As a result, four Italian soldiers surrendered. That same night, Chips alerted the platoon to ten additional enemy soldiers attempting to slip through the lines under cover of darkness, leading to their capture as well.

Chips did not escape the encounter unscathed. He suffered burns around his mouth and eye and a wound to his scalp. His actions, however, quickly became national news. Captain Edward G. Parr, the company commander, recommended Chips for the Distinguished Service Cross, citing his âcourageous action in single-handedly eliminating a dangerous machine gun nest and causing surrender of its crewâ. On November 19, 1943, Major General Lucian K. Truscott Jr. awarded Chips the Silver Star, and accounts differ slightly on whether the Distinguished Service Cross was also formally conferred or only recommended. What is well documented is that Chips also received a Purple Heart for his wounds.

In 1945, Chips met General Dwight (Ike) D. Eisenhower, who bent down to pet the famous dog. Chips, true to his sentry training, nipped the generalâs hand. The incident became one of the more good-humored footnotes in his legend.

Washington reacted less good-humoredly to the idea of a dog receiving human military honors. After public objection to the precedent of awarding animals medals intended for soldiers, the War Department revoked Chipsâs Silver Star, Distinguished Service Cross, and Purple Heart in early 1944. His platoon nonetheless unofficially awarded him a Theater Ribbon with Arrowhead, an honor reserved for assault landings, along with eight battle stars, one for each campaign in which he served. Chips was honorably discharged on December 10, 1945, and returned to the Wren family in Pleasantville. He died a few months after returning home, from complications related to his wartime wounds.

In January 2018, more than seven decades after his service, the United Kingdomâs PDSA posthumously awarded Chips its Dickin Medal, the animal equivalent of the Victoria Cross, in a ceremony at the Churchill War Rooms in London on the 75th anniversary of the Casablanca Conference. John Wren, then 76, traveled from the United States to accept the medal on Chipsâs behalf. PDSA Director General Jan McLoughlin remarked that the honor finally allowed Chips to âtake his place in the history books as one of the most heroic dogs to serve with the US Armyâ.

Chips is estimated to have been one of more than 10,000 dogs who served in the American military during World War II. His story, and the controversy his medals caused, shaped military policy for decades: no American war dog would again receive an official human combat decoration, a policy that held until working dogs began receiving other forms of formal recognition much later in the twentieth century.

Every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

Support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

Keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

Follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

These dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

Among the dogs of the 26th Infantry Scout Dog Platoon, one German Shepherd stood out for the length and success of its combat record. Scout Dog York is credited with taking part in 148 combat missions without a single man in his patrol being killed, a record that made him one of the war's most celebrated scout dogs.

Morgan Farr is a writer, graphic designer, and advocate who has spent her career telling the stories of working dogs and the people who love them. She serves as the Social Media Coordinator for both the Military Working Dog Heritage Museum and the National Service Animals Monument. She previously served as the social media manager for the U.S. Army Military Working Dog Program.

Together with her husband, an Army veterinarian, Morgan co-founded Canine Advancement Group, which offers education on canine wellness and welfare for both working and companion dogs. She is a member of the American Veterinary Medical History Society, the American Historical Association, the American Association for State and Local History, and the Society for Military History. In 2025, she was named the Armed Forces Insurance Military Spouse of the Year for Joint Base San Antonio.

At home, Morgan is a military spouse, a homeschooling mother of four, a small business owner of Dog-Eared Press, and a co-op instructor. She shares her household with a high-drive Dutch Shepherd and a spirited Bombay cat, who remind her daily that every animal, working or companion, deserves understanding, partnership, and thoughtful care.

You can find her across social media platforms using her handle @morgandfarrauthor.

#7834. Shrubs Steal the Show in Bonnie’s Colorado Garden

Hi GPOD! Yesterday we enjoyed some beautiful fall color in Nancy’s Massachusetts garden, and today we’re heading west to see what fall looked like in Colorado this year.

Bonnie took these photos in mid-November after an unusually long fall. While the trees certainly put on a show, Bonnie says the shrubs were the real stars this year. Here’s Bonnie:

Colorado put on a spectacular fall color display this year. My garden was filled with so many vivid hues that I had to capture them in photos. Some years are more colorful than others, and this was certainly a good one! The standout colors came not from the trees, but from the shrubs.

Welcome to my fall garden! Just walk through the arch and see the colors beyond. ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) starts in spring with dark burgundy leaves, turns green by late summer, and finishes the season in bright yellow. I love this tree!

Other stars in my fall garden are the barberries, hydrangeas, dwarf smokebushes (Cotinus coggygria cvs., Zones 4–8), and spireas. Oh, and the Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) in the back turned a lovely red this year.

Barberry, dwarf smokebush, and spireas in the back make a nice composition.

I’m in love with these ‘Annabelle’ smooth hydrangeas (Hydrangea arborescens ‘Annabelle’, Zones 3–9). They are all over my yard.

Another hydrangea vignette with viburnum, boxwood, and Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra, Zones 5–9) in front.

I love the beautiful colors of this barberry.

Around the other side of our yard, the dwarf smokebush shines among the evergreens and the orange leaves of the mountain ash and honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos, Zones 3–8) trees.

Looking toward the front yard, the dwarf smokebush steals the show!

A weeping Norway spruce (Picea abies, Zones 3–7) and barberry make a beautiful combination.

Thanks for sharing your beautiful fall garden with us, Bonnie! The trees are gorgeous, but I agree that the shrubs really stole the show this year.

Have photos to share? We’d love to see your garden, a particular collection of plants you love, or a wonderful garden you had the chance to visit!

#7832. Former Garden Center Manager Reveals the Gifts Gardeners Love – and the Ones They Secretly Hate

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Beautiful plants and ideas to brighten your garden.

Expert tips for growing fruit, vegetables and herbs at home.
