Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Skip the garden-themed trinkets and give them something they'll actually use. Here, I share the gifts gardeners really want (and the ones they'd rather skip).

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Buying a gift for the gardener on your list seems easy enough. Head to the garden center, find something cutesy with flowers on it, maybe a packet of seeds, add a few assorted tools, and call it a day. They’ll appreciate the thought behind any gift, of course, but if you want to make a gardener really happy, skip the cute and go for something useful.

After years of working with gardeners as a garden center manager and an avid gardener myself, I can tell you the gardening gifts they really want: boots that can handle mud, pruners that cut without a fight, and tools that solve a problem, hold up over time, or make the job easier. Gardening may be a hobby to some, but its actual work and the right tools make all the difference.

If you’re shopping for a gardener this year (or for yourself), let me share my garden center secrets to help you look past the gifts that merely look pretty in a gift bag and find the ones they’ll actually use, appreciate, and think of you every time they reach for them.

The pattern may be cute, but pretty garden shoes aren’t always cut out for real gardening tasks. They may not hold up long-term and may leak.

Give them real gardening boots that are waterproof, durable, comfortable, and warm enough for cold weather. We want something that can handle mud, wet grass, mulch, snow, and a full day outdoors without leaving our feet wet and miserable.

The boots from The Original Muck Boot Company check all of those boxes. Oh, and some have those cute prints, too!

This waterproof, easy-wear chore boot is built for gardening, yard work, and everyday outdoor tasks.

Gardeners do not need more tools that do just one thing. They want tools that earn their place in the shed and are useful for more than one task.

A hori hori knife is one of those tools they don’t realize how much they’ll use until they have one. It digs, weeds, cuts roots, transplants, divides plants, and tackles countless other jobs. It even has markings to help correctly plant or space seeds and bulbs. They will reach for this one over and over again.

Features both serrated and straight edge blades, and is a fantastic gardening and landscaping tool.

A Garden Weasel Oversized Potting Scoop, like this one from Amazon, is another multi-use tool that can be used for scooping soil, digging, planting, or even filling bird feeders with seed.

For gardeners who love wildlife, another basic, oddly shaped container to fill with seed isn't very exciting. They want to get more out of the experience than that.

Instead, bring the birds closer with a smart feeder that captures photos and videos of their feathered visitors. They'll practically get to know their daily regulars (and probably a few squirrels, too) up close, all from their phone or tablet, rather than having to wait around by the window.

The Kiwibit Solar Smart Bird Feeder With Camera is an upgraded, fully solar-powered model that captures 8MP photos and crisp 4K Ultra HD video, with real-time alerts when birds visit the feeder. Plus, it works with the Kiwibit app to identify more than 10,000 bird species.

If you're on a tighter budget, then the Birdfy Bird Feeder with Camera for Beginners offers Lifetime Bird ID and 2K HD for a great price.

The Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 works with the Kiwibit app to identify over 10,000 bird species with real-time alerts.

Just because the package shows a pair of pruners doesn't mean they're up to the task. Cheap pruners with dull blades can crush stems or struggle to cut even thin branches. They're frustrating for the average gardener and often end up in the trash after just a few uses.

Gift them a pair of sharp, quality bypass pruners. They don't even need to be expensive. Gardeners simply want a pair that makes clean cuts, feels comfortable in their hands, and lasts for years with just a little maintenance.

While the F-2 pruning shears from Swiss brand Felco, available here on Amazon, are a favorite among gardeners, the affordable 5/8-inch Fiskars Bypass Pruning Shears are also well-reviewed and happen to be one of my personal favorites.

Self-cleaning sap groove prevents sticking with a non-slip grip for cutting stems & branches.

Speaking of maintenance, they could also benefit from a quality sharpening tool to keep not only their pruners but also their loppers and hedge clippers in good working order, such as this Corona Blade Sharpener from Amazon

If you've spent the day pruning the thick, tough stems of panicle hydrangeas, fruit trees, or thorny roses, you know how quickly your hands can tire from the repetitive cutting. Gardeners don't need more tools that make these time-consuming jobs harder than they already are.

They want tools that save time and effort, such as cordless electric pruners, mini chainsaws, and other battery-powered garden tools that make repetitive tasks faster, easier, and less physically demanding. Many of these compact tools are small enough to fit right into a gardener's tool caddy, making them easy to carry around the yard and keep close at hand.

These types of tools can be a real game changer, especially for gardeners who spend hours tackling demanding pruning and trimming jobs.

Equipped with two rechargeable batteries, our cordless pruning shears provide extended runtime for continuous cutting.

Equipped with a WORKPROX 20V 2.0Ah battery, providing up to 30 minutes of continuous runtime.

2-in-1 functionality and a 5/16" cut capacity, making it ideal for trimming where other tools can't reach.

Gardening already involves plenty of bending, kneeling, and repeatedly getting up and down, especially when it comes to weeding. While there are plenty of weeding tools on the market, many still require gardeners to spend long periods bent over or kneeling. It's no wonder backs and knees start to ache!

Give gardeners a tool that lets them work smarter, not harder. Long-handled, stand-up weed pullers help take the strain off backs and knees while making it easier to tackle weeds without constantly bending, kneeling, or getting down on the ground. Their back will thank you!

Remove weeds without bending, pulling, or kneeling.

Cute gloves made of thin fabric with funny sayings and colorful floral prints may look good in a gift basket, but they don't necessarily get the job done. Ill-fitting, flimsy gloves offer little protection and often end up shoved in a drawer and forgotten. On the other hand, gloves that are too bulky can make even simple gardening tasks difficult.

What gardeners really want are gloves that fit properly, offer the right protection, and are comfortable enough to wear for hours.

Breathable gloves with a nitrile-coated palm provide excellent protection for all sorts of gardening jobs, from digging and pulling weeds to pruning roses and planting delicate seeds.

Look for pairs that fit well and come in bright, easy-to-spot colors. That way, when gardeners inevitably set them down and forget where they left them, they're much easier to find!

And here's a little gift-giving tip: Buy a set of four or more! Gardeners can never have too many pairs of gloves.

The unique form-fitting, ergonomic design fits like a second skin, allowing for unmatched precision.

Gnomes, gazing balls, and flower stakes can make wonderful gifts if you know the gardener collects them. But if you're not sure, yet another garden ornament may not be the best use of your money.

Consider giving them something functional, such as a comfortable garden kneeler that flips over into a cushion-lined seat. It makes planting, working close to the ground, and tending raised beds much more comfortable. Plus, having a place to sit and take a break is always welcome after a few hours in the garden!

Equipped with two large tool pouches, perfect for keeping your gardening tools conveniently within reach.

Those little novelty herb-growing kits that use a mason jar might be cute and offer a fun way to grow something during the winter, especially when gardening with kids. However, those small containers have limited room for roots and simply won’t produce a full, lush plant. Gardeners who enjoy growing their own fresh greens and herbs are likely looking for something a little more worthwhile and practical.

A good microgreens planter is a great option, allowing them to grow fresh, nutritious greens right in the kitchen or just about anywhere, regardless of the weather outside. It’s easy, practical, and provides something fresh to harvest week after week, even in the middle of winter.

Skip the dirt and daily watering—this planter is made for simple, indoor growing.

I’ve been really enjoying my EZ Microgreens Planters from Vego Garden. I had fresh greens ready to harvest in just a little over a week, even as temperatures started dropping here in Ohio.

I’d add in a few packets of high-quality microgreens seeds from Botanical Interests to complete this gift set.

Small hoop houses, low tunnels, and pint-sized greenhouses can certainly be useful, but flimsy covers that don’t hold up to the wind, offer very little protection, or barely provide any room to grow can leave gardeners wanting something bigger and better.

What they really want is a proper greenhouse or a well-built growing structure that can help extend the growing season, protect their plants, and give them more opportunities to grow in early spring and late fall. They want something with usable space and practical functionality, not just a flimsy cover that barely makes a difference. And if it looks gorgeous in the backyard, that's an added bonus!

Extend your growing season for half the price of other premium greenhouses.

For those who don't have the space or whose budget doesn't quite allow for a full-size greenhouse, a tiered, all-in-one greenhouse shelving unit, like this Home-Complete 4 Tier Mini Greenhouse with Locking Wheels and PVC Cover from Walmart, may do the trick. But let's be honest, they'll probably still be dreaming about that beautiful glass greenhouse!

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter so you never miss the best gardening deals. We check the latest sales and only recommend products we'd genuinely buy ourselves.

Amy Draiss, Digital Community Manager at Gardening Know How since 2021, seamlessly blends her hands-on gardening experience with a digital green thumb. With roots in family landscaping and management at a garden center, Amy has cultivated expertise in plants, supplies, and customer relations. Residing in the Midwest, Amy tends to her two-acre haven, showcasing a diverse range of trees, shrubs, and perennials. As the Hydrangea Queen, she shares her love for these blooms and imparts gardening wisdom through videos and social media. Beyond gardening, Amy enjoys quality time with her family, travel, and theme parks. Amy's mission is to inspire and advise plant enthusiasts, fostering flourishing gardens for both seasoned and budding gardeners alike.

Don't despair if your tree looks awkward when you get it home. A little strategic trimming can help – if you know what to cut, what to leave, and when to stop.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Unless you’re willing to settle for an artificial Christmas tree, you’re unlikely to find one that’s perfectly symmetrical. We've all been there: you choose one that looks promising at the lot, then get it home and discover it's too tall or wide for your living room – or simply looks much more awkwardly shaped than you remembered. It’s enough to make you open the bottle of sherry you left out for Santa.

All of the best Christmas tree care in the world won’t help with these shaping issues. But a little careful pruning can make a big difference. Here, we will explain the steps to trim a too-tall, too-wide, or lopsided Christmas tree into a balanced, attractive centerpiece. We’ll also lay out the tools you need and the techniques you should use.

Of course, knowing how to pick a Christmas tree with a good natural shape can save you some work in the first place. Before you begin trimming, remember that removing branches is much easier than putting them back. Work gradually, and try repositioning or fluffing branches before reaching for your pruners.

A beautifully shaped Christmas tree should have a straight central trunk, a strong top branch to support a star or angel, and evenly spaced branches that create a full, balanced appearance.

Commercial Christmas tree growers tend to encourage the classic conical Christmas tree shape through occasional pruning. They aim for a base width of around 60 to 70 percent of the tree's height, although a slimmer tree may be more practical for smaller rooms.

Branch density matters, too. Large gaps between branch tiers can make a tree look sparse, while more closely spaced tiers create a fuller appearance – though denser branch tiers mean less space to hang ornaments.

The first step, once you bring the new tree into your home, is to make a fresh, straight cut about half an inch (1.3 cm) from the base of the trunk. Some sellers will do this for you before you load it into your car, but it needs to be fresh. If you're doing it yourself, a pruning saw, like Fiskars' Pro 10-Inch Pruning Saw, available on Amazon, will make the job easier. Then, put the tree straight into a sturdy container of water. This is one of the most important steps to make your Christmas tree last longer and prevent premature needle drop.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Let the tree settle before doing any further trimming. Give the tree a few hours, or ideally overnight, to relax its branches. This is particularly important if the tree has been tightly wrapped in netting. Its branches need time to spread back into their natural positions, and what initially looks like an awkward gap or uneven section may become much less noticeable.

Once the branches have relaxed, walk around the tree and look at it from several angles. Identify any protruding branches, bare patches, or uneven growth before deciding what actually needs cutting.

You’ll need clean, sharp tools to prune a real Christmas tree into a pleasing cone shape. With the right tools and techniques, you can create a full, appealing tree no matter how tall, wide, or wonky it started out.

You can buy a hundred different tools for pruning trees, but you really don’t need more than a handful to prune a real Christmas tree. For smaller branches, a pair of budget-friendly pruners, like Fiskars Bypass Pruning Shears, will give you the control needed to make clean, precise cuts. For thicker branches, use loppers, like Corona ComfortGEL Bypass Loppers, which provide extra cutting power.

For cutting through the trunk, use a sharp pruning saw or handsaw. Make sure the cut is straight so the tree sits securely in its stand.

Is your Christmas tree too tall for your space? That’s usually one of the easiest Christmas tree problems to deal with, so don’t fret. First, measure your ceiling height, then subtract the height you need for the tree stand and tree topper, plus at least 1–2 inches (2.5–5 cm) of clearance. This is the perfect height for your new tree. Then measure the tree to see how much you need to remove.

If you only need a modest reduction (say, a few inches), cut the excess length from the bottom of the trunk. Just make sure enough bare trunk remains to fit securely into the stand without forcing the lower branches against its rim. Then put the tree into its stand – ideally one with a built-in water reservoir, like the Krinner Genie Christmas Tree Stand.

If your tree is significantly too tall, removing a large section of the trunk could also mean losing its attractive lower branches. In this case, you may need to shorten the central leader at the top instead. This is the upright shoot that forms the tree's tip.

Sometimes the leader is disproportionately tall and can easily be shortened without spoiling the tree's shape. Other times, cutting off the original tip can ruin its natural outline and remove the little knobbly buds and side shoots that help hold a tree topper in place. Indeed, it might be better to go without a topper rather than making a drastic cut. So treat trimming the tip of your Christmas tree as a last resort, and only if you think it will work with its natural shape.

If you do decide to take this step, trim the leader carefully to the desired height. Then assess the tree's new shape and, if necessary, selectively shorten the surrounding branches until you achieve a symmetrical, conical outline. Work gradually, stepping back regularly to check your progress.

When a tree is too wide to fit gracefully in your home, you can trim its branches. A traditionally shaped Christmas tree has a base width of around two-thirds its height. But it’s a good idea to measure the floor space where the tree will stand to make sure that the “ideal” shape will work for you.

Start by positioning the tree where you want it to stand and turning it to find the most attractive side. If branches at the back prevent it from fitting neatly against the wall, trim these first. Then, look at the tree from the front and sides, shortening any branches that stick out too far or spoil its overall shape.

Work gradually, removing a little at a time, and step back often to check the results. You don't need to trim every branch to the same length – the aim is to create a balanced, natural-looking tree that fits comfortably in its space.

For branches that genuinely need shortening, make cuts within the green, needle-covered portion of the growth. Avoid cutting too deeply into the bare, woody sections, as this can leave obvious gaps in the foliage that won't fill out.

Remember that different types of Christmas trees naturally have different shapes. Some firs have a dense, compact outline, while certain spruces and pines have more open branching. Work with the tree's natural form rather than trying to force every variety into exactly the same silhouette.

It’s easier to talk about a too-tall or too-wide Christmas tree than one that’s just kind of weird. Whether it's lopsided or just plain wonky, you can still improve that uneven Christmas tree shape to make it presentable.

First, check that the trunk is standing straight in its base. Sometimes a tree that looks lopsided simply needs adjusting in the stand rather than pruning.

To shape a lopsided Christmas tree, keep a cone shape in the front of your mind. Prune the upper branches shorter than the lower ones, and remember that the base width should be about two-thirds the tree's height. To achieve these goals, keep stepping back to see how things look.

Take off any dead or damaged branches, then clip back any that protrude too far and spoil the tree's outline. If one side is particularly dense, you can selectively shorten a few branches to create a more balanced appearance. Work gradually, as it's easy to remove too much.

Some unevenness comes from the way the tree grew. Christmas trees produce successive tiers of branches as they develop, and the amount of growth between these tiers influences how dense or open the finished tree appears. If one section has widely spaced branches, pruning alone won't necessarily make it look fuller.

Start by fluffing nearby branches or gently repositioning longer ones to disguise any gaps. You can also fold flexible branches into place and secure them with twine. If one side is woefully sparse, turn the tree so that this side is against the wall.

Alternatively, you can borrow a branch from a particularly dense area of the tree and use it to fill an obvious gap. Simply cut the branch and secure it to the trunk or a sturdy neighboring branch with green wire, like this Pauleen floral wire from Amazon, positioning it to blend in with the surrounding foliage. Make sure it's firmly attached before adding any decorations.

If you'd rather not cut branches from elsewhere on your tree, artificial Christmas tree filler branches or greenery picks can work just as well. Look for ones that closely match the color and texture of your tree's needles, like these Hananona faux pine branches, and tuck them into sparse areas to create a fuller, more balanced appearance.

You may also be able to disguise a sparse section by trimming back some of the heavier surrounding growth, helping the branches appear more evenly distributed. However, avoid cutting away too much greenery in an attempt to fill a gap – you could end up creating another one.

The only time you have to worry about a tree’s health is when it is alive. If you have a cut Christmas tree, it is no longer growing. That means that you do not have to worry about its health. Instead, trim the tree to fit well and look nice in your home.

However, excessive Christmas tree shearing can still affect its appearance and stability. Removing too many lower branches may leave the trunk exposed, while cutting away large sections of the crown can make it difficult to achieve a natural shape.

If, however, you buy a living Christmas tree you wish to plant, you do have to worry about keeping the tree healthy. Over-trimming can send the tree into shock or even kill it. The general rule is never to take off more than a quarter of the foliage annually. For most trimmings, stick to 10 percent.

Don't cut conifers back to the woody inner branches. Most will not sprout new needles from these branches. Limit your pruning to green, needle-bearing growth. The only exception is if you remove an entire branch back to the trunk.

If you're growing your own Christmas tree in the garden or keeping a living tree to use again in future years, pruning requires a different approach. Unlike a cut tree, a living evergreen needs to maintain healthy growth and develop a strong, balanced structure.

Young Christmas trees generally need only light corrective pruning during their first few years. This might involve removing damaged branches, correcting an uneven shape, or dealing with two competing upright shoots. Ideally, the tree should have one dominant central leader to maintain a straight trunk and a natural pointed crown.

More regular shaping can begin as the tree becomes established, often around its third growing season. For many Christmas tree species, growers carry out their main shearing once the new shoots have finished extending but before the fresh growth becomes fully firm. The timing varies according to the species and growing conditions.

For a living Christmas tree you hope to keep for years, though, it's best to prune conservatively. Focus on correcting problems rather than heavily shearing the entire tree, and always check the pruning requirements of the particular species you're growing.

Many people get overexcited when they start pruning a Christmas tree and are shocked to find out they have cut off too much. If this is you, take a breath. It’s only a Christmas tree. Resist the temptation to keep cutting elsewhere to even things up. A few strategically placed decorations will usually disguise the problem more effectively than further pruning.

If you have snipped a few times too many and created a bare spot (or two!), here are a few tips for covering up the damage:

As you move through the necessary pruning, you’ll want to keep these few key rules in mind:

She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#7828. When a Pet's Final Goodbye Becomes a Nightmare: The Philippines Crematorium Scandal

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

For families who have just lost a beloved pet, arranging cremation is often one of the last acts of love they can offer. They choose a service, pay for the arrangements, and believe that their companion will be treated with dignity and respect. They may never see what happens behind the crematorium doors, but they trust that their furry family member is in caring hands.

Sadly, for hundreds of families in the Philippines, that trust has been destroyed.

What began as a neighborhood concern over a foul smell quickly turned into a disturbing discovery. On October 29, 2026, residents of Barangay Minuyan in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan, were disturbed by a strong, suffocating, and foul odor coming from a nearby vacant lot. The terrible stink prompted a report and closer inspection, leading to the nightmare-worthy discovery of seven large sacks containing the remains of 26 dogs and three cats; each one wrapped in plastic bags bearing identification labels with their names and weights.

The investigation eventually led to Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium in Bacoor, Cavite, where many families had entrusted their deceased pets for cremation.

By November 4, authorities had recovered 29 animal carcasses, while 20 containers of ashes surrendered by families were undergoing forensic examination. The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is investigating possible fraud and other violations, and at least 250 pet owners have reportedly filed complaints against the company.

The questions are heartbreaking. Were these families given the ashes of their own pets? Were some animals never cremated at all? How did companions entrusted to a professional aftercare service end up in plastic bags beside a road?

For grieving pet owners, discovering that their furry family member's final arrangements may have been mishandled is an especially cruel betrayal.

Sadly, this is not the only case, or the only country, where fraud and deception have pervaded what should be a sacred service. In 2025, the Casa XibalbÃ¡ case in Quintana Roo, Mexico, exposed a similarly disturbing situation. Authorities investigating a Chetumal pet crematorium found that families had paid to have their beloved companions cremated, only to receive urns containing soil instead of their pets' ashes. Even worse, more than 180 animal carcasses were reportedly discovered during searches connected with the investigation. The case involved allegations of fraud and improper disposal of animal remains, with legal proceedings continuing into 2026.

Different countries, different businesses, but an eerily similar betrayal. And in both cases, the damage potentially reaches far beyond the families who were deceived.

Another disturbing side of these horrific stories is the environmental impact. Improperly discarded animal remains can create environmental hazards, particularly when several carcasses accumulate in unmanaged locations.

As tissues decompose, bodily fluids and organic material are released. These substances can contribute to leachate, a liquid that may move through soil with rainfall and drainage. Depending on soil conditions, groundwater depth, and proximity to wells or waterways, this can create pathways for environmental contamination.

Biohazardous runoff, odors, and potential groundwater pollution are among the concerns associated with improperly managed animal carcasses. If investigators discover that remains were repeatedly discarded at multiple locations, removing the visible carcasses may not be enough. Surrounding soil, drainage systems, and nearby water sources may also need assessment.

The deceived pet owners deserve justice, but residents also need answers about the conditions around their homes.

Exposed animal remains can attract scavengers, including free-roaming dogs, cats, and wildlife. Insects may also come into contact with decomposing material and potentially spread infectious agents between locations.

Not every deceased animal carries an infectious disease, and finding carcasses does not automatically mean disease will spread. However, when the cause of death is unknown, there may be no way to determine whether the remains contain infectious agents that could expose other animals.

There is another potential hazard that pet owners may not immediately consider: euthanasia medications.

Pentobarbital, commonly used for humane euthanasia in veterinary medicine, can remain in an animal's tissues after death. Wildlife that consumes the remains of an animal euthanized with this drug can suffer secondary poisoning, with scavenging birds being particularly vulnerable.

And this is where the consequences can extend much further. Scavengers play an essential role in maintaining healthy ecosystems by removing animal carcasses before they become sources of environmental contamination and disease transmission. Vultures, for example, can consume remains that might otherwise attract other scavengers or allow infectious agents to persist in the environment. When scavenger populations decline, carcasses can remain accessible for longer, potentially increasing opportunities for pathogen transmission and disease spread.

A carcass that should have been cremated could therefore become a source of danger to another animal. The irony is that the very animals helping keep ecosystems clean could be exposed to a potentially lethal drug simply because someone failed to dispose of a pet's remains responsibly.

The scandals also raise questions about oversight of the pet aftercare industry. A business permit cannot demonstrate that every animal entrusted to a facility has been handled properly.

Families should be able to expect accountability throughout the process, from collection and identification to transportation, cremation, and the return of ashes. Records should establish which animal was received, where it was taken, and what happened to its remains.

The Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) says the case has also highlighted a potential legal gap. According to the organization, the alleged deception may not fall directly under the Animal Welfare Act because the animals were already deceased when entrusted to the crematorium. However, the alleged conduct may constitute âestafaâ, or fraud by deceit, under the Revised Penal Code.

Affected families have been encouraged to preserve receipts, cremation certificates, photographs, messages, and other documentation that could support their complaints.

The Casa XibalbÃ¡ case in Mexico revealed a similarly disturbing situation, with more than 180 animal carcasses reportedly discovered and families allegedly receiving urns filled with soil instead of their pets' ashes. Two countries, two scandals, and far too many grieving families betrayed by businesses they trusted.

The death of a beloved pet is already a difficult time. Families make end-of-life decisions, discuss euthanasia with their veterinarians, arrange transportation, and decide how they would like to remember their companions.

For some, receiving an urn containing their pet's ashes brings comfort. It becomes something tangible to keep beside a favorite photograph or in a special place at home. And while emotional cost is the most painful aspect for the affected pet owners, itâs also worth noting that individual cremation usually comes at a premium price; a price paid for a service not performed. But regardless of whether these pets were to have undergone individual or commingled cremation, families deserve honesty about the service they purchase.

They should never have to question whether the ashes they brought home belong to their furry family member.

There is something particularly upsetting about the possibility that an animal cherished throughout life, treated as family, and surrounded by affection could have its remains handled so carelessly.

People entrust pet aftercare providers with something deeply personal. They are saying goodbye to someone they loved. That deserves respect.

All it takes is a few thoughtful tweaks to turn your yard into a pit stop for these beautiful birds...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Long tied to forest and earth deities, woodpeckers are some of the most fascinating (and symbolically-laden) birds to welcome into your backyard.

That's right, folks; the birth month bird for August babies everywhere, the woodpecker represents curiosity, persistence, and determination. (And don't even get us started on what it means if they're the first bird you spot on January 1st!).

Whether you believe in that or not, though, there's no denying that woodpeckers are considered one of the world's most popular birds for a reason... so, yes, it makes sense you'd like to befriend one!

Oh sure, they might seem like woodland-only visitors, but there are actually several things you can do to encourage woodpeckers into your yard. In fact, whether you're hoping to spot a great spotted woodpecker, downy woodpecker, or another local species, a few simple changes can make your outdoor space a more welcoming place.

Suet is one of the easiest foods to use to attract woodpeckers, especially during colder months when birds need extra energy and natural food sources become harder to find. Make sure, though, that you use a sturdy suet feeder designed to allow clinging birds to feed comfortably, and position it somewhere quiet where birds feel safe.

You should also take care to choose quality suet cakes (you want the kind with seeds or nuts in!) and keep feeders clean. It may take a wee bit of time and patience for woodpeckers to discover your new offering, but once they find a reliable food source, they may return regularly.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Suet isn't the only food worth serving, as woodpeckers also enjoy peanuts and sunflower seeds, particularly black oil sunflower seeds, so long as you pop them in the sort of feeders that allow woodpeckers to perch or cling while feeding. (They don't like it one bit when you scatter food across the ground).

As ever, we must stress that you should never offer salted or flavored nuts to wildlife.

It's all well and good teasing them in, but if you want woodpeckers to stick around, you need to think beyond feeders. And the best way to do this? By planting trees that provide insects, places to forage and shelter in abundance, of course!

Take care to choose a tree that suits your available space and growing conditions, and remember that even a young tree can contribute to a more wildlife-friendly garden over time. Something like an oak is an excellent long-term habitat investment, while a birch offers lots of opportunities for birds to search for insects.

A smaller ornamental tree that offers spring flowers, berries for birds, and beautiful fall color is also a good option for gardens with less room. Something like a serviceberry could work really well!

I've said it before and I'll say it again, but a perfectly tidy garden isn't necessarily the most wildlife-friendly one. Dead branches, logs and tree stumps might not be the prettiest to look at (although that's changing; they've been stealing the spotlight at the RHS Chelsea Flower Show across the pond for years) but they can provide valuable habitat for insects and other invertebrates that woodpeckers forage for.

If you have a dead tree or limb that can safely remain, then, consider leaving it in place rather than removing it automatically. You could also create a small log pile or stumpery in a quiet corner of your yard. As the wood decays, it can add visual interest and become a bug buffet for woodpeckers and other birds.

If you'd love to attract green woodpeckers in particular, consider giving your lawn a little more freedom, as these birds are particularly fond of ants ; in fact, they love nothing more than to use their long tongues to dig into nests and crevices to sccop them out and gobble them up.

Avoid pesticides, then, and leave a patch of grass to grow longe if you can. You don't need to abandon lawn care completely, but creating a less manicured patch? It will encourage much more natural wildlife activity.

Just like other backyard birds, woodpeckers need fresh water for drinking and bathing. A shallow birdbath with gently sloping sides is a must, then, especially during hot weather or when natural water sources freeze.

Be sure to pop it somewhere relatively quiet, with nearby trees or shrubs where birds can retreat if startled, but without dense cover immediately beside it where predators might lurk. A fine balance to strike, but a vital one, as I'm sure you'll agree.

Look, attracting woodpeckers isn't about transforming your yard overnight. By providing reliable food, planting trees, preserving natural habitat and offering fresh water, though, you can make your outdoor space a place where wildlife feels welcome. And when that distinctive drumming or flash of color finally catches your eye? Well, then you'll know the effort was all worth it.

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

#7826. Paws Off the Stuffing: A Guide to Safe Thanksgiving Foods for Dogs

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Letâs face it: despite its somewhat complicated and controversial history, these days,Thanksgiving is built around food, which makes it one of the trickiest holidays for dogs that want to join you around the table, since many common dishes contain ingredients that are toxic to them. Some foods are fine to share in small amounts, while others can cause anything from an upset stomach to life-threatening illness. Knowing which is which makes it easy to include a dog in the day without risking an emergency.

Turkey is safe and healthy for dogs, with a few conditions. The skin is fatty and usually coated in bastings and spices, and too much fat can lead to obesity and pancreatitis. Turkey bones can splinter and damage a dogâs mouth and digestive tract, so they should be avoided. Seasonings, including salt, can cause toxicity, so processed turkey should be skipped too. Plain meat is the safe choice, with no sauces or gravy.

Plain pumpkin is considered healthy, which is why so many dog foods contain it. Canned or fresh both work, provided the canned kind isnât pre-seasoned and nothing has been added. Pumpkin pie, with its spices and sugar, is a definite no.

Sweet potatoes are full of nutrients and vitamins, but they should be cooked and served in small amounts, without marshmallows, seasoning, or butter. Green beans offer vitamins, fiber, and manganese. They can be steamed, raw, canned, or cooked, as long as they are plain and not part of a casserole.

Corn is healthy without butter or salt, but only if it's been taken off the cob. Corn cobs are a relatively common source of intestinal blockage in dogs. Carrots, celery, and peas are fine cooked or raw and unseasoned, and carrots and celery should be cut into bite-sized pieces to prevent choking.

Plain cranberries are safe in moderation, though cranberry sauce and juice contain too much sugar. If they come from a dried fruit pack, only the cranberries should go to the dog. Apple slices are healthy and tasty, but the core and seeds should go in the trash. The seeds contain small amounts of cyanide that wonât harm a dog unless it eats too many, but itâs best to be cautious. The pie is for the people.

Cheese makes a tasty treat unless a dog is lactose intolerant, and low-fat versions suit dogs watching their weight. A small piece of plain bread is safe unless the dog has a grain allergy. It should have no raisins, seeds, or nuts, and since bread offers few nutritional benefits, it should only be an occasional snack.

Onions are highly toxic to dogs, along with everything in the onion family, including shallots, chives, and leeks, as they can cause anemia and liver damage. Garlic should also be avoided, and garlic powder is especially potent. It can also cause anemia, among other problems, so it shouldnât be anywhere near your pet.

Stuffing is also off limits. It usually contains onion, and it often carries a large amount of butter, which makes it too fatty for a dogâs diet. Mashed potatoes are fine if completely plain, but most are made with plenty of salt, butter, and other ingredients that arenât good for dogs, so itâs best to skip them. Gravy is a problem because of its high sodium, and it usually contains onions or garlic.

Chocolate is toxic because of two chemicals, theobromine and caffeine. It can lead to death if left untreated, and the signs can appear relatively quickly. Caffeinated drinks are risky for the same reason. Dogs are smaller and lighter than people, so it doesnât take much caffeine to cause trouble, and that rules out coffee, tea, and soft drinks.

Yeast-based bread dough is dangerous even though small amounts of baked bread are fine. The yeast expands in a dogâs stomach and can lead to bloat, which can progress to a life-threatening condition called gastric dilatation-volvulus. Alcohol of any kind causes poisoning in dogs, whether itâs a drink, rubbing alcohol, or hand sanitizer.

A final but deadly ingredient to be aware of is the artificial sweetener, xylitol. Sometimes listed as birch sugar, even in small amounts, this seemingly minor ingredient causes severe hypoglycemia, and even if dogs survive this, irreversible liver damage can finish them off. Always keep an eye out for this one, commonly included in sugar-free mints, gums, candy, and peanut butter, to name a few.

A dog caught eating something toxic needs to go straight to a vet or the nearest emergency animal clinic. Bringing the packaging, along with a sample of whatever the dog ingested, helps the vet treat that particular substance. When itâs unclear whether something was toxic, the ASPCA Animal Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 and the Pet Poison Helpline at (855) 764-7661 can help. Both charge a fee, but they can guide the next steps and get a pet immediate help.

When it comes to ingested toxic ingredients, timing is everything. If you know your dog has eaten something potentially dangerous, or even if you just suspect it, donât wait for clinical signs to appear. By then, it may already be too late. Far better to pay for an overcautious detox than risk the life of a four-legged family member.

Thanksgiving can be enjoyable for the whole family, dogs included, as long as ingredients and leftovers arenât left out for a dog to gobble down. Be familiar with ingredients that are harmful to pets, particularly anything toxic. A little care with what gets shared keeps the day safe and lets everyone relax.

#7825. Connie’s Garden in Griffin, Georgia

Hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Griffin, Georgia, for an update from Connie Raines. We first visited Connie’s garden shortly after she moved into her new home and transplanted many of her plants. Now, a little over a year later, she’s back with a few highlights from spring and late summer. Here’s Connie:

I have lived in this house and garden for a little over a year. When I moved here, I worked hard to transplant many of my plants, and the garden continues to be a work in progress.

Delphinium (Delphinium cvs., Zones 3–7) with coleus (Coleus scutellarioides, annual)

Native swamp rose mallow (Hibiscus moscheutos, Zones 5–9) and zinnias

Perennial begonia (Begonia grandis, Zones 6–9), a soft mahonia bush just planted this spring, and amaranth

A watermelon my husband grew in our garden area created by a new stepped retaining wall.

A work in progress… I transplanted this hearts-a-bustin’ (Euonymus americanus, Zones 6–9) from a different spot where I originally had it. It was crowded in and now will be able to spread out.

This celosia (Spicata group) actually grew from seeds of plants that were in a pot last summer. The ground in this area is where a tree used to be, and the roots are rotting and creating wonderful soft soil.

Thanks for sharing another update from your garden, Connie! And I have to know: What variety of watermelon did your husband grow? It’s huge and oblong! I hope it was delicious. Looking forward to the next update! 🙂

If you're wondering how to protect plants from the winter weather, start by winterizing these favorites for plenty more flowers next summer.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With winter just around the corner, your garden is busy adjusting to the changes in light and temperature and, while some plants won’t fail to return next year, others are more vulnerable and need your help to survive. Many of our favorite flowering plants are the most susceptible to harm from changing temperatures, deep freezes and drying winter winds, so if you want lots of blooms again next year, give them the winter protection they need.

Some of these garden stalwarts are tender perennials that simply won't survive outdoors in winter, while others are technically hardy but still a little vulnerable, so overwintering these plants well is vital. From protecting shrubs growing in the ground to digging bulbs up to take indoors, here's how to protect plants through winter so they wake up healthy in spring, ready for another bumper season of blooms.

Dahlias are some of the most varied and prized flowers of a late summer and fall garden, but they’re really only hardy in zones 8 through 11. Their tuberous roots are susceptible to getting mushy in wet conditions and frozen in cold winter ground so leaving them in the ground is risky, especially in zones 6 and colder.

The best way to protect these plants for flowers next year is to lift dahlia tubers out of the ground after the first deep frost blackens the foliage. Cut the stems back to a couple inches, then carefully dig around and lift out the crown and tubers. Let these dry for a few days to cure and then store dahlia tubers in a box of wood shavings – a compressed bale of natural pet bedding such as this from Amazon is a cheap and convenient way to buy. Keep the box in a cool but frost-free, dry storage area such as an unheated garage, and you'll overwinter dahlias to replant next spring.

Another plant that benefits from lifting is canna, which is only generally hardy in zones 7 through 10 because it grows from rhizomes that are vulnerable in freezing winter ground. Exact hardiness depends on the variety, so know your type and growing zone.

Once the foliage has blackened after a frost, cut the stems back to four to six inches (10 to 15 cm) and then carefully dig up canna rhizomes to store for the winter. As with dahlias, it’s best to let these dry for a few days before storing them in a material like wood shavings. Overwinter canna rhizomes in a dark, cool and dry storage area until spring weather has warmed up enough to replant them outdoors.

One of the most popular hydrangeas for its bright blue or pink flowers, bigleaf hydrangeas, also known as mophead hydrangeas, are typically hardy in zones 5 through 9. However, while the shrubs themselves cope with cold weather just fine, the issue with overwintering hydrangea shrubs that flower on old wood is the potential damage to next year’s flower buds that have developed before winter arrives. A cold snap can damage these buds, reducing the number of flowers you get next summer.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

To protect hydrangea buds, you’ll need to do more than simply covering the roots zone with mulch. Place four stakes in a square around the shrub and wrap burlap like this from Walmart for protection. In a very cold climate, increase the insulation by filling the space between the burlap and the plant with dry leaves.

Hybrid tea roses can be hardy from zones 4 through 9, but there is some variation by cultivar, and they're still a little vulnerable to cold weather compared to other types of roses. So, to overwinter roses in a region with a harsh climate, give them some winter protection to ensure they make it through to spring in a healthy state, ready for strong growth.

Your roses are vulnerable to damage caused by freeze-thaw cycles in the soil and winter damage to canes. First, clean up any plant debris on the ground to reduce the risk of disease, then loosely tie the canes together for extra support in damaging winter winds. Mound soil or compost around the base of the plant and for a final layer of insulation, top with a natural mulch such as Miracle-Gro All Natural Mulch, available from The Home Depot.

Rosemary is a Mediterranean herb that's generally hardy in zones 8 through 10. The best way to overwinter rosemary in colder climates is to bring it inside: trying to protect this plant outside with mulch is risky as it's very susceptible to wet, cold soil and drying winter winds. However, using a mulch is helpful in zones 7 or 8 to give the roots a little extra insulation.

In colder areas, dig up your rosemary plant and move it into a pot that you can bring it indoors. Even better, grow rosemary in a pot year-round as it won’t appreciate being dug out of the ground once established. This Mediterranean herb is one of those plants that grow better in terracotta pots because of the well-drained conditions the porous clay walls create. And because the pot won't be left outside in freezing temperatures, a cheap terracotta planter like this from Lowe's is all you need.

Rosemary doesn't tolerate soggy roots so to improve drainage, mix perlite like Back to the Roots Organic Perlite, available from Walmart, into any all-purpose potting mix at a ratio of 1:3. Indoors, give your potted plant a cool, bright spot and avoid overwatering.

Species and varieties of Colocasia and Alocasia offer large, striking, tropical leaves in summer but are only hardy in zones 8 through 11. Elephant ears grow from corms (large underground structures similar to tubers) which should be dug up for winter in colder growing zones.

To store Elephant ear corms over winter, let the foliage die back after a frost, then cut back the stems and leaves. Dig around the corm and lift it from the ground, allowing it to dry for up to two weeks before storing in wood shavings in a cool, dry spot. If your Elephant ear is growing in a pot, and small enough, the other option is bring it indoors for winter. While some types can be kept actively growing to enjoy as a houseplant, it's more usual to trim and overwinter tropical plants indoors in a semi-dormant state in a bright but cool spot.

Many salvias are winter hardy up to zone 3, but in regions with cold winters, more tender varieties are usually grown as annuals. Alternatively, you can try to protect these tender salvia varieties like Brazilian sage or gentian sage from winter weather, and this strategy works best in borderline zones like 6 or 7.

To overwinter tender salvias outside, use a thick layer of an airy natural mulch such as long-needle pine straw mulch like this from Amazon around the root zone and crown. In a more exposed garden, bark chips like these Pine Mulch Nuggets, also from Amazon, are heavier but create the same airy conditions. Leave the stems in place as they're hollow and trap air that can help insulate the crown.

If you're growing tender salvias in containers, simply bring them inside for the winter, placing them in a spot with bright light and reduce watering as growth will slow.

Timing for winter protection depends on the plant and your local climate and weather in your USDA zone. Tender plants should be brought inside before the first frost, but for plants that grow from tubers, rhizomes or corms that need lifting from the ground, wait until after the first deep frost.

For mostly hardy perennials that simply need a little protection to remain healthy outside, you need to strike a balance between acting before the ground freezes and waiting until the plant goes dormant. Insulating these plants from the cold by mulching or covering too early can delay dormancy and encourage growth that's quickly damaged once temperatures drop.

Protecting your precious plants before winter arrives isn't complicated or difficult. You simply need to know what you're growing and how the plants tolerate your local winters, then protect them accordingly. A little effort now will reward you next year with strong new growth as soon as temperatures rise in spring, and an abundant display of flowers.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

#7823. War Dogs of History: York and the 26th Infantry Scout Dog Platoon

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

The Korean War is often called Americaâs Forgotten War, with the dogs who served in it forgotten right along with it. Yet one platoon, and one dog in particular, quietly reshaped how the military would think about scout dogs for the rest of the twentieth century.

When North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950, the United States military had almost nothing left of the war dog program that had served so effectively in World War II. After 1945, the Army had gutted its dog units, and only one platoon, the 26th Infantry Scout Dog Platoon (26th ISDP), based first at Fort Riley, Kansas, survived intact. Before the war, this platoonâs main job was public demonstrations that showcased military dog capabilities to American audiences.

Scout dogs in Korea were not attack dogs in the way many people imagine war dogs to be. Their central task was to give a silent alert, typically by freezing, raising their hackles, or pointing, when they detected enemy soldiers ahead of a patrol, at an observation post, or forward of the front lines. Nearly all of these patrols took place at night, when human senses were least reliable, and the risk of walking into an ambush was highest.

Over the course of the war, the 26th ISDP conducted more than 1,500 combat patrols. A Review of after-action reports credited scout dog teams with reducing casualty rates among the patrols they accompanied by 65 percent, an extraordinary figure for a single battlefield innovation.

The dogs became well known, even feared, on the other side of the line, too. Historical accounts describe Chinese forces using loudspeakers along the front to broadcast messages to American troops that reportedly included the line, âYankee, take your dog and go home!â

Among the dogs of the 26th ISDP, one German Shepherd stood out for the length and success of its combat record: Scout Dog York, service number 011X. York is credited with taking part in 148 combat missions without a single man in his patrol being killed, a record that made him one of the war's most celebrated scout dogs.

Other dogs in the platoon earned similar renown. Arlo, another German Shepherd, is remembered for helping his patrol avoid what is believed to have been a near-certain ambush. Handler accounts and unit histories also mention dogs named Happy, Champ, and Hasso as part of the platoonâs roster of effective scout teams during the conflict.

The 26th ISDP served in Korea from June 1951 until the July 1953 armistice. Over that time, its members, both human and canine alike, were awarded a total of three Silver Stars, six Bronze Stars for Valor, and thirty-five Bronze Stars for Meritorious Service. On February 27, 1953, the Department of the Army formally recognized the platoonâs accomplishments in General Order No. 21.

Unlike the individual medal controversies that followed Chips during WWII, official recognition of the Korean War scout dogs came largely through unit citations rather than personal decorations for the animals themselves, an approach that seems to have avoided the same public dispute over honoring dogs with human military awards.

Before the Korean War, the scout dog program had all but disappeared. In 1946, the Armyâs Committee on Organization at Fort Benning debated whether to keep infantry war dog platoons active. Committee chairman Brigadier General Frederick McCabe recommended retaining them and attaching them to infantry training units; a recommendation that was largely ignored. Instead, the Quartermaster Corps shifted toward purchasing dogs directly from breeders rather than sustaining a broader loan program with the public. Had the 26th ISDP not survived this postwar contraction, the United States might have entered Korea with no scout dog capability at all.

The success of the 26th ISDP in Korea, epitomized by dogs like York, helped ensure scout dogs would never again be allowed to disappear from the Armyâs order of battle as they had after 1945. When American forces deployed to Vietnam a little more than a decade later, the Army reactivated its scout dog program in 1965, drawing directly on lessons learned in Korea.

Every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

Support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

Keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

Follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

These dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

He had just been shot through the face. He had lost an eye.

And still, Nemo crawled back to his wounded handler and lay across him, guarding him from anyone who came near.

This is the story of the Vietnam War's most famous sentry dog.

Morgan Farr is a writer, graphic designer, and advocate who has spent her career telling the stories of working dogs and the people who love them. She serves as the Social Media Coordinator for both the Military Working Dog Heritage Museum and the National Service Animals Monument. She previously served as the social media manager for the U.S. Army Military Working Dog Program.

Together with her husband, an Army veterinarian, Morgan co-founded Canine Advancement Group, which offers education on canine wellness and welfare for both working and companion dogs. She is a member of the American Veterinary Medical History Society, the American Historical Association, the American Association for State and Local History, and the Society for Military History. In 2025, she was named the Armed Forces Insurance Military Spouse of the Year for Joint Base San Antonio.

At home, Morgan is a military spouse, a homeschooling mother of four, a small business owner of Dog-Eared Press, and a co-op instructor. She shares her household with a high-drive Dutch Shepherd and a spirited Bombay cat, who remind her daily that every animal, working or companion, deserves understanding, partnership, and thoughtful care.

Grow fresh herbs and veggies at home, whatever the season. Our experts reveal which indoor gardens make it easiest – and which are worth buying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you love home cooking, then what could be more appealing than picking fresh herbs and lettuce leaves – or even flavorful cherry tomatoes or chilis – right from your kitchen countertop? The best indoor garden systems let you grow your own organic produce year-round, even when it’s freezing outside. And unlike a backyard veggie garden, they take up hardly any space: just a small corner near a free power outlet.

Offering features like built-in grow lights, automated watering, and often hydroponic setups, indoor growing systems make it easy to produce fast and surprisingly substantial harvests. Prices, features, and growing capabilities vary considerably, but most systems are straightforward to use and designed with beginners in mind. Some models have a small footprint, while others offer more capacity for bigger harvests.

With so many systems to choose from, finding the right one for your needs can be confusing. The Gardening Know How team has tested some of the leading models and shares firsthand experiences with setup, growing performance, maintenance, and harvesting in this guide. We will help you compare the models, identify the features that matter most, and choose the best system for your space, budget, and growing ambitions.

Here we round up three of the best indoor garden systems. Scroll down to read more detailed reviews from testing each product hands-on. You can also use the links to jump to the indoor garden that interests you the most.

If you're new to indoor growing, the Click & Grow Smart Garden 9 is an easy way to get started, ideal for fresh herbs, salad greens, and even dwarf tomatoes. With automatic lighting and self-watering capability, it uses pre-seeded pods, making it easy to get started and delivering great results. Just bear in mind that the replacement seed pods add to the ongoing cost.

The Auk Mini combines a compact footprint with a stylish Scandinavian-inspired design, making it ideal for smaller kitchens (especially if you're fond of the IKEA aesthetic). It's exceptionally easy to use, and you can grow your own choice of seeds without buying special pods. With room for just four plants, though, it's better for fresh herbs as opposed to more substantial harvests.

If you love the idea of enhancing your growing with the latest tech, then the LetPot LPH-Max is the indoor garden for you. This impressive hydroponic system fits a variety of herbs, greens, and vegetables. Its advanced smart features offer plenty of control, but setup can be fiddly for some users, and some automated functions require extra equipment.

Drawing on our extensive gardening experience, we evaluated each system for ease of setup and use, build quality, efficiency, crop performance, and overall value for money. Each reviewer tested their indoor garden for at least eight weeks in their own kitchen, assessing everything from initial setup to ongoing maintenance and harvesting. As the systems were tested by different experts in their own homes, growing conditions varied slightly, but all reviewers followed the same assessment criteria.

From stylish, compact designs to more advanced hydroponic systems, here's how they performed in our kitchens – and who we'd recommend them for.

After four months of testing the Click & Grow Smart Garden 9, I can honestly say it's so low-maintenance it feels illegal. Setup took about 10 minutes, including time to read the instructions. Growing tomatoes, lettuce, herbs, and flowers is as easy as loading a coffee pod into a capsule machine: just pop the pre-seeded pods into the reusable grow cups and click them into place. It's completely mess-free, and the built-in grow light means you don't need a sunny windowsill.

Watering is just as easy. I refill the reservoir about once a week, and the system handles the rest. A handy water-level indicator takes away the guesswork. I even went out of town for two weeks, and my plants kept growing without any care.

I grew basil, lettuce, dwarf tomatoes, and marjoram. The lettuce grew quickly and made delicious summer salads, and the basil brought wonderful flavor to my Italian dishes. I was most impressed, though, by the cherry tomatoes. I transplanted a few spare seedlings into standard pots under grow lights, but the Smart Garden tomatoes grew much larger and produced fruit about two months earlier.

The only disappointment was the marjoram. It sprouted well but barely grew, possibly because the larger basil and tomato plants blocked its light.

Overall, the Smart Garden 9 has been a really fun, easy, and delicious project. Its sleek design looks great in my kitchen, and I'd highly recommend it to beginners or experienced gardeners looking for a hassle-free way to grow fresh produce year-round.

Reviewed by Kathleen Walters. Read the full review for more details.

The Auk Mini is easily one of the most stylish indoor growing systems I've come across. With its sleek Scandinavian design featuring wooden supports and a choice of black or white finishes, it's a world away from the more clinical-looking hydroponic systems on the market. You can also choose from three base finishes – cork, oak, or walnut – so it's easy to find one that looks at home in your kitchen.

Setting it up couldn't have been simpler. I just pushed the wooden supports into either side of the base, threaded through the power cable, and attached the adjustable grow light on top. Then it was a case of filling each of the four mini planters with the supplied coco coir and planting the seeds. Mine came with basil and parsley, so I was ready to start growing straight away. Adding the coir was a little messy, and there aren't any convenient pre-seeded pods like you get with some other systems. However, the big advantage is that you can use whatever seeds you like (within reason), rather than being tied to a brand's refills.

The water reservoir has an indicator that tells you when it's full or needs refilling, and you also get two little bottles of nutrients labeled Grow and Flavor – which felt delightfully Alice in Wonderland! You just pump these into the reservoir as directed. The grow light has different settings and a timer, and I particularly liked being able to position it low over the seedlings, then raise it as the herbs grew taller.

Within six to seven weeks, I was harvesting fresh herbs, which was very pleasing. I also loved how neat and self-contained the whole system was once it was set up. It's attractive enough to leave out on display rather than hide away in a utility room, and it has taken pride of place on my kitchen countertop.

The main limitation is its size. With room for just four plants, it's really designed for growing a few fresh herbs rather than producing substantial harvests. But if you want something compact, easy to use, and great-looking, then the Auk Mini is a lovely choice. There's now a newer Mini 2, but the original Mini is still available while stocks last.

The LetPot LPH-Max makes it easy to grow plenty of edible plants indoors year-round. With 21 small pods and an alternative tray for two larger plants, you can grow practically a whole garden right in your kitchen. It's mess-free, too – no dirt required. Just fill the tank with water, add plant food, and sow your seeds in the sponge-like pods.

The system was pretty easy to set up, though it took me about an hour to read the directions and work out how everything fit together. I was genuinely shocked by how well my basil grew in just water and plant food. Hydroponics is kind of amazing!

However, I did run into a few frustrations. I wanted to try the automatic watering and feeding, but it requires an extra 7-liter reservoir to refill the tank. With a rambunctious cat, limited space, and newly refinished hardwood floors, that wasn't practical, so I used manual mode instead. The top tray didn't fit properly, and I was also disappointed that seeds weren't included.

Ultimately, I think the LetPot LPH-Max is a good choice for those with hydroponics experience or who enjoy integrating technology into gardening. The app provides helpful growing information and remote controls, though a few features didn't work as expected. For beginners or anyone short on space, I'd recommend starting with a simpler system.

Reviewed by Laura Walters. Read the full review for more details.

The AeroGarden Harvest is a compact, beginner-friendly hydroponic system that grows up to six herbs, vegetables, or flowers, with a 20W LED grow light, automatic lighting, and handy reminders for adding water and nutrients.

The Ahopegarden Hydroponic Growing System has a double-layer design that offers a space-efficient alternative to other countertop gardens, with space for 44 pods.

The iDOO Hydroponic Growing System packs plenty of features into an affordable countertop garden, including Wi-Fi app control, adjustable LED grow lights, automatic timers, and a built-in fan and water pump, with space to grow up to 12 plants.

Indoor garden systems can make it easy to grow fresh herbs, salad greens, and even vegetables, but there's quite a difference between compact countertop systems and larger, fully automated hydroponic systems. Before buying, think about what you want to grow, how much space you have, and how much time you're willing to spend looking after your plants. These are the main things to consider.

Start by deciding where to position your indoor garden. Countertop systems are ideal for kitchens, but check the dimensions carefully – including the grow light's maximum height. These are often height-adjustable, but not always. You'll need enough clearance for plants to grow, as well as easy access to refill the water reservoir and harvest your crops.

Plant capacity is another important consideration. Smaller systems, such as the four-pot Auk Mini, are ideal for keeping a few fresh herbs on hand, while larger models can grow a wider variety of crops. However, just because an indoor garden has 20 growing positions doesn't mean you can actually grow 20 mature tomato plants. Larger crops like tomatoes need more room for their roots and foliage, so you may need to leave some planting spaces empty. But you can plant several herbs and lettuces as cut-and-come-again crops.

Indoor garden systems are mainly used for herbs and leafy greens, including basil, parsley, lettuce, and arugula. These grow relatively quickly, don't need much space, and can provide repeat harvests.

However, if you're hoping to grow tomatoes, peppers, or strawberries, you'll need to be more selective. Fruiting crops generally need more lighting, more growing space, and a longer growing period. Look for a system with an adjustable grow light and enough height to accommodate mature plants. Compact or dwarf varieties are usually the best choice.

Many indoor garden systems use hydroponics, meaning plants grow without traditional soil. Instead, their roots receive water with nutrients added using liquid feed, and they are often supported by sponges or another growing medium. These systems can be very efficient, but you'll need to keep the water reservoir topped up and add nutrients regularly.

Other systems use specially formulated growing media, such as Click & Grow's pre-seeded Smart Soil pods or the coco coir supplied with the Auk Mini. These can be particularly straightforward for beginners.

It's also worth checking whether you're restricted to the manufacturer's own seed pods. Some systems require you to buy compatible refills, while others allow you to use your own seeds, giving you more freedom to experiment with different varieties and potentially saving money over time.

One of the biggest advantages of an indoor garden system is that you don't need a sunny windowsill. Built-in LED grow lights provide all the light the plants need, and most systems include a timer to switch them on and off automatically.

Look for adjustable light height, particularly if you want to grow anything taller than herbs or lettuce. Some systems also offer different lighting modes for leafy growth and flowering or fruiting crops.

More advanced models include touchscreen controls, smartphone apps, automatic nutrient dosing, and water-level alerts. These features can be convenient, but they aren't essential for successful growing. A simpler system with reliable lighting and watering is often a better choice if you're new to indoor gardening.

Although indoor garden systems are low-maintenance, they aren't completely hands-off. You will still need to refill the water reservoir, add liquid fertilizer where required, prune plants, and harvest regularly. Hydroponic systems may also need periodic cleaning to prevent algae buildup and keep pumps and water lines working properly.

Consider how easy the reservoir is to access and clean, whether the system has a water-level indicator, and how often you'll need to refill it. If you travel frequently, a larger reservoir or automatic watering feature could be particularly useful.

Indoor garden systems range range from fairly affordable countertop models to high-tech setups costing several hundred dollars or more. However, the initial purchase price isn't the only expense to consider.

LED grow lights use electricity, although they're generally more energy-efficient than older lighting technologies. You can check the wattage and daily operating time to estimate running costs.

You'll also need to factor in the cost of replacement seed pods, the growing media, nutrients, and potentially other accessories. Proprietary pods can make planting wonderfully convenient, but the costs can add up if you're growing continuously.

Finally, think about what you actually want from your indoor garden. If your main goal is to save money on groceries, a small system growing a handful of herbs may take a long time to pay for itself. But if you enjoy gardening, want fresh ingredients year-round, or simply love watching things grow, the convenience and enjoyment can make it a worthwhile investment.

Yes. Indoor garden systems can be a worthwhile investment if you enjoy growing your own food and want a to be harvesting fresh herbs and leaves throughout the year. They're particularly useful if you don't have a garden or want to keep growing through winter. However, they're unlikely to save you a fortune on groceries, especially once you factor in electricity, nutrients, and replacement growing supplies. The real value lies in the convenience, enjoyment, and satisfaction of harvesting your own produce whenever you need it.

Indoor garden systems are ideal for growing herbs such as basil, parsley, cilantro, mint, and chives, along with leafy greens like lettuce, arugula, spinach, and kale. Some systems can also be used to grow smaller vegetables, including dwarf tomatoes, peppers, and even strawberries. The key is choosing plants that suit the available growing space and lighting. Fast-growing, compact crops tend to give the best results.

Most small indoor garden systems are inexpensive to run, thanks to energy-efficient LED grow lights. For example, a 20-watt light running for 16 hours a day uses approximately 9.6 kWh of electricity per month. At an electricity rate of $0.17 per kWh, that works out to around $1.63 a month. Larger systems with more powerful lighting, pumps, and automated features will use more electricity.

Yes, but you'll need the right system and varieties. Compact or dwarf tomatoes are particularly well suited to indoor growing, provided they receive enough light and have room to develop. Strawberries can also grow successfully indoors, although they need sufficient light, nutrients, and pollination to produce fruit. Look for a system with adjustable lighting and enough space for mature plants, and avoid overcrowding.

Yes. Because hydroponic plants grow without traditional soil, they rely on nutrients dissolved in the water to provide the minerals they need. Most systems come with a starter supply of specially formulated liquid nutrients. Avoid using ordinary garden fertilizer unless the manufacturer specifically recommends it, as it may not contain the right balance of nutrients or dissolve properly. Some systems automate nutrient dosing, while others require you to add it manually.

Absolutely. In fact, many indoor garden systems are designed specifically for people with little or no gardening experience. Models with pre-seeded pods, automatic grow lights, and self-watering reservoirs take much of the guesswork out of growing plants. The Click & Grow Smart Garden 9 is a particularly beginner-friendly option, while systems such as the Auk Mini offer more flexibility to experiment with your own seeds. Start with easy crops like basil or lettuce, follow the instructions, and you'll soon be enjoying your first homegrown harvest.
