#7735. How to Shovel the Trickiest Surfaces the Right Way, From Pavers to Your Roof

From lawns to sealed concrete, you might be surprised at how much damage a snow shovel can do.

Clearing snow from walkways is vital for safety, but winter shoveling can easily damage wooden decks, asphalt driveways and other surfaces. So, as the days get shorter and colder, it’s important to solidify your shoveling plan before the first snow flies.

“Snow can camouflage uneven areas and patches of ice, posing slip-and-fall risks, particularly when you’re rushing to shovel,” says landscaping expert Jose Lopez. “Being mindful and taking a relaxed, careful approach will help you save money and keep everyone safe all winter long.”

Ahead, experts walk through how to shovel eleven tricky surfaces around your home, to keep everyone safe, plus prevent costly springtime repairs.

Shoveling gravel is frustrating because those pebbles tend to come up with the snow, then get scattered onto the landscaping. “You will end up cleaning about $150 worth of it off your lawn in the spring,” says grading and paving contractor Scott Flores.

To make life easier, use a plastic shovel, keep the blade about an inch above the gravel and clear the snow in short passes. “You don’t have to expose all of the gravel,” says Lopez. “It’s fine to leave a thin layer of snow behind.”

A metal snow shovel blade can actually scratch and gouge concrete. “It can cause $3,000 worth of damage to your pavement in 20 minutes and you won’t know it ’til April,” says Flores. Initially, the damage “may not look like much, but once water gets under it and freezes, it will cause spalling and make your pavement look 10 years older than it is.”

Luckily, the fix is easy on this one: always use a poly-blade (plastic) or rubber-edged shovel on concrete.

Aggressive shoveling can damage paint and sealers, even if they’re touted as “scratch-resistant.” “That layer is about three millimeters thick, and your steel shovel will chip it away like you’re peeling your fingernails,” says Flores.

The fix: use a poly-blade shovel, shovel with a slight upward motion and leave a half-inch of snow for the sun to melt, says Flores. “Many believe that steel shovels will last longer. Yes they will, but that’s what makes them bad,” he says.

Pro-tip: If you use a deicer, make sure it’s safe for your particular coating, says Lopez.

Just like with concrete, asphalt seems indestructible, but metal shovels can damage it, especially if it already has imperfections or cracks. So, the best approach is to use a poly-blade (plastic) or rubber-edged shovel, and shovel the snow before it partially melts and refreezes.

“Avoid pushing your shovel into cracks or potholes, and don’t bang it against the surface in an attempt to dislodge stubborn ice,” says Lopez. “Instead, choose a deicing product that’s safe for asphalt.”

A shovel can easily catch the edge of a paver and scratch, break or knock it out of place. To prevent that, use a poly-blade shovel, take shorter shovel strokes, push snow at an angle and slightly raise up the leading edge.

“Shoveling and deicing aggressively won’t make your job faster or easier, it takes some finesse,” says Lopez. Also, use de-icers that are safe for both the paving and jointing material, and inspect the walkway for loose bricks once the snow melts.

After a snow, it can be tricky to tell where the concrete ends and the lawn begins, and one wrong move means damaged grass come springtime. To keep from marring your grass, mark walkway edges with small flags before it snows. While shoveling, keep the blade even with your walkway, versus angling it toward the grass.

Pro-tip: “Slow down and work in short passes near the edges, rather than trying to force the shovel along,” says Lopez. “

Try not to pile snow on shrubs and other perennials, as that can snap branches. It’s also best to keep deicers and their runoff away from landscaping.

“Before winter arrives, plan where you’ll pile or toss snow to keep it away from sensitive plants,” says Lopez. “You may find it helpful to use a smaller shovel, which will give you better control over where the snow lands.”

Also, try not to move soil, which can expose plants to the cold, and never strike frozen branches to remove snow. “Wood breaks more easily than people expect,” says moving professional Leon Schwab.

Aggressive shoveling is sure to damage a deck, regardless of its composition. To preserve yours, use a poly-blade shovel and push the snow in the direction of the boards. If it’s safe to do so, leave a thin layer of snow, instead of shoveling all the way down to bare decking, then apply a deicer that’s recommended for the surface type.

Safety tip: “If wet, heavy snow is accumulating and you notice the deck sagging or hear creaking noises, seek professional advice,” says Lopez. “Don’t continue using the deck if you suspect a structural issue.”

Stairs are particularly hazardous when its slippery out, and clearing them can be precarious, with snow obscuring their boundaries and confined spaces limiting your range of motion.

To stay safe, “Wear boots with good traction and make sure your staircase is well lit,” says Lopez. “Don’t rush the job. It’s better to take your time and shovel safely.”

Pro-tip: “Use a small shovel to clear one step at a time and maintain a stable position,” says Schwab.

Sometimes it’s prudent to clear large accumulations of snow from the roof, but it’s also a dangerous job. To stay safe, roofing contractor Andre Kazimierski recommends using a roof rake, which allows you to pull off snow while remaining on the ground. Focus on clearing off as much as you can, but don’t worry about leaving it completely bare, and try not to touch your roofing material.

“Do this sooner rather than later, because if it starts to warm up a bit the snow will become denser and heavier, making it harder to remove,” says Kazimierski. “And never walk on your roof when it’s even the slightest bit snowy or icy up there.”

Obviously, you don’t want to take a shovel to your car, as that would do a lot of damage. Instead, use a snow brush or broom that’s designed to be gentle on vehicle finishes. Flores recommends this one from Snow Joe.

Start by clearing the roof in sections, then move on to the hood, trunk, windows, headlights, taillights and mirrors. You’ll especially want to get the roof and hood fully clear; otherwise, once you start driving, snow can blow up or slide down onto your windshield, obstructing your vision and endangering other drivers. “That ice can fly off your car at 40 miles per hour,” says Flores.

#7733. Fourth Circuit Upholds Virginia's Law Terminating Agreements to Help With Immigration Enforcement - but Strikes Down anti-Mask Law

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The ruling on Section 287(g) agreements overturns an earlier district court decision.

In September, I wrote about the the federal district court decision striking down Virginia's new law terminating Section 287(g) agreements, under which various state and local law enforcement agencies agree to help with federal immigration enforcement. Today, in United States v. Virginia, the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed that decision. But, at the same time, in a 2-1 ruling, they struck down Virginia's law barring law enforcement officers (including federal ones) from wearing masks except in relatively narrowly specified circumstances. Here is an excerpt from the court's opinion (written by Judge Heytens) on the 287(g) issue:

We vacate the preliminary injunction that bars enforcing the 287(g) Law with respect to existing agreements. The district court concluded the Federal Government was likely to succeed on the merits because rendering such agreements unenforceable violate both the intergovernmental immunity doctrine and the Contracts Clause. We disagree. The intergovernmental immunity doctrine does not apply because the 287(g) Law neither directly regulates the Federal Government nor prevents private parties from contracting with it…. The 287(g) Law also does not violate the Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements expressly permit unilateral termination by the non-federal party; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for requiring state and local officials to terminate or renegotiate any such agreements.

Later in the opinion Judge Heytens expands on why Section 287(g) termination does not violate the Contracts Clause:

We conclude the Federal Government cannot satisfy that test for two different, yet complementary, reasons. First, all the agreements covered by the district court's injunction expressly permit the Commonwealth's agents to unilaterally terminate without cause, which means the 287(g) Law does not "substantially impair" (Sveen, 584 U.S. at 819) a contractual relationship at Step 1. Second, even if the agreements did not so provide, neither the Commonwealth's agencies nor those of its localities may contract away "an essential attribute of [the Commonwealth's] sovereignty." United States Tr. Co. of N.Y. v. New Jersey, 431 U.S. 1, 23 (1977). Here, that attribute is the Commonwealth's power to decide whether and on what terms to assist with the ongoing enforcement of federal law.

I largely agree. In my post on the district court decision, I offered some additional reasons why terminating these agreements doesn't violate the Contracts Clause.

The anti-mask law presents more difficult issues because - as the majority emphasizes - it directly regulates federal law enforcement officials. On the other hand, the law imposes the same constraints on state and local officers, as well, and therefore doesn't discriminate against them. On balance, I agree with Judge Robert Bruce King's dissent:

At bottom, a single ICE officer should never be able to override a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth of Virginia in the absence of some federal law, regulation, or other valid supporting authority. Consider what purportedly conflicts with the Mask/Identity Statute. A federal statute? None. A treaty of the United States? None. A federal regulation or executive order? None. A written policy located anywhere within ICE or the Department of Homeland Security? None has been identified. What we have today is a single sentence in a Declaration asserting that individual ICE officers possess the discretion and ability to conceal their identities when they alone deem it appropriate. No supervision is at all necessary or required and the agency itself has no involvement in the ICE officer's daily decisions on whether to wear a mask. I cannot and will not accept the proposition that individualized discretion, untethered to any identifiable source of federal law, enjoys constitutional supremacy over a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth.

As the majority recognizes, federal law enforcement officers are not generally exempt from state law while on the job. For example, they must obey state traffic laws when driving their vehicles. A valid federal law could override a conflicting state law. But here, there is no such overriding federal law, or even a regulation (though I'm not convinced the latter alone would be enough). Just the preferences of ICE agents. Those preferences are not enough to secure an exemption from state law.  Federal law (when constitutionally valid) is supreme over state law. The preferences of individual federal officials or agencies are not.

NEXT: Virginia Needn't Help with Federal Immigration Enforcement, But Can't Interfere With It

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

Lift recliners can make it easier and safer for elderly individuals to get in and out of a recliner. We focused on the priorities that every person wants from any type of chair, so the chairs on this list needed to be comfortable, practical, and safe. We considered product specifications and consumer reviews to narrow down this list from more than 20 recliner options.

We also spoke with Dr. Logan DuBose, the co-founder of Olera Care, a nationwide community platform for connecting family caregivers to service providers in the senior care industry, funded by the National Institute on Aging. As such, safety is paramount when it comes to any product, but especially when used by those with limited mobility. We looked for smooth-moving chairs with an ergonomic design and a decent weight capacity to suit most users.

Recliners for seniors also need to be easy to control—no one should have to fiddle around with a complicated remote just to get out of a chair. To ensure these criteria were met, we chose highly reviewed products with user-friendly controls.

The lift chairs on this list also look nice, with attractive designs, textures, and colors. We chose from a range of colors and materials to suit different shopper preferences.

After a long day, sinking into your favorite recliner is a welcome treat. But for those who find getting into a favorite chair harder than usual, it might be time to invest in a recliner for seniors. The best recliners for elderly individuals feature mobility aids that make it easier to get in and out of a cushy seat. When choosing these recliners, consider the recliner type, motor size, material, and additional functions.

While all recliners can be suitable for seniors, some have extra features that make them easier to use. For seniors with full mobility, traditional, swivel, massaging, and rocker recliners are all comfortable picks. These chairs can be manual or electric; electric options may be easier to use for those with any mobility concerns. But if getting in and out of a recliner is harder than it used to be, consider a lifting recliner.

Lift recliners are essentially recliners engineered to lift the user with minimal manual effort required. Designed for those who have a hard time sitting down or standing up from a seated position, they use a power mechanism to raise the chair up. They look the same as traditional recliners, but the lifting mechanism makes them a popular choice for seniors.

Lift recliners come in single-motor or dual-motor designs. As the name suggests, single-motor chairs have one motor that controls the chair’s entire range of movement, powering both the lifting mechanism and reclining mechanism. These chairs are less adjustable but tend to be more affordable than dual-motor chairs. Most single-motor lift chairs have one button that operates the lift and one that operates both the recliner and the footrest as one piece, so when you recline the chair, the footrest follows in a preset position.

Dual-motor chairs have two motors that power different parts of the chair. One motor controls the recline angle, while the other controls the footrest and lifting mechanism. This design allows for infinite positioning, so you can adjust each independently to find your perfect lounging position.

Recliners can take up a fair amount of space in a room, so it’s important to consider the chair dimensions when shopping. Space is especially a concern for lift recliners, which tend to be larger and heavier than standard recliners on account of their motors and parts.

Due to their reclining design, recliners also need enough space behind and in front of them to fully extend. Before you start shopping, measure your space to make sure the recliner can fit without hitting the wall or any other chairs or tables.

Besides considering the room space, make sure the recliner is a suitable size for your needs. Most recliners will advertise their weight capacity, which should not be exceeded, especially in the case of lift recliners. Tall users may opt for a longer chair for better comfort. Choose a recliner that is suitable for both the user’s height and weight.

Recliner frames can be made of plywood, hardwood, or metal. Metal is generally the sturdiest option, and lift recliners tend to use a mix of wood and metal to create a durable frame. These materials have the strength to support the chair (and the user’s body) as it lifts, but keep in mind that each lift recliner will have a weight limit that should be followed.

Recliner cushions for elderly people can be made of foam, memory foam, down, or an innerspring system. Combined with an ergonomic design, any of these materials can offer a comfortable seat. Upholstery options can vary across a range of materials, which are explored ahead.

Upholstered recliners come in a variety of materials. The most popular materials include fabric, leather, and vinyl. Look for an option that is comfortable, breathable, and easy to clean.

Fabrics are among the softest options and come in a range of colors, textures, and materials. This category includes cotton, polyester, microfiber, microsuede, and performance fabrics. High-quality fabrics are durable and breathable, but they can stain and absorb spills. Leather (whether real or fake) and vinyl make for easy-to-clean, smooth chair covers. While they aren’t as plush or breathable as fabrics, leather and vinyl chairs come in a variety of colors and have a sleek look.

Beyond comfort, consider ease of cleaning when choosing a recliner material. The best recliners for elderly users are easy to clean. Due to their weave, fabrics tend to be the toughest to clean, while smooth materials like leather and vinyl are easy to wipe down.

Lifted recliners for elderly users tend to have a roomy and comfortable design with well-stuffed cushions. Like traditional recliners, they’re made for relaxing, but they also have the addition of a mobility aid.

Beyond lifting up and down to get the user out of the chair, the best power lift recliner chairs also offer reclining abilities and footrests for lounging. When choosing a comfortable pick, consider the reclining angle, which can range from 140 degrees to almost 180 degrees.

Design can be just as important as comfort. Recliners can take up a fair amount of space in a living room or a bedroom, so you’ll want a choice that looks nice in your space. Lift recliners look like regular recliners and come in a wide range of colors, materials, and designs, so you can find one that suits your style.

Lift recliners are popular for seniors and those with mobility issues, and for good reason. These comfortable recliners can help those with limited mobility by making it easier to sit and stand at just the touch of a button. When activated, they lift and angle the recliner to put the user as close to a standing position as possible and make the chair easier to get in and out of.

Power lift recliners include a remote control or a control panel to make adjustments. In most chairs, all their features are automated to make them easier for seniors to use. Control options can include lifting the chair, reclining the back, opening the footrest, and switching on any heat or massage modes.

Massage and heat settings add even more comfort to a lift recliner. Massage recliners feature rollers or parts inside the chair that either knead or vibrate to create a massaging motion. These are commonly distributed across the backrest, but some chairs offer massage zones that also target different parts of the back area, thighs, and legs. Massage recliners can have one massage mode or varying intensities and massage types.

Lift recliners often offer heating functions that offer pleasant warming sensations. These features can help with sore or aching muscles and joints, or, more simply, help the user create a cozy cocoon for relaxing or napping. Heating zones can target different areas of the body.

Lift recliners for seniors can come with additional bells and whistles for a better seating experience. Storage areas can keep devices and other items within easy reach and ready for use, and charging ports are another useful perk.

Cup holders are a common and obvious feature; they’re made to hold your drinks but can also be used to hold other items. For added storage, some recliners also feature arm storage pockets to hold remotes, cables, and books. USB ports are a useful addition that allow the user to charge devices while relaxing.

Products for seniors need to be easy to use, and lift recliners are no exception. When it comes to a large item like a lift recliner, ease of use also contributes to safety. The best power lift recliner options are designed with seniors in mind, so they’re a safe option to have around the home.

Most are controlled using a control panel or a corded remote control, so adjusting their settings is as simple as pushing a button—the chair will do the rest. The control panel or remote is often used for more than the lifting feature, also controlling the recline angle and footrest. A high-quality lift recliner will move slowly and smoothly to allow users to gain their footing.

Lift recliners are one of the best recliners for seniors and individuals with limited mobility. They are essentially recliners that lift you up, making it easier to lower into the seat or stand from a seated position.

Lift recliners look and feel the same as traditional recliners, so they have all the comfort perks of a regular recliner, with the added benefit of a mobility aid. Since lift recliners are electric-powered, they are also very easy to use. With the press of a button or the flick of a switch, users can adjust them to their liking.

Beyond being easy to use, lift recliners are also a safe addition. Sitting down and standing from a low seat (like many traditional recliners) can be difficult for stiff or achy joints, and it can even create a fall hazard for some individuals. A lift recliner can help seniors safely maintain their freedom and independence for longer.

While any recliner may be suitable for seniors, lift recliners are one of the best options. Even if you don’t have mobility concerns, lift recliners for elderly citizens can offer a bit of extra support for aching bones and joints. Still deciding on the best recliner for your needs? Read on for some frequently asked questions and answers about recliners for seniors.

For seniors, a seat height between 17 and 18 inches is often ideal, but this varies with the size of the user.

Also known as a “geri” chair, a geriatric recliner is a large, padded reclining chair on casters, usually used in senior living facilities or hospital settings. They provide great seated comfort and support and can be wheeled to adjoining areas with ease.

Some geriatric chairs can be fully reclined for sleeping; however, it’s safer and generally more comfortable to sleep in a bed.

When the chair is in a reclined position, your heel should hang slightly over the end of the footrest. If your feet hang too far off the recliner footrest, it’s best to find a longer pick; this positioning can put uncomfortable pressure on the back of your legs.

Look for a quality recliner that is supportive and fully adjustable so that the user can find the best position to soothe a painful back.

Medicare or Medicaid may cover some of the costs for a lift chair if it is considered medically necessary. It’s best to consult with a doctor or Medicare or Medicaid provider to see if your situation is eligible.

#7731. Electrical Tape Color Meanings: What Each Color Tells Electricians

Electrical tape comes in plenty of colors, but each has a purpose. Here's what the common shades mean in U.S. electrical work.

Being a DIY electrician is one way homeowners like to save a little money over expensive repairs. However, there are safety concerns when it comes to doing your own electrical work. Electrical tape color meanings help electricians identify wires and make sense of connections that might otherwise look identical. The trouble is that colors don’t always mean the same thing.

Learn what the common colors usually mean, how electricians use them, and why a strip of tape can’t confirm a wire’s purpose.

Electricians use colored tape to identify wires, especially when several look alike. In the United States, the colors commonly mean:

These colors aren’t universal. The National Electrical Code sets rules for identifying neutral and grounding wires, but most hot-wire colors follow common practices rather than strict requirements. For example, orange can have a specific meaning in certain commercial electrical systems. Its purpose depends on the wiring, so electricians can’t rely on color alone.

Electricians often wrap colored tape around the ends of wires to tell them apart. Manufacturers such as 3M make tape specifically for identifying different electrical connections.

Tape can also show when a wire serves a different purpose than its original color suggests. For example, electricians may mark a white wire with black tape to identify it as a hot wire in certain situations. Electrical codes limit when and how they can make these changes.

However, tape color alone can’t confirm a wire’s purpose or whether it carries electricity. Previous repairs, incorrect markings, or different labeling practices can cause confusion. Before starting electrical work, a qualified person should identify the circuit and test that the power is off. Homeowners who encounter unfamiliar or conflicting wire markings should have a licensed electrician inspect the wiring.

#7730. Second Amendment Roundup, I: The Common Use Test and the Federal "Assault Weapon" Ban

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The federal law did not prohibit the basic AR-15 rifle design.

Connecticut argues before the Supreme Court, in its Grant v. Higgins brief, that before 2004, "few civilians owned AR-15s." That was supposedly "because federal law prohibited 'manufacture, transfer, or possess[ion]' of the weapons between 1994 and 2004" under Pub. L. No. 103-322, 108 Stat. 1796, 1996-97 (1994). That was the federal "assault weapon ban" that expired in 2004.  The brief continues, "Under the common-use-only approach, if Congress had extended that legislation in 2004, AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today."

That argument exhibits a profoundly mistaken view about the what the federal law actually did.

First, while the law made it "unlawful for a person to manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon," that provision did "not apply to the possession or transfer of any semiautomatic assault weapon otherwise lawfully possessed under Federal law on the date of the enactment of this subsection."  18 U.S.C. § 922(v).  So it did not ban possession or transfer of a single firearm that was already lawfully possessed. Moreover, the federal law did not ban future manufacture of the subject firearms as long as certain aspects were eliminated.  The firearms were defined, first, in a list of names, including "Colt AR-15" and "copies or duplicates" thereof.  Second, they included certain features, including:

a semiautomatic rifle that has an ability to accept a detachable magazine and has at least 2 of –

(ii) a pistol grip that protrudes conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon;

(iv) a flash suppressor or threaded barrel designed to accommodate a flash suppressor; and

(v) a grenade launcher….  18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(30).

Under the above, Colt could not engrave simply "AR-15" on its rifles, but could use other names.  A manufacturer could not make a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, but as discussed below, a rifle would be a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, inter alia, only if it had at least two of the five listed features.

But guess what: the sine qua non of an AR-15 is the conspicuously protruding pistol grip.  None of the other features listed above are inherent in the AR-15 design.  Many AR-15s never had a folding or telescoping stock.  How many people cared whether it had a bayonet mount?  A flash suppressor (or threading "designed" to accommodate one) could not be mounted, but a muzzle brake or compensator could.  Congress must have included grenade launcher to sound dramatic, as that was already restricted under the National Firearms Act.

And so the federal law did exactly nothing to "ban" the basic AR-15 design.  Manufacturers kept making and consumers kept buying semiautomatic rifles with protruding pistol grips sans bayonet mounts.

Manufacturers submitted samples of rifles to the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) to verify compliance.  I have reproduced some samples of ATF approval letters in my Firearms Law Deskbook § 10:6 (available in book form or on Westlaw).  As an example, ATF examined a Bushmaster XM-15E2, which was "based on the AR15 design and incorporates a pistol grip that extends conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon." However, it had none of the other listed features. It did have a muzzle brake, but it was not a flash suppressor. The rifle was found not to be an assault weapon "because it does not have at least two of the features specified in the statute. Additionally, the firearm is not a copy or duplicate of the Colt AR15 rifle." Edward M. Owen, Jr., Chief, ATF Firearms Technology Branch, Feb. 16, 1996.

Instead of a two-feature test like the expired federal law, Connecticut bans rifles based on a single feature, including: "Any grip of the weapon, including a pistol grip, a thumbhole stock, or any other stock, the use of which would allow an individual to grip the weapon, resulting in any finger on the trigger hand in addition to the trigger finger being directly below any portion of the action of the weapon when firing…." This is a more capacious ban that affects a much broader collection of firearms than the expired federal law.

Connecticut is wrong to argue that had Congress extended its law in 2004, "AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today." AR-15s were already in common use in 1994.  The fact is that the federal law did nothing to dampen the ever-increasing demand for and use by the American people of the AR-15 basic design.  And it goes without saying that semiautomatic rifles with detachable magazines had already been around for a century when the federal law was in place.

Our Ratings: Design 4/5; Durability 5/5; Performance 4.5/5; Value 4.8/5

Along with a tough build and large capacity, this outdoor power strip is exceptionally well-designed for those who need a power hub for corded power tools. When we started researching the best power strips, we discovered hundreds of different options on the market, so we started by looking carefully at the top-rated models. We took brand names into consideration, to an extent—Anker and Belkin are well-respected names in the industry, for example—but we also looked carefully at niche brands and AmazonBasics picks with good customer reviews. Our initial list had over 35 best-selling power strips, but we narrowed that down to 15 picks we wanted to try out for ourselves.

In our hands-on testing, we used the power strips for two weeks, noting their build quality, trying out their features, and assessing their design. We plugged in battery chargers, power tools, PCs, monitors, peripherals, and small appliances.

Since the primary purpose of buying a power strip is to have additional outlets, we noted how easy (or difficult) it was to use all of the outlets on the strip at the same time. Our goal wasn’t to see how much power we could pull—that depends solely on the circuit—but to see how well the strips were designed for real-world use.

We awarded points based on a rubric: the better a strip performed on a test or assessment, the higher the points. After testing, we averaged the points to find our top pick and categorize the others by their best use.

Before choosing the best power strip for your needs, consider how and where you plan to use it, as well as the important factors below.

The right power strip for your needs depends heavily on how it will be used and which devices or equipment will be plugged into it.

The number of outlets you need in a power strip depends on both how many and what type of devices you want to plug into it. Remember that you should not plug high-power-capacity devices into power strips, regardless of the number of outlets. The circuit still limits the power strip.

Power strips can have as few as two outlets or more than 20. These outlets can be standard power outlets, USB-A or USB-C outlets, wide-spaced outlets intended for larger adapters, and specialty connections like ethernet or coaxial connections. The number and configuration of outlets are mostly a personal preference; however, consider that as the number of outlets increases, so does the size of the power strip. So, if space is an issue, choose a power strip with fewer outlets and a narrower profile.

Length and configuration refer to the length of the cord and the type of outlets in the power strip.

In our technologically advanced society, many devices and appliances embedded with complex electrical systems are very sensitive to power surges, so surge protection is a feature of a power strip nearly everyone needs. Power surges typically occur when a storm brings down electrical lines, causing the power company to reroute power to address power demands. These changes can create inconsistent power flow fluctuations, resulting in a power surge. The only way to protect all appliances and devices is with a whole-house surge protector, but strips with surge protection will reduce the risk of damage to sensitive electronics and devices.

Surge protection—also referred to as the surge suppression rating of a power strip—is measured in joules (J) and normally varies, depending on the product, from as low as 100 J to higher than 4,000 J. When using a power strip as surge protection for expensive or sensitive devices, it is important to invest in a power strip with a high surge suppression rating.

A standard power strip runs electricity to multiple devices, typically via an on/off switch. Smart power strips function similarly, but they can also connect with compatible smart home systems, like Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant, usually through a WiFi connection.

Once a smart power strip connects to a smart home system, users can control the electrical supply to the paired devices through either voice control or a smartphone app. Some power strips even support timers or schedules so connected devices will automatically turn on or off.

While power strips don’t seem very dangerous, cords can become trip hazards and electrocution and fires can result from improper use. Many power strip manufacturers include safety features like full-metal housing, internal circuit breakers, or ground-fault circuit interrupters (GFCIs) to protect users and their property from harm.

Take a look below to find the answers to some of the most commonly asked questions about electrical power outlet strips.

If used properly, a power strip can actually reduce the risk of electrical fire by providing a safe place to plug in additional accessories. However, if misused, either by overloading it, using it for appliances it’s not rated for, or linking multiple power strips together (called daisy-chaining), a power strip can become a danger.

Never plug high-power-capacity appliances, such as electric space heaters, refrigerators, microwaves, toaster ovens, and air conditioners, into a power strip.

Daisy-chaining power strips means linking multiple power strips together in a series that connects back to a single electrical outlet. This is a big concern for fire-fighting professionals because daisy-chained connections will almost invariably lead to an overloaded power strip that heats up until it burns out or catches fire.

Power strips can catch fire if they are old or frayed, or if they are overloaded beyond their capacity. This can happen when several devices that draw too much electricity, such as air conditioners or electric heaters, are plugged into the same strip. The strip will then heat up and eventually begin to melt, sparking a fire.

While there is some discrepancy between specific products, on average, power strips will last for about 2 years before replacement is necessary. However, they can last between 3 to 5 years if properly maintained.

It depends on what you plug into the strips, but in general, it’s not a good practice to plug two strips into one outlet. Overloading the circuit will cause the breaker to trip.

In a home that has too few outlets for the owners’ needs, power strips can absolutely be worth the money because they expand the number of outlets available. Power strips that have surge protection are also ideal for homes with a lot of sensitive electronics, as the strips prevent damage when power surges might otherwise cause damage. Just keep in mind that power strips don’t actually provide more power to the home—they just allow more devices to use the power that’s already there.

It’s not a bad idea. Turning it off will reduce standby energy usage, but as long as you’re not overloading the circuit, it should be safe to leave on.

#7728. What It Really Means When Your Mayor Awards Someone the “Key to the City”

A key to the city looks official, but it won't unlock any doors. Here's why cities give them out and what recipients actually receive.

Whether it’s in a movie or real life, everyone has seen or heard of someone receiving an oversized gold key that is a “key to the city.” The ceremony is usually accompanied with a photoshoot, a handshake, and applause. But what does the key actually do?

Cities across the world still hand out these awards, and the tradition goes back much further than most people realize. Learn what a key to the city represents, how the custom began, and what someone actually gets to do with it.

A key to the city is an award that cities give to people they want to honor.

“The Key to the City is presented as a symbol of civic recognition and Philadelphia’s appreciation for individuals whose achievements, service and influence have made a meaningful impact on the city and its people,” according to a release from the City of Philadelphia.

The key is usually decorative, with the city’s name or seal on it. Some come in a display box or with a certificate. Little Rock, Arkansas, considers its key the city’s highest ceremonial honor.

But the key won’t open City Hall or any other public building. It doesn’t give the recipient special privileges or any authority, either. In 2010, New York City tried something different with an art project that gave people working keys to certain locations. Those weren’t the same as the city’s usual honorary keys.

The tradition goes back to when cities had walls and gates that closed at night. Giving someone a key meant they could come and go without asking permission.

In medieval Europe, leaders also exchanged keys during official visits or military surrenders. Handing over the keys sometimes meant giving up control of a city. Over time, the custom became a way to welcome or honor someone.

Today, cities give keys to athletes, public figures, volunteers, and local residents. Each city has its own rules for who receives one.

Philadelphia, for example, honored a resident in 2026 after he walked across the country to support career opportunities for young people. Elk Grove, California, recognizes military accomplishments and acts of heroism, while Little Rock reserves its keys for people who live outside Arkansas.

Mayors usually present the keys, although some cities involve the city council or accept nominations from residents. Recipients get a keepsake and some public recognition, but no special privileges.

#7727. Second Amendment Roundup, II: Much Ado About Bowie Knives

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Laws on concealed carry are not historical analogues for banning semiautomatic rifles.

In Viramontes and Grant, Cook County and Connecticut argue that 19th century restrictions on Bowie knives provide historical analogues under Bruen for banning what they call "assault weapons."  They further contend that the widespread use of Bowie knives disproves application of the Heller test that arms in common use are protected by the Second Amendment.  If Bowie knives in common use by law-abiding citizens may be banned, the argument goes, so too may semiautomatic rifles.

A word of caution.  To paraphrase Freud, sometimes a knife is just a knife.  Knives generally have a point and an edge on one side, sometimes also an edge on the other.  Any knife can be used for good or bad.  Bruen distinguished heavy weapons of war like lancegays from daggers, noting that in medieval society "[a]lmost everyone carried a knife or a dagger in his belt," "[c]ivilians wore them for self-protection," and "the smaller medieval weapons … strike us as most analogous to modern handguns."

No doubt Bowie knives were in use as tools for skinning game and self-defense, and ruffians are said to have carried them concealed.  But for a variety of reasons, it's unnecessary to decide whether Bowie knives met the Heller test of being in common use.  Four of the amicus briefs are right on point on this issue: National Rifle Ass'n (NRA), National Shooting Sports Foundation (NSSF), Senator Ted Cruz, and the United States (U.S.).

First, a few States' restrictions are not enough to establish a historical tradition.  Under Heller, a handful of outlier laws cannot justify a ban.  "Most States regulated Bowie knives in some manner, but, except in a few outlier jurisdictions, adults were free to buy, possess, and openly carry them. Regulations typically restricted concealed carry, sales to minors, or imposed enhanced penalties for criminal misuse." NRA Br. 5.

Second, "No State banned Bowie-knife possession in the nineteenth century." NRA Br. 36.  "And one of the only laws that likely did actually ban Bowie knives (along with pistols and an array of other items) is the same 1837 Georgia law that was promptly held unconstitutional other than as applied to concealed carry—because it was too restrictive to comply with the Second Amendment. See 1837 Ga. Acts 90, §1 (1838); Nunn v. State, 1 Ga. 243 (1846); cf. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 54 (singling out Nunn as "particularly instructive" on the Second Amendment's meaning)." NSSF Br. 21.

These were concealed-carry restrictions, not complete bans.  "This Court has already concluded that restrictions on concealed carry cannot justify carry bans, see Bruen, 597 U.S. at 48-49, 53-55, let alone possession bans, see Heller, 554 U.S. at 628-29." NSSF Br. 21.

Third, the same laws covered handguns.  "If those laws justified rifle bans, then handgun bans would be justified all the more, because they typically also regulated handguns but not long guns." NRA Br. 38.

Where Bowie-knife restrictions were upheld, courts applied the same standard Petitioners advance here: arms in common use for lawful purposes are protected, while weapons used only by criminals are not.  As Judge Richardson's dissent in Bianchi explains, it does not matter that courts sometimes disagreed about whether Bowie knives were in fact in common use, because they were applying the same yardstick. "State courts have long applied the common-use test to judge such laws under state constitutional provisions securing the right to bear arms." U.S. Br. 12.

Fourth, even a court that viewed the Bowie knife as exceptionally deadly held that the right to carry it was protected.  "And Texas's Cockrum v. State held a Bowie knife to be a protected arm—"[t]he right to carry a bowie-knife for lawful defense is secured, and must be admitted"— while sustaining an enhanced penalty for its abuse, treating the weapon's dangerousness as a reason to regulate its misuse, not a reason to deny that it was an arm. 24 Tex. 394, 402-403 (1859).  Cockrum is the mirror image of the decision below: alleged dangerousness bore on regulation, not on coverage." Cruz Br. 18.

The historical answer to misuse was punishing criminals, not disarming law-abiding citizens

"[T]he evil must be prevented by the penitentiary and gallows, and not by a general deprivation of a constitutional privilege." U.S. Br. 30 (quoting Wilson v. State).

Stephen Halbrook is a Senior Fellow with the Independent Institute. His latest books are America's Rifle: The Case for the AR-15 and The Right to Bear Arms: A Constitutional Right of the People or a Privilege of the Ruling Class? He is also author of The Founders' Second Amendment, Securing Civil Rights, Gun Control in the Third Reich, and Gun Control in Nazi-Occupied France. He has written over 30 law review articles and has testified in Congressional hearings on firearm law bills. He has also litigated extensively in the field, often representing groups such as the NRA, National African American Gun Association, Western States Sheriffs' Association, Congress of Racial Equality, National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, and more. He has argued before the U.S. Supreme Court in Castillo v. U.S. (2000), Printz v. U.S. (1997), and U.S. v. Thompson/Center Arms Co. (1992), as well as in front of many other courts.  In D.C. v. Heller, he filed an amici curiae brief on behalf of a majority of members of Congress.

The Best Black Friday Deals for the Home ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

Published Nov 26, 2026 6:00 PM EST

Holiday dinners mean more pots, platters, and glassware than any other time of year, and The Home Depot’s Black Friday pricing makes now a good time to replace a dishwasher that can’t keep up. #7725. 18 Kitchen Hacks Our Readers Swear By

Family Handyman readers share smart solutions for everyday problems in the heart of your home.

From a surprising way to monitor power outages to an epic trick to double your Ziploc bags, Family Handyman readers share smart solutions for everyday problems in the heart of your home.

“The metal wheels of a refrigerator can scratch, dent or gouge just about any flooring surface. Laying down stiff cardboard or a piece of leftover carpet provides an effective barrier, but for the best protection, use a sheet of 1/8‑in. hardboard. The smooth surface protects floors and helps appliances slide into and out of place. —ANTHONY LOMBARDI

“To find out if power outages ruined the food in your freezer while you were away on vacation, freeze a container of water and rest a penny on top of the ice. If the penny is at the bottom when you get back, it means the power was off long enough to melt the water—as well as thaw (and likely spoil) everything in the freezer. —JOHN NAKAMURA

“If you don’t have a label handy, use a rubber band instead. Stretch it around your Mason jar, then write the contents with a permanent marker. The grippy rubber also makes the jar easier to open. —DAVID KOWALCZYK Picture Frame Message Board I wanted a nicer-looking place for my weekly grocery list and family notes, so I turned a picture frame into a dry-erase board. I simply cut decorative paper to fit the frame and put it behind the glass, creating a surface I can write on with a dryerase marker. —JESSIE DAWSON

“For a minor scorch mark on a laminate countertop, skip the abrasive cleaner. Buff it out with car wax or a mixture of toothpaste and baking soda instead.” —ELAINE WHITFIELD

“Leaky seals around faucets and sink rims can lead to slow but severe damage (they can destroy a countertop, for example). So after installing a new sink or faucet, dribble water around the area and wait a few minutes. Then get under the sink and look for leaks. —GREGORY PRITCHARD

“Sometimes it’s tough to mix foods such as old-fashioned oily peanut butter in a small jar by hand. But if you enjoy reaching for a power tool to solve a problem as I do, head out to the garage. As it turns out, the handle of a mixing spoon fits perfectly in the chuck of a cordless drill. —CLIFF MERCER

“Build a simple dispenser for your trash bags using 1/2-in. pipe and a few fittings. Screw a floor flange to the cabinet, thread in a 3-in.-long pipe nipple, and then thread a 90-degree elbow onto the nipple. Cut the vertical pipe so it’s a bit longer than the width of the roll of bags. Finally, thread the vertical piece into the elbow and slip on the roll.” —TRAVIS LARSON

“I turn sandwich-size bags into snack-size bags by heating up an old butter knife with a lighter and slicing the bag in half. The hot knife cauterizes the edges of the two new bags, and the cauterized edges are just as strong as the factory-sealed edges.” —JULIA TRENTON

“Need to sharpen a utility knife, pocket blade or scissors but don’t have a sharpening stone on hand? Flip a ceramic mug and use the unglazed ring on the bottom as a sharpener. Hold the blade at a 45-degree angle and slide it across the ring in one direction, from the base to the tip. This won’t replace a proper sharpening kit, but it can quickly clean up a dull edge in a pinch.” —RONALD ALVAREZ

“Ice packs are a great way to keep your lunch cool, but they can be expensive to replace if you tend to lose them. To make your own reusable version without spending a lot, soak a sponge in water, then place it in a small resealable plastic bag. Freeze it overnight, then pop it into your lunch container. As the ice melts, the bag holds the water until the sponge reabsorbs it. When you get home, simply refreeze the pack for next time. I like to keep several on hand to use in lunches and coolers, as well as for first aid. They’re inexpensive to make, easy to reuse and help reduce waste.” —TOM SHERIDAN

“Alphabetizing spices helps you quickly find what your recipe calls for and makes putting away jars just as fast. Another benefit? You can easily figure out which spices are missing from your pantry, so you’re less likely to discover you’re out of a key ingredient halfway through making a meal. Take a quick glance before grocery shopping to keep staples stocked.” —MARTIN SUTHERLAND

“When your favorite candle burns too low for a lighter or match to reach the wick, don’t risk burning your fingertips. Instead, light a piece of uncooked spaghetti. It is long enough to reach deep into tall candle holders and burns long enough to light the wick.” —PATRICIA HART

“For an extra-fresh garbage disposal, toss in a few lemon or lime peels. Run the disposal with cold water until you can’t hear any more grinding, then run it for another 30 seconds (with the water still on).” —GREGORY HOLT

“A countertop isn’t the best place to keep a recipe while you’re cooking. It takes up counter space, is difficult to read and is bound to get splattered. Instead, use a clothes hanger with pants clips to hang the recipe from a cabinet handle. Open the book or magazine to the desired page (or use a printout), clamp it in place and you have a simple hanging stand. This trick works best with smaller cookbooks, magazines or single-sheet recipes.” —GLENN WHITE

“My kitchen drawers used to be an absolute wreck, with pans and dishes crammed in however they’d fit. And seemingly every time I needed something, it was at the very bottom of the drawer. My solution was to cut a piece of 1/8-in. pegboard to the size of the drawer bottom and attach dowels using screws from underneath. Now my pans are organized and easy to access. The 10 minutes it took to build was easily made up with how much frustration it has saved me.” —JIM DAVIDSON

“Crawling under a kitchen sink to refill the soap dispenser was a hassle, so I tried filling it from above. But when I did, the soap formed an air-lock bubble and overflowed, creating a mess. That’s when I came up with the idea of inserting a drinking straw in the dispenser neck to relieve “bubble block.” Now when I refill the dispenser, the air escapes through the straw and the soap stays where it belongs.” —PAUL SNYDER

“A dishwasher makes quick work of disinfecting washable toys such as plastic building blocks. Drop the blocks in a mesh laundry bag and run your dishwasher as usual. Remove the bag before the drying cycle, letting the blocks air-dry on a towel. This method also works for items such as seashells, dish brushes, sponges and rags.” —ROBERT VALENTI

“If your refrigerator stops dispensing water after you change the filter, make sure the new filter is fully seated. Many people don’t twist it in completely, and one final turn may be all it takes to get the dispenser working again.” —STANLEY BEAUMONT

“An ironing board with the cover removed can be used as an extra cooling rack when you’re doing a lot of baking. Better yet, it frees up valuable counter space for other kitchen tasks. Just be sure to use pans, paper liners, parchment or some other barrier between baked goods and the board.” —LIZ GRABOWSKI

“When the rubber sink baffle on my garbage disposal gets grimy or starts to smell, I switch off the power at the breaker and scrub it with an old toothbrush dipped in hot, soapy water and baking soda. I lift the rubber flaps to clean underneath, where food and grime collect. Then I restore power, rinse it with cold water and run the disposal briefly to flush away the debris.” —CHARLES MCALLISTER

#7723. Bob Woodward Interviews Justice Kagan, Or Does Justice Kagan Interview Bob Woodward

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Kagan sheds some light on her view about leaks, Dobbs, and the Court.

Last month I wrote about an excerpt from Bob Woodward's new book that reveals sources. Most of the sources are deceased, so there is little harm outing them. But Justices Kagan and Breyer are alive and well. Woodward reveals a remarkable conversation with the former. As Woodward would observe, it is less clear that he was interviewing Kagan than Kagan was interviewing him.

"Well, the conclusion of The Brethren was that the center of the court was in control," I said, meaning neither the left nor the right was in charge. "Yes, I prefer it that way," Kagan said. "That's exactly what it should be." That's not the way it is now, I noted. It is not, Kagan confirmed. How did you get such detail in the book? We had time, I said. Of course, it was a different era in which Scott and I were doing the reporting in the late 1970s. I started to tell her about Scott and how he had really discovered the Nixon Tapes because he found Alexander Butterfield. Not letting me off the hook, Kagan asked again, "How did you do it?" Well, we interviewed five sitting justices and 170 law clerks. We got documentation. That's extraordinary, Kagan said. How did you get the documents? The justices must have approved the clerks giving you the documents? I shook my head. Not that we were aware. You make clerks now sign nondisclosure agreements, I noted. "Yes," she said.

Over the years, I've speculated that Justices have authorized their clerks to leak information to the press. The premise of Kagan's questions is that Justices had authorized their clerks to speak with Woodward and Bernstein. But no, the clerks went rogue. If the clerks acted alone in the 1970s, perhaps they did so in 2022 with the Dobbs opinion.

I told her that Brennan and Marshall, the liberal justices on the court, would not help us. Well, who did? Rehnquist and White, I said. Kagan seemed surprised. I recounted the story of calling Justice Lewis Powell at the court one morning and him agreeing to meet. I said when and he said now. "I was in my pajamas, but told him I'd be there in half an hour." You must be fast, Kagan said. I was then, I joked. I was 79 now and slow.

Justice Kagan clerked for Justice Marshall, who apparently never discussed the sourcing for The Brethren.

Is all of this known about The Brethren? Kagan asked. I didn't have an answer so instead I dived into Blackmun's role in Roe v. Wade and how he had drafted the opinion at the Mayo Clinic library. "I thought the leak of the Dobbs decision was a public service," I told her, referencing the decision that had overturned Roe the previous year. I can't say I agree with that, Kagan said. Why do you think it's a public service? Well, the court took away a right that had been there for 50 years. The public needed to know so there could be a debate. Kagan didn't say anything.

I find it odd that Kagan said nothing in response. This is not the sort of statement that could trigger a recusal. She might have said "that debate nearly got my colleague assassinated." But she stayed silent.

I said from reporting more than 50 years on 10 presidents, I thought there was such a concentration of power in the presidency. Too much power.

She nodded. It's why Trump was able to get away with so much, I said. Kagan did not respond. Then I said, there's too much power in the Supreme Court maybe. She noticeably reacted to that, her head held a little higher, her posture stiffening. Her only reply was, "That's interesting."

She mustered a response here, but not to the leak question. Interesting?

"Are you happy on the court?" I asked her. No, I'm not, given the situation, Kagan replied. I was surprised at her candor.

Kagan likely didn't think she would be quoted.

As we parted ways, she smiled warmly and said she respected my work and I said I respected hers. Late that night I recorded a detailed voice memo of my conversation with Kagan for my assistant to transcribe. It is hard to tell who was interviewing who.

On Saturday, October 21, 2023, Elsa and I attended a dinner for the 50th anniversary of the Saturday Night Massacre hosted by the former Watergate special prosecutors at the WilmerHale law firm in downtown Washington. The main speaker was retired Supreme Court justice Stephen Breyer, who had been a junior Watergate prosecutor. Elsa sat next to Breyer at the dinner before switching seats with me. He had served 28 years on the Supreme Court and told her he was "forced out" so someone younger could take his place.

No one forced him out. He has life tenure. Instead, Breyer surrendered to the pressure. So much for judicial independence. Justices Alito and Thomas are often charged with being MAGA partisans, but they exhibited robust independence from political forces.

Woodward offers this anecdote about the Thomas confirmation hearing:

Later Gray told me it took five years for Clarence Thomas to recover. Justice Thomas's wife, Ginni Thomas, a conservative activist, approached me at a conference in Washington one day. She said after the hearings her husband was never really a whole person again. He hardened. Many conservatives, including attorney general for George H. W. Bush and for Donald Trump, Bill Barr, have said the hearings pushed Thomas to the hard right.

I couldn't find any references to other current justices.

I will read the chapters on The Brethren with interest.

#7721. The Reason Some Parking Lots Have Angled Spaces Instead of Straight Ones

Angled parking spaces aren't just a design choice. Their layout can make turning easier, control traffic, and change how a lot uses space.

Navigating a new parking lot can be confusing and stressful. Some have one-way traffic, some have different parking rules. Even the parking spaces themselves can vary, with some lots using straight spaces and others using diagonal parking spaces. It turns out that small difference is intentional.

Parking lot designers think about how vehicles enter spaces, where drivers back out, and how much room cars need between rows. Learn why some parking lots use diagonal spaces, how the layout affects traffic, and what drivers should watch for.

Diagonal parking spaces are easier to pull into because drivers don’t have to make as sharp a turn. This is especially helpful in busy lots where cars are frequently coming and going. These spaces usually face one-way lanes, allowing drivers to pull in from the same direction. This helps keep traffic moving and reduces the chance of cars approaching each other head-on.

Drivers still need to follow the arrows, though. Entering from the wrong direction makes it harder to pull into a space and can put drivers in the path of cars backing out.

Not always. According to the Iowa Statewide Urban Design and Specifications, “One-way angled parking provides fewer spaces than perpendicular for the same length of aisle.”

The benefit is that one-way angled parking allows for narrower driving lanes, since drivers don’t need as much room to turn. Two-way angled parking is also possible, though Iowa’s guidelines say it’s generally less efficient than other layouts.

There’s also a downside to consider. Backing out of an angled space can be difficult when neighboring cars block the view, especially larger trucks and SUVs.

Some streets use back-in angled parking to address this problem. Drivers back into a space so they can pull forward when leaving. According to the University of Kentucky, Kentucky Transportation Center, “With the front of their vehicle facing the street, a motorist has improved sight distance when leaving a parking space.”

Back-in parking also lets passengers get out toward the sidewalk and keeps loading and unloading away from traffic. For regular diagonal spaces, drivers should back out slowly and watch for approaching cars and pedestrians. Backup cameras can help, but they shouldn’t replace checking the surrounding area.

#7720. Setting the Record Straight On Senator Cornyn And The N.D. Tex. Seat (Updated)

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

At the outset of President Trump's second term, there were a number of vacant district court seats throughout Texas. A reasonable person might have predicted that given two Republican senators, those seats would be filled quickly, but no such luck. The first nomination--Nicholas Ganjei for S.D.Tex--was not made until November 2025. Yes, while Missouri quickly filled all the seats, Texas lagged behind. Two more nominations in the Western District were made in January 2026--Andrew Davis for the Austin seat and Chis Wolfe for the Waco seat. It's worth noting that both Ganjei and Davis served as Chief Counsel for Senator Cruz. And the story of the Waco seat is enough for another post. In April 2026, two more nominations were made for S.D. Tex. seats in the Valley: John Marck and Arthur Jones.

Up to this point, none of the vacancies in the Northern District of Texas were tapped. Finally, in May 2026, Kasdin Mitchell was nominated to one of the seats in N.D. Tex. At that time, Angela Colmenero was tapped for another seat in Houston. Four more months would lapse. In September, Richard Bennett was nominated for a seat in Houston and Courtney Coker was nominated for a seat in Dallas.

But there were still two open seats. The critical vacancy was the Western District of Texas seat in Austin, which had remained open for some time. Virtually all of the litigation against the state government is filed in Austin. And, for reasons that continue to elude me, David Ezra, a senior judge from Hawaii, brings the Aloha Spirit to muck up Texas jurisprudence.

Shortly after the midterm election, President Trump nominated Justice James Sullivan of the Texas Supreme Court for the Austin seat. Around the same time, Trump nominated Elliot Gaiser for the remaining N.D. Tex. in Dallas. Ultimately, Senator Cornyn would block Gaiser's nomination, and urged the White House to nominate Steve Fahey. That's where thing stand now.

Many people, even those in Texas, cannot make sense of this situation. Why on earth did it take so long to fill all of these seats? Why did nominations for the final two seats only come after the election? Why did Trump pick Gaiser if Cornyn had objections?

Let me try to set the record straight on a few matters here.

Traditionally, Texas District court nominees have gone through something called the Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee (FJEC). Senators Cornyn and Cruz have used this structure to allow local attorneys (now about 30) to make recommendations on potential judicial candidates. The committee will screen applications, conduct interview, and recommend finalists to the Senators. Generally, if both senators sign off on a finalist, they recommend the name to the White House. At that point, the White House will conduct an interview, and if things work out, a nomination is made. I hedge slightly, because sometimes the process goes in a different order. It can happen that the White House really likes a particular candidate, and speaks to them in parallel, or even before the FJEC process goes through. But FJEC remains a central cog in any district court nomination.

For more than a year, there has been something of a standoff concerning the N.D. Tex. seat. There were two relevant finalists from FJEC. The first was Michael Berry, a Marine Veteran, longtime attorney with the First Liberty Institute, and--perhaps most importantly--former Chief Counsel to Senator Cruz. The second was Steve Fahey, a lawyer I did not know. He was an assistant United States Attorney until 2021, and now has a solo private practice. I'm told one of his most significant case was seeking a writ of coram nobis to protect an illegal alien from deportation. (The petition was denied.)

Senator Cornyn blocked Berry. Or to be more precise, Cornyn's Chief Counsel, Franci Becker, blocked Berry. The exact reason is not entirely clear. I've heard some rumors that Becker blames Berry for blocking another district court nominee, but that never happened. Senator Cruz supported that nominee. The White House found problems in that nom's record that would have made confirmation impossible. Ultimately, she withdrew from the search, and took a lucrative in-house position. Another explanation is that Becker, and Cornyn, opposed Berry because he was too conservative. Whatever the reasons, Berry had deep ties to Texas. The White House had interviewed Berry, and was prepared to make the nomination, but Cornyn kept saying no. The Washington Examiner reports on this story.

What about Fahey? I'm told that Cruz never actually blocked Fahey, but the White House had reservations about the nominee--especially his work defending illegal aliens. Ultimately, the decision was made to just let the seat stay open and it would be filled once Cornyn is out of office. The Austin seat was vital, as it involves so much state-wide litigation, but the Dallas division seats are interchangeable. This is not Amarillo or Wichita Falls. Indeed, even if Paxton were to lose the election, the Senate was likely to stay in Republican control, and a deal could be made with Senator Talarico for the Dallas seat. Alas, the election day bloodbath changed things.

The Sullivan nomination for the Austin seat was made quite quickly, even though it had been in the works for a while. Sullivan had already gone through the background check, as well as the FJEC approval. But what about Elliot Gaiser? It is true that Gaiser did not go through FJEC, but he had something very important: a recent FBI background check and Senate confirmation. He could (in theory) be slotted into the final confirmation hearing planned for November 18.

Despite my best efforts, Senator Cornyn blocked Gaiser's nomination. Cornyn (or at least someone on his staff) put out this social media post to explain his actions:

If President Trump wanted to fill a judicial vacancy in Dallas, why did he wait until after the midterms to nominate someone? The seat has been vacant since 2025. Then, without any consultation, he nominates a non-Texan with little connection to the Lone Star State, with no trial court experience, and who has not been appropriately vetted for a lifetime job. The Senate has a constitutional responsibility to provide "advise and consent," which is impossible without consultation.

Still, I would like to work with the President to fill the seat while we still have a Senate majority. I have forwarded an outstanding candidate who was highly rated by Senator Cruz's and my bipartisan Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee, and who has now been interviewed by White House Counsel. All that is needed is an FBI background check with they stand ready to do on a timely basis.

Back to you, Mr. President. Time is of the essence.

This post is misleading. Why did Trump wait until after the midterms to nominate someone? The short answer is that Cornyn blocked the White House's and Cruz's preferred candidate, and the White House did not want to pick Cornyn's candidate. That's how things work. Senators can withhold consent by not returning a blue slip. But they can't force the White House to make a nomination they don't wish to make. The White House then tried a list-ditch effort to get someone into the seat before the new Congress concluded. I'm sure the administration was hoping that Senator Cornyn would realize that a filled seat is better than an empty seat, but he refused, and blocked Gaiser. Moreover, Cornyn refused to even meet with Gaiser, so he is no position to complain about a "lack of consultation." FJEC could have performed a review of Gaiser on short notice, but it was never convened.

Cornyn says Fahey was "was highly rated by Senator Cruz's and my bipartisan Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee." But that does not mean Senator Cruz himself approved of Fahey. Indeed, Senator Cruz can still withhold a blue slip of Fahey. That comeuppance would be just, after Cornyn blocked both Berry and Gaiser unreasonably. Cornyn has earned no favors at this point--especially after cursing at Cruz on the Senate floor and calling him a "fragile thing" on social media. After the events of the past few weeks, I think James Talarico would be a more trustworthy partner on nominees than Cornyn. Remember, Cornyn aided and abetted the spiking of Lee Rudofsky's nomination to the Eighth Circuit. Soon enough, Judge Ada Brown's NDTX seat will become open--either through resignation or impeachment. I can see a deal being made with Cruz gets one of the Dallas seats and Talarico gets the other. All Cornyn could do that point is grouse.

The bigger problem is that there is no time left for a hearing. The November 18 hearing was the end of the show. Cornyn's stunt is now putting pressure on Senator Grassley to break even more China by holding a December nomination hearing. There is no reason that Grassley should give Cornyn this courtesy--especially after the recent stunts Cornyn has pulled.

This post is based on my best understanding of some complex deliberations over the course of nearly two years. If you spot any errors, please send me an email.

Update: Tuesday evening, the press secretary from Senator Cornyn's post reached out and said "It's inaccurate to say that Franci Becker is responsible for blocking Mike Berry's nomination." She asked me to post a statement, which I will do:

Attributable to a Cornyn spokesperson, Franci Becker did not block Mike Berry's nomination, as staff in Senate offices do not have the authority to make decisions about a nominee, and the claims in this story were not corroborated by Sen. Cornyn's office.

Of course, the ultimate decision to sign a blue slip belongs to the Senator. In any office, a staffer cannot take a final action. So in a hyper-technical sense, no staffer is capable of blocking any nominee. But Chief Counsels routinely make decisions about candidates that their senators defer to.

What the statement does not say is far more important than what it actually says. There is no denial along the lines of, "Franci Becker played no role in Mike Berry not receiving a blue slip." I also posed a few other questions about Becker's involvement with the Dallas seat, that the press secretary did not answer.

I stand by what I wrote, which is something I have heard from multiple sources in the Senate over the course of nearly a year. Staffers from other Senator's offices thanked me for this post. Two federal judges who are familiar with the situation thanked me for writing this. People I trust and who are familiar with the situation reviewed it and found no errors.

#7718. 7 Surfaces You Should Never Use Ice Melt On

Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.

Ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface. Applying ice melt to certain materials can cause significant damage and should be avoided. Ahead, learn which surfaces are most vulnerable to damage from ice melt, why it happens and what safer alternatives you can use to keep outdoor areas free from ice.

Ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage. The type of damage will depend on the surface and how it interacts with ice melt.

Ice melt contains rock salt, calcium chloride and/or magnesium chloride to melt ice faster and at lower temperatures. While all melting salt is corrosive and can damage outdoor surfaces, ice melt products can react differently than rock salt alone.

Ice melt seeps deeply into porous cement-based materials. The calcium chloride in ice melt can react with elements of concrete or brick to form calcium oxychloride crystals. As the crystals grow, they generate extreme pressure that can cause cracks, surface spalling and crumbling.

De-icing products accelerate freeze-thaw cycles in porous cement-based surfaces, causing them to break down. “It makes the freezing and thawing cycle more aggressive, which is what causes the surface to break up,” Murphy says.

Though less damaging than rock salt, ice melt can still contribute to deterioration. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride attract and retain moisture, increasing the potential for freeze-thaw damage.

Conversely, ice melt draws moisture out of organic materials, causing them to dry out. Over time, this moisture loss can lead to warping, cracking, splitting and other forms of deterioration.

Ice melt accelerates metal oxidation to create rust. It can corrode rebar embedded in concrete, potentially causing cracks and structural damage, as well as rusting exposed metal stairs and railings.

It’s best to avoid applying salt to these salt-sensitive surfaces.

“New concrete is the most vulnerable because it takes weeks to fully cure, so salt on the surface will cause the top few millimeters to flake off,” Murphy says. To be safe, avoid salting new concrete for the first season.

“Cracked concrete opens up for water to get inside, and salt in the water will only make that worse because it will freeze and thaw more aggressively,” Murphy says.

All ice melt products will damage hard-scape surfaces due to chemical reactions and freeze-thaw cycles. “If you are using them, use them sparingly and remove them as soon as possible to decrease continuous exposure for your hardscape areas,” Zurcher says.

Natural stone like limestone and flagstone can react to ice melt compounds. The porous surface is vulnerable to damaging freeze-thaw cycles as well.

Harsh de-icers can damage dyed, painted or stamped concrete surfaces by breaking down color pigments.

Metal stairs and railings will rapidly rust when salt is applied to them, so it’s best to avoid it.

Ice melt draws moisture from wood, causing cracking, warping and raised fibers. It also degrades paint and stain and leaves behind chalky white salt stains.

Sand: Sand doesn’t melt ice, but does provide traction to prevent slips.

Wood ash: Instead of throwing away wood ash, use it as a salt alternative to melt ice and also provide improved traction.

Electric mats: Installed before cold weather sets in, electric melting mats warm up and prevent ice from ever forming. These can be very effective on stairs and sidewalks.

Weed torch: Weed torches are handy when you need to melt a lot of ice quickly. Do not use one to melt ice on wood and avoid painted or stained concrete as well.

“The best way to reduce damage from these chemicals is to shovel snow as soon as possible,” Zurcher says, so you can use less of them. Use ice melt sparingly, and only as directed. A handful is enough to treat three square yards. Instead of using ice melt alone, mix a small amount with sand to treat surfaces.

Regular sealing protects cement-based products.  “Reseal every three to five years to make sure no water can get in, salty or not,” Murphy says. Additionally, use chloride-free de-icing products, or those labelled as “concrete-safe”.

Newly poured concrete is the most vulnerable to salt damage, but all concrete surfaces will experience damage with enough prolonged exposure to salt.

It depends on the extent of the damage. Major cracks and breakage mean concrete needs to be removed and repoured, Zurcher says, while surface damage could be skim-coated, with potentially limited results.

Pet-safe products will have similar effects on hardscape areas, Zurcher says, as they still contain salt.
